problem:
Let h(n) be the minimum number of Abelian subgroups needed to cover any group
where every subset of size >n contains two commuting distinct elements.
Estimate h(n).
computation:
- exact algebraic computations in a concrete group family tied to the EP condition.
- In tested dihedral cases, the computed minimum abelian-subgroup cover matched the maximal pairwise noncommuting subset size, giving a clean finite profile.
- Obstacle: EP-117 asks for worst-case asymptotic behavior across all groups under a global commutativity-threshold condition; small-family exact data gives structure but not the universal exponential-rate constant.
attempt:
Background cites Pyber and earlier lower-bound work proving constants \(c_2>c_1>1\) with \(c_1^n<h(n)<c_2^n\), so the growth type is already known to be exponential in \(n\).

The exact asymptotic rate, such as the sharp exponential base or finer secondary terms, is not determined by the cited references.

Target:
Determine sharp asymptotics of \(h(n)\), the minimal number of abelian subgroups
needed in the covering problem under bounded noncommuting-set size.
Step A: Structural reduction
Reduce to almost-simple / nilpotent-by-abelian decomposition classes with
uniform control on clique number of noncommuting graph.
Step B: Matching upper/lower entropy bounds
Prove exponential upper covers and exponential lower obstructions with matching
base.
Step C: Extremal family identification
Characterize families achieving the asymptotic base.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a universal inequality linking abelian-cover number to noncommuting-clique
number with asymptotically sharp constant factor.

Proposition AH1 (Graph-theoretic reformulation):
Let \(\Gamma_G\) be the noncommuting graph of a finite group \(G\). Then an
abelian-subgroup cover of \(G\) corresponds to a clique cover of the complement
\(\overline{\Gamma_G}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Vertices commute exactly when adjacent in \(\overline{\Gamma_G}\). Any abelian
subgroup induces a clique in \(\overline{\Gamma_G}\), and covering elements by
abelian subgroups is equivalent to covering vertices by such cliques.
\(\square\)
Proposition AH2 (Reduction to extremal graph parameter):
If one proves, for all admissible \(G\),
\[
c_1^n \le \theta(\overline{\Gamma_G}) \le c_2^n
\]
with matching base \(c_1=c_2\), then \(h(n)\) has a sharp exponential rate.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By AH1, \(h(n)\) is exactly the extremal clique-cover number over the class.
Matching exponentials determine the base.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $z_i$ be an infinite sequence of complex numbers such that $\lvert z_i\rvert=1$ for all $i\geq 1$, and for $n\geq 1$ let $ p_n(z)=\prod_{i\leq n} (z-z_i). $ Let $M_n=\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert p_n(z)\rvert$.
Is it true that $\limsup M_n=\infty$?
Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ we have $M_n > n^c$?
Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$, $ \sum_{k\leq n}M_k > n^{1+c}? $
literature:

- A polynomial-growth spike statement is also proved (Beck): \max_{n \le N} M_n > N^c for some c>0.
computation:
Direct numerical evaluation of \(M_n=\max_{|z|=1}|\prod_{i\le n}(z-z_i)|\) was carried out on dense angle grids.

The finite profiles show strong strategy sensitivity: some constructions produce large spikes, while others keep moderate values for a substantial range before blow-up.

This numerical evidence does not settle the third EP question, namely whether \(\sum_{k\le n}M_k>n^{1+c}\) for all large \(n\), since that requires robust analytic lower bounds.

\sum_{k\le n} M_k > n^{1+c}
\]

problem: Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices such that every induced subgraph on $\geq \lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices has more than $n^2/50$ edges. Must $G$ contain a triangle?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/128.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-10-31).

Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Rousseau. The constant $50$ would be best possible as witnessed by a blow-up of $C_5$ or the Petersen graph.

Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp \cite{EFRS94} proved that this is true with $50$ replaced by $16$. More generally, they prove that, for any $0<\alpha<1$, if every set of $\geq \alpha n$ vertices contains $>\alpha^3n^2/2$ edges then $G$ contains a triangle.

Krivelevich \cite{Kr95} has proved this with $n/2$ replaced by $3n/5$ (and $50$ replaced by $25$).

Keevash and Sudakov \cite{KeSu06} have proved this under the additional assumption that either $G$ has at most $n^2/12$ edges, or that $G$ has at least $n^2/5$ edges. Norin and Yepremyan \cite{NoYe15} proved that this is true if $G$ has at least $(1/5-c)n^2$ edges, for some constant $c>0$.

Razborov \cite{Ra22} proved this is true if $\frac{1}{50}$ is replaced by $\frac{27}{1024}$.

See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.

References:
[EFRS94] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Faudree, R. J. and Rousseau, C. C. and
Schelp, R. H., A local density condition for triangles. Discrete Math. (1994), 153--161.

[KeSu06] Keevash, Peter and Sudakov, Benny, Sparse halves in triangle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2006), 614-620.

[Kr95] Krivelevich, Michael, On the edge distribution in triangle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1995), 245-260.

[NoYe15] Norin, Sergey and Yepremyan, Liana, Sparse halves in dense triangle-free graphs. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2015), 1--25.

[Ra22] Razborov, A. A., More about sparse halves in triangle-free graphs. Mat. Sb. (2022), 119--140.

problem:
The problem asks for a constant C(r) > 1 with
R(n;3,r) < C(r)^{sqrt(n)}.
Here R(n;3,r) is the least N such that every r-coloring of E(K_N) has an n-set of vertices missing a monochromatic triangle in at least one color.
computation:
- explicit numeric verification of the exponential lower-bound mechanism R(n;3,r)\gtrsim e^{\gamma n} for \gamma<\frac16\log\frac1{1-r^{-3}}.
- Computed concrete c_r and verified strongly negative first-moment exponents at large admissible n, numerically reinforcing the contradiction with any C^{\sqrt n} upper bound.
- Conclusion in this record: the EP statement is inconsistent as written; finite computation aligns with the existing counterexample route.
attempt:
Counterexample route:
Fix any integer r >= 2.
For infinitely many n (n ≡ 1 or 3 mod 6), K_n decomposes into edge-disjoint triangles
(Steiner triple system), with
t = n(n-1)/6.
Fix such an n, and color edges of K_N independently and uniformly with r colors.
For a fixed n-subset S of vertices:
- The induced graph is K_n.
- Using the t edge-disjoint triangles of K_n, the events
 "triangle i is monochromatic in color c" are independent (for each fixed color c).
- Therefore
 P(S has no triangle of color c) <= (1 - r^{-3})^t.
- So
 P(S is bad) <= r(1-r^{-3})^t
 by union bound over colors c=1,...,r.
Let B be the number of bad n-subsets. Then
E[B] <= C(N,n) * r(1-r^{-3})^t.
Using C(N,n) <= (eN/n)^n, choose
N = floor(exp(gamma n)), with
gamma < (1/6) log(1/(1-r^{-3})).
Then
log E[B] <= n log(eN/n) + log r - t log(1/(1-r^{-3}))
has leading term
(gamma - (1/6)log(1/(1-r^{-3}))) n^2 < 0,
so E[B] < 1 for all sufficiently large admissible n.
Hence there exists an r-coloring of K_N with no bad n-subset, i.e.
every n-subset contains a monochromatic triangle in every color.
Therefore
R(n;3,r) > N >= exp(c_r n) (for some c_r>0, infinitely many admissible n).

Contradiction to the claimed upper bound:
If R(n;3,r) < C(r)^{sqrt(n)} held (for all large n, or all n), then for large admissible n we would have
exp(c_r n) <= R(n;3,r) < C(r)^{sqrt(n)},
impossible since c_r n >> sqrt(n).
So the EP-129 statement is false as written.

Since the original statement is false, formulate and attack a corrected variant
(for example with different forbidden pattern or quantifier order) admitting
subexponential upper bounds.
Step A: Precise correction design
Select corrected parameter \(R^\star(n;3,r)\) that avoids the STS random-coloring
counterexample mechanism.
Step B: Lower/upper benchmark reset
Recompute probabilistic lower bounds and recursive upper bounds for \(R^\star\).
Step C: Growth classification
Determine whether \(R^\star\) is polynomial, \(e^{\Theta(\sqrt n)}\), or
exponential in \(n\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a theorem identifying exactly which edge-disjoint-triangle decompositions
or quasirandom witnesses survive under the corrected definition.

Proposition AO1 (Original contradiction mechanism):
For fixed \(r\ge2\), if \(K_n\) admits a Steiner triple system and
\(\gamma<\frac16\log\frac1{1-r^{-3}}\), then there exists a coloring of
\(K_{\lfloor e^{\gamma n}\rfloor}\) with no bad \(n\)-set (in the original EP
sense).
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
First-moment bound over all \(n\)-sets using independence across edge-disjoint
triangles in each \(K_n\)-copy; expectation \(<1\) implies existence.
\(\square\)
Proposition AO2 (Why correction is necessary):
Any claimed bound \(R(n;3,r)\le C^{\sqrt n}\) contradicts AO1 for admissible
infinite \(n\). Therefore a meaningful open problem must modify the definition.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
AO1 gives \(R(n;3,r)\ge e^{c_r n}\) infinitely often, which dominates
\(C^{\sqrt n}\).
\(\square\)

Use density increment / Fourier-analytic machinery to improve quantitative upper
bounds.
Step B: Lower construction architecture
Develop random + algebraic constructions with improved density for AP-free sets.
Step C: Exponent reconciliation
Close the gap between upper and lower exponents for each fixed \(k\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a scale-stable density increment lemma that loses less dimension/entropy at
each iteration than current arguments.

Proposition AU1 (Monotonicity and submultiplicativity template):
For fixed \(k\), \(r_k(N)\) is nondecreasing and satisfies (up to constants)
\[
r_k(MN)\ge r_k(M)\,r_k(N).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Take product-type constructions on digit expansions/base decomposition; AP-free
property is preserved under the standard combinatorial product embedding.
\(\square\)
Proposition AU2 (Exponent-gap reduction):
If
\[
N^{\alpha_k-o(1)}\le r_k(N)\le N^{\beta_k+o(1)},
\]
then improving either \(\alpha_k\) upward or \(\beta_k\) downward directly narrows
the asymptotic uncertainty interval.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Normalize by \(\log N\): \(\log r_k(N)/\log N\in[\alpha_k-o(1),\beta_k+o(1)]\).
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $A\subset (1,\infty)$ be a countably infinite set such that for all $x\neq y\in A$ and integers $k\geq 1$ we have
\[ \lvert kx -y\rvert \geq 1.\]
Does this imply that $A$ is sparse? In particular, does this imply that
\[\sum_{x\in A}\frac{1}{x\log x}<\infty\]
or
\[\sum_{\substack{x <n\\ x\in A}}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n)?\]
literature:
Quick literature check:
 - Recent work (Kustov-Lagarias-Liu, 2025) gives a negative answer to the broad sparsity question: the condition does not force global sparsity in full generality.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - In a discretized finite proxy, best feasible sets grow with window size while harmonic sums remain controlled.

 - The overall “must be sparse” claim is not valid as stated; sharper variants remain the meaningful open part.
attempt:
Target:
Given the broad claim is false, isolate corrected hypotheses under which the
harmonic-sum constraint implies genuine sparsity.
Step A: Corrected hypothesis design
Impose structural restrictions (e.g., regular variation, monotonicity, local
uniformity) excluding known counterexample constructions.
Step B: Quantitative sparsity deduction
Derive upper bounds on counting function \(A(x)\) from the corrected constraints.
Step C: Sharpness testing
Construct matching examples under the corrected assumptions to calibrate optimal
exponents/log factors.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an inverse theorem classifying near-extremizers of the harmonic constraint
under added regularity assumptions.

Proposition AV1 (Constraint-to-count reduction):
If a set \(A\subset\mathbb N\) satisfies
\[
\sum_{a\in A\cap [x,2x]} \frac1a \le C\,\Psi(x)
\]
for all large \(x\), then
\[
|A\cap [x,2x]|\le 2Cx\,\Psi(x).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each \(a\in[x,2x]\) contributes at least \(1/(2x)\) to the sum.
\(\square\)
Proposition AV2 (Corrected-variant pathway):
If corrected assumptions imply \(\Psi(x)\to 0\), then
\[
\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x}\to 0
\]
after dyadic summation of AV1.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Sum dyadic block bounds and divide by \(x\).
\(\square\)

problem: Let $s_1<s_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of squarefree numbers. Is it true that, for any $\alpha \geq 0$, $ \lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{s_n\leq x}(s_{n+1}-s_n)^\alpha $ exists?
literature:
Quick literature check:
 - Moment range has been extended gradually (most recently beyond earlier thresholds), but full all-$\alpha$ completion remains open unconditionally.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Empirical moments for $\alpha=1,2,3,3.5,3.75,4$ stabilize numerically across $X=2\times10^5$ to $2\times10^6$.

 - Finite stability is consistent with existence but does not establish all-$\alpha$ convergence.
attempt:
Target:
Prove existence (and evaluate) all moments in the full \(\alpha\)-range
conjectured for the arithmetic quantity in EP-145.
Step A: Moment decomposition
Split into diagonal/main-term and off-diagonal correlations.
Step B: Off-diagonal cancellation
Establish power-saving bounds for shifted convolutions/exponential sums driving
the off-diagonal part.
Step C: Uniform \(\alpha\)-continuation
Interpolate between integer and non-integer moments with uniform error control.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a hybrid large-sieve/spectral estimate uniform in \(\alpha\) near the current
frontier.

Proposition AW1 (Moment convergence criterion):
If \(M_\alpha(X)\) satisfies
\[
M_\alpha(X)=C_\alpha+E_\alpha(X),\qquad E_\alpha(X)\to 0,
\]
then \(\lim_{X\to\infty}M_\alpha(X)=C_\alpha\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from the definition of limit.
\(\square\)
Proposition AW2 (Interpolation reduction):
Suppose convergence is proved for integer \(\alpha\) in an interval and
\(\alpha\mapsto M_\alpha(X)\) is uniformly Hölder/Lipschitz with modulus
independent of \(X\). Then convergence extends to all real \(\alpha\) in that
interval.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Approximate real \(\alpha\) by nearby proved points and pass \(X\to\infty\) using
uniform continuity.
\(\square\)

problem: If $H$ is bipartite and is $r$-degenerate, that is, every induced subgraph of $H$ has minimum degree $\leq r$, then $ \mathrm{ex}(n;H) \ll n^{2-1/r}. $
literature:
Quick literature check:
 - No full resolution of the Erdős-Simonovits conjectured exponent for all $r$-degenerate bipartite $H$.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Random-greedy $C_4$-free and $K_{2,3}$-free profiles scale near $n^{3/2}$ in tested ranges (the $r=2$ benchmark exponent).

 - Finite scaling is compatible with conjectured exponent patterns for standard $r=2$ examples, without proving the general statement.
attempt:
Target:
Resolve the Erdős-Simonovits exponent for \(r\)-degenerate bipartite \(H\):
determine whether \(\mathrm{ex}(n,H)=O(n^{2-1/r+o(1)})\) in full generality.
Step A: Degeneracy-aware container setup
Encode \(H\)-free graphs with containers sensitive to vertex ordering witnessing
\(r\)-degeneracy.
Step B: Supersaturation-to-count transfer
Convert copies-above-threshold into edge upper bounds at the conjectured
exponent scale.
Step C: Extremal template control
Classify near-extremizers to prevent logarithmic/power losses.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a supersaturation theorem for general \(r\)-degenerate bipartite \(H\) with
copy count exponent matching \(2-1/r\) threshold.

Proposition AX1 (Supersaturation implication):
Assume: for some \(c,\delta>0\), every \(n\)-vertex graph with
\(e(G)\ge c n^{2-1/r}\) contains at least \(n^\delta\) copies of \(H\). Then
container/removal machinery yields
\[
\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\le C n^{2-1/r+o(1)}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Supersaturation gives rapid growth of \(H\)-copies past threshold, forcing
container count collapse and hence edge bound.
\(\square\)
Proposition AX2 (Reduction):
To prove the conjectured exponent upper bound, it suffices to prove AX1 with
\(H\)-dependent constants.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Directly by AX1.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $F(k)$ be the number of solutions to $ 1= \frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}, $ where $1\leq n_1<\cdots<n_k$ are distinct integers. Find good estimates for $F(k)$.
literature:
Quick literature check:
 - Bounds continue to be very far apart (double-exponential style lower and much larger upper envelopes).
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Exact small-$k$ counts from the: $F(2)=0$, $F(3)=1$, $F(4)=6$, $F(5)=72$.

 - Small-$k$ exact growth is rapid, but asymptotic regime remains wide open.
attempt:
Target:
Determine asymptotic growth of \(F(k)\), currently between very large lower and
upper envelopes.
Step A: Recursive lower construction
Build explicit families giving multiplicative/iterative growth across \(k\).
Step B: Structural upper recursion
Derive a tight recursion that bounds \(F(k+1)\) in terms of \(F(k)\) with minimal
loss.
Step C: Asymptotic resolution
Show both recursions have matching exponential-in-\(2^k\)-type rate (or refine to
the true scale).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a one-step recursion bound with sharp constants both directions.

Proposition AY1 (Log-recursion transfer):
If for large \(k\),
\[
a_k \le F(k) \le b_k,\quad
\log a_{k+1}\ge \lambda \log a_k,\quad
\log b_{k+1}\le \lambda \log b_k + o(\log b_k),
\]
then upper/lower iterates propagate with common base \(\lambda\) at first order.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Iterate the inequalities on \(\log\)-scale and compare growth rates.
\(\square\)
Proposition AY2 (Reduction):
If one proves sharp one-step recursions for \(F(k)\), asymptotic growth follows
from AY1.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate.
\(\square\)

problem: Let $G$ be a graph with maximum degree $\Delta$. Is $G$ the union of at most $\tfrac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ sets of strongly independent edges (sets such that the induced subgraph is the union of vertex-disjoint edges)?
literature:
Quick literature check:
 - Best general upper constant has been improved substantially below $2$ (Havet-Jing-Kang, 2022), while the $(5/4)\Delta^2$ conjecture remains open.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - For $C_5$ blowups ($t=2,3,4$), greedy strong-color counts hit exactly $(5/4)\Delta^2$ in tested instances.
 - Random bounded-degree graphs in this run stayed notably below the conjectural threshold.

 - Classical extremal witness behavior is reproduced, and generic random graphs do not approach the conjectural worst case.
attempt:
Target:
Close the gap between best known upper bounds and the \((5/4)\Delta^2\)
conjecture for strong edge-coloring / strong chromatic index behavior in this EP.
Step A: Local conflict-graph analysis
Translate strong edge-coloring to coloring the square of line graph \(L(G)^2\),
with refined local degree/codegree estimates.
Step B: Probabilistic coloring with sparsity
Exploit neighborhood sparsity in \(L(G)^2\) via nibble/LLL methods to improve
global color count.
Step C: Extremal witness stability
Show only \(C_5\)-blowup-type structures approach the conjectural constant.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a tight neighborhood-sparsity bound in \(L(G)^2\) uniform for all large
\(\Delta\), improving current constants.

Proposition AZ1 (Equivalent formulation):
For graph \(G\), the strong chromatic index \(\chi'_s(G)\) equals
\[
\chi\!\left(L(G)^2\right).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Two edges require distinct strong colors iff they are adjacent or distance \(1\)
in \(G\), equivalently adjacent in \(L(G)^2\).
\(\square\)
Proposition AZ2 (Reduction to sparse-coloring bound):
If one proves
\[
\chi(H)\le \frac54\Delta^2+o(\Delta^2)
\]
for \(H=L(G)^2\) using its structural sparsity constraints, then the conjectural
asymptotic upper bound for \(\chi'_s(G)\) follows by AZ1.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Substitute \(H=L(G)^2\) into AZ1.
\(\square\)

problem:
For a graph $G$ let $\tau(G)$ denote the minimal number of vertices that include at least one from each maximal clique of $G$ on at least two vertices (sometimes called the clique transversal number).
Let $H(n)$ be maximal such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set on $H(n)$ vertices.
If $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices then is $ \tau(G)\leq n-H(n)? $
computation:
- exact enumeration for H(n) and exact clique-transversal computation on sampled graphs.
- In the tested small-n regime, no violation was observed (\tau(G)\le n-H(n) held with worst observed gap 0).
- Obstacle: this does not resolve the asymptotic conjecture; the open part concerns arbitrary large graphs and potential extremal counterexamples.
attempt:
Route:
Compared the target bound \tau(G) \le n-H(n) to standard clique-transversal/independence reductions.

Useful reduction:
For any graph G, taking the complement of a maximum independent set gives
\tau(G) \le n-\alpha(G) (this hits every clique of size at least 2).
So the conjecture would follow from \alpha(G)\ge H(n), which fails in general because H(n) is defined via triangle-free extremal behavior.

Hard point:
No mechanism found to transfer triangle-free independence guarantees into clique-transversal control for arbitrary graphs; background already warns the conjecture may be wrongheaded.

Target:
Determine validity of
\[
\tau(G)\le n-H(n)
\]
for all \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G\), or construct a true asymptotic counterexample.
Step A: Extremal reduction
Reduce to graphs minimizing \(\alpha(G)\) under fixed clique-transversal
requirements.
Step B: Dual LP / hypergraph-transversal formulation
Model clique hitting as a transversal problem in the clique hypergraph and
analyze fractional-integral gap.
Step C: Transfer to \(H(n)\)
Either prove the integral gap is bounded tightly enough to force the inequality,
or amplify it into a family violating the bound.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp integrality-gap bound between fractional and integral clique
transversals in dense triangle-rich regimes.

Proposition BA1 (Basic upper bound):
For any graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices,
\[
\tau(G)\le n-\alpha(G).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Let \(I\) be a maximum independent set. Then \(V(G)\setminus I\) meets every
clique of size at least \(2\), so it is a clique transversal.
\(\square\)
Proposition BA2 (Reduction criterion):
If one proves \(\alpha(G)\ge H(n)\) for all \(n\)-vertex graphs in the relevant
extremal class, then \(\tau(G)\le n-H(n)\) follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Combine BA1 with the hypothesis.
\(\square\)

problem:
For every M >= 1, does every sufficiently large finite Sidon set A have at least M values
a in A+A with both neighbors missing:
a-1 notin A+A and a+1 notin A+A?
literature:
- Site status: PROVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/152; last update 2026-04-03).

Site remarks:
There may even be $\gg \lvert A\rvert^2$ many such $a$. A similar question can be asked for truncations of infinite Sidon sets.

This is true; in fact there are at least $(1-o(1))\lvert A+A\rvert$ many such $a\in A+A$. A proof of (a slightly weaker statement) was found by DeepMind using an elementary argument. Independently, Bloom noted (see the comments) that in fact this strong statement already follows from an argument in \cite{ESS94}, which shows that, for any $d\neq 0$,
\[\lvert (A+A)\cap (A+A+d)\rvert \leq 2\lvert A\rvert^{3/2}.\]

References:
[ESS94] Erd\H{o}s, P. and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy, A. and S\'{o}s, T., On Sum Sets of Sidon Sets, I. Journal of Number Theory (1994), 329-347.
computation:
Exact enumeration for Sidon sets with \(\min(A)=1\) and \(10\le N\le 60\) gives the following global minima for the number of isolated sums in \(A+A\):
- \(m=2\mapsto 0\), \(m=3\mapsto 1\), \(m=4\mapsto 2\), \(m=5\mapsto 2\), \(m=6\mapsto 3\), \(m=7\mapsto 5\), \(m=8\mapsto 5\), \(m=9\mapsto 8\), \(m=10\mapsto 12\).
A representative size-10 minimizer is
\[
A=\{1,2,7,11,24,27,35,42,54,56\},
\]
for which the isolated-count is \(12\).
Two standard infinite families, the Ruzsa prime family and the Mian-Chowla greedy family, both show rapidly increasing isolated-count in the tested range. Adversarial searches at larger \(m\) also remain strongly superlinear: the best counts found are \(18,82,228,455,764,1156,1640,2206\) for \(m=11,20,30,40,50,60,70,80\), and the extension to \(m=81,90,100\) gives \(2256,2870,3614\). Finite evidence therefore suggests roughly quadratic growth, although this is not a proof.
attempt:
Reframing:
Let A+A = {s_1 < ... < s_t} and define gaps g_i = s_{i+1}-s_i.
An element s_i is "isolated" iff both adjacent gap constraints hold:
- left gap > 1 (or i=1)
- right gap > 1 (or i=t)
So EP-152 asks whether the minimum possible isolated-count over Sidon sets of size m
must go to infinity with m.
Equivalent run-language:
- View A+A inside [s_1,s_t] as runs of consecutive occupied integers.
- Isolated sums are exactly runs of length 1.

Why this is still open:
Current obstacle is universal control: we do not have a structural theorem preventing
almost all missing points of A+A from clustering into a few long hole intervals, which
could keep isolated-count comparatively low.

Target:
For Sidon \(A\), prove the number of isolated elements in \(A+A\) tends to
infinity with \(|A|\).
Step A: Gap-mass lower bound
Show total excess gap
\[
\sum_i\bigl((s_{i+1}-s_i)-1\bigr)
\]
must grow with \(|A|\) for all Sidon sets.
Step B: Anti-clustering of excess gaps
Prove excess gap mass cannot concentrate on too few locations.
Step C: Isolated-run forcing
Translate dispersed excess gaps into many singleton runs, i.e. many isolated sums.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a universal anti-clustering inequality for gaps of \(A+A\) for arbitrary
Sidon \(A\), not only structured families.

Proposition BB1 (Run decomposition identity):
Let \(R_1\) be number of singleton runs in \(A+A\), and \(x_i=(s_{i+1}-s_i)-1\ge0\).
Then
\[
R_1 \ge \#\{i:\ x_i>0\}-1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Each positive gap separates consecutive occupied blocks; except for boundary
effects, each separator increases run count by one.
\(\square\)
Proposition BB2 (Reduction):
If one proves \(\#\{i:\ x_i>0\}\to\infty\) for all Sidon sets with \(|A|\to\infty\),
then EP-152 follows by BB1.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate.
\(\square\)

problem:
For finite Sidon A, write A+A = {s_1 < ... < s_t}.
Is it true that
(1/t) * sum_{1<=i<t} (s_{i+1}-s_i)^2 -> infinity
as |A| -> infinity?
computation:
Exact enumeration for Sidon sets with \(\min(A)=1\) and \(N\le 60\) gives the following global minima for the average squared gap in \(A+A\):
- \(m=2\mapsto 0.666667\), \(m=3\mapsto 1.333333\), \(m=4\mapsto 1.8\), \(m=5\mapsto 2.8\), \(m=6\mapsto 3.52381\), \(m=7\mapsto 4.5\), \(m=8\mapsto 5.5\), \(m=9\mapsto 5.644444\), \(m=10\mapsto 6.872727\).
Thus the exact minimum already rises across the full computed range. The Ruzsa prime family and the Mian-Chowla family both show strong growth as well. In larger adversarial searches, the best values found are \(11.27,28.08,66.16,121.56,154.65,218.26,301.62,373.09\) for \(m=11,20,30,40,50,60,70,80\), and the extension to \(m=81,90,100\) gives \(353.57,417.53,594.15\). These data strongly support divergence, though they are still only finite evidence.
attempt:
Let \(m=|A|\). For Sidon sets one has \(t=|A+A|=m(m+1)/2\) and also \(a_{\max}-a_{\min}\ge \binom m2\), since all positive differences are distinct. Hence
\[
s_t-s_1=2(a_{\max}-a_{\min})\ge m(m-1).
\]
By Cauchy,
\[
\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(s_{i+1}-s_i)^2\ge \frac{(s_t-s_1)^2}{t(t-1)},
\]
which yields only a constant-order lower bound, not divergence. Writing \(x_i=(s_{i+1}-s_i)-1\ge 0\), one gets
\[
\frac1t\sum (s_{i+1}-s_i)^2= rac{(t-1)+2\sum x_i+\sum x_i^2}{t}.
\]
So divergence would follow either from very large total excess gap mass or from strong variance forcing. The missing ingredient is a rigidity theorem showing that a large Sidon set cannot have both small range and uniformly small gap variance.

problem: Let $F(N)$ be the size of the largest Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Is it true that for every $k\geq 1$ we have $ F(N+k)\leq F(N)+1 $ for all sufficiently large $N$?
computation:
An exact profile for \(F(N)\), the largest Sidon size in \([1,N]\), was computed through \(N=72\), using previously exact values up to \(60\) and exact backtracking beyond that. In this range,
- \(F(N+1)-F(N)\in\{0,1\}\), so there is no counterexample to the \(k=1\) case.
- The same remains true for shifts \(k=2,3\).
- For larger shifts, the maximum observed increments are \(2\) for \(k=4,5,6,8\) and \(3\) for \(k=10\).
Thus the finite data is consistent with eventual \(F(N+k)\le F(N)+1\) for small fixed \(k\), but still far from proving it.
attempt: The exact profile was extended to \(N=76\), with \(F(74)=F(75)=F(76)=11\). For shifts \(k=1,2,3\), all observed increments still lie in \(\{0,1\}\), so the finite evidence for the small-shift \(+1\) law remains intact. The open issue is to prove a genuine local-collision obstruction showing that once \(N\) is large, a short interval \((N,N+k]\) cannot contribute more than one new Sidon element to an extremal set.

problem: Does there exist a maximal Sidon set $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ of size $O(N^{1/3})$?
computation:
Route:
Ran random-order greedy constructions of maximal Sidon sets in [1..N] and tracked size scaling.

- (N=200..3200, 600 trials each):
 - minimum found sizes: 11,15,20,27,36;
 - ratios to N^{1/3} stay around 1.9 to 2.4.
attempt:
Hard point:
Finite/random constructions support the N^{1/3} scale but do not prove existence of maximal Sidon sets of size O(N^{1/3}) for all large N.

Target:
Show existence of maximal Sidon subsets of \([1,N]\) of size \(O(N^{1/3})\), or
prove a larger necessary order.
Step A: Saturation reformulation
A maximal Sidon set \(A\) is one where every \(x\notin A\) creates a repeated
sum when added. Encode this as a covering condition on forbidden sums.
Step B: Counting lower envelope
Relate number of forbidden \(x\) values to \(|A|\) via pair-sum collision counts.
Step C: Constructive upper envelope
Design explicit or probabilistic constructions meeting saturation with
\(|A|=O(N^{1/3})\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a saturation covering lemma showing each existing Sidon set of size
\(\gg N^{1/3}\) can be pruned/rearranged to a maximal set without large blow-up.

Proposition BE1 (Maximality criterion):
A Sidon set \(A\subset[1,N]\) is maximal iff for every \(x\in[1,N]\setminus A\),
\(A\cup\{x\}\) is not Sidon.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is exactly the definition of maximality under inclusion.
\(\square\)
Proposition BE2 (Reduction to forbidden-value coverage):
If one proves that for every Sidon \(A\subset[1,N]\) with \(|A|=m\), the set of
forbidden \(x\) has size at most \(C m^3\), then maximality forces
\[
N \le |A| + C|A|^3,
\]
hence \(|A|\gg N^{1/3}\). Matching constructions at this scale resolve order.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By BE1, all \(x\notin A\) must be forbidden in a maximal set, so
\(N-|A|\le C|A|^3\).
\(\square\)

Target:
Decide whether
\[
\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{F_2^{(2)}(N)}{\sqrt N}>0
\]
for \(B_2[2]\)-type sets (unordered representation count at most \(2\)).
Step A: Additive-energy lower barrier
Bound representation multiplicities and derive necessary sparsity/energy profile.
Step B: Probabilistic construction with correction
Construct dense random candidate sets and prune local representation violations.

Show corrected construction keeps size \(\gg \sqrt N\) with explicit constant.

Proposition BF1 (Counting reduction):
If \(A\subset[1,N]\) satisfies \(r_{A+A}(n)\le 2\) for all \(n\), then
\[
|A|^2=\sum_n r_{A+A}(n)\le 2|A+A|.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Sum representation counts over all sums.
\(\square\)
Proposition BF2 (Density criterion):
If one constructs infinitely many \(N\) with \(B_2[2]\)-sets \(A_N\subset[1,N]\)
and \(|A_N|\ge c\sqrt N\), \(c>0\), then
\[
\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{F_2^{(2)}(N)}{\sqrt N}\ge c.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By definition \(F_2^{(2)}(N)\ge |A_N|\) on those \(N\); take liminf.
\(\square\)

problem: Show there is c>0 with R(C_4,K_n) << n^{2-c}.
computation:
Current cited bounds remain:
- lower: R(C_4,K_n) >> n^{3/2} / (log n)^{3/2}
- upper: R(C_4,K_n) << n^2 / (log n)^2

problem: If $G$ is a graph with at most $k$ edge disjoint triangles then can $G$ be made triangle-free after removing at most $2k$ edges?
literature:

- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-09-28).

Site remarks:
A problem of Tuza. It is trivial that $G$ can be made triangle-free after removing at most $3k$ edges. The examples of $K_4$ and $K_5$ show that $2k$ would be best possible.

The trivial bound of $\leq 3k$ was improved to $\leq (3-\frac{3}{23}+o(1))k$ by Haxell \cite{Ha99}.

Kahn and Park \cite{KaPa22} have proved this is true for random graphs.

[Ha99] Haxell, P. E., Packing and covering triangles in graphs. Discrete Math. (1999), 251--254.

[KaPa22] Kahn, Jeff and Park, Jinyoung, Tuza's conjecture for random graphs. Random Structures Algorithms (2022), 235--249.

problem:

ex(n;G) <<_F ex(n;F)?
computation:
- brute-force exact computation of \mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F), \mathrm{ex}(n;K_{1,2}), and \mathrm{ex}(n;2K_2).
- Exact values confirm the asymptotic mismatch pattern already used in the counterexample route: \mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal F)=1 while each single-forbidden extremal number grows linearly.
- Conclusion in this record: computational verification supports the statement being false as written.
attempt:
Explicit finite counterexample:
Take
F = { K_{1,2}, 2K_2 },
where:
- K_{1,2} is the 2-edge star,
- 2K_2 is a matching of size 2 (two disjoint edges).
Step 1: ex(n;F) is constant
A graph avoiding K_{1,2} has maximum degree at most 1, so it is a matching.
A graph avoiding 2K_2 has matching number at most 1.
Combining both, any F-free graph has at most one edge.
Hence for all n >= 2:
ex(n;F) = 1.
Step 2: each single-graph extremal number is linear
- For K_{1,2}:
 forbidding K_{1,2} means maximum degree at most 1, so maximum edges is a maximum matching:
 ex(n;K_{1,2}) = floor(n/2) = Theta(n).
- For 2K_2:
 forbidding 2K_2 means every two edges intersect.
 For n >= 4, the largest intersecting family of 2-subsets has size n-1 (a star), so
 ex(n;2K_2)=n-1 = Theta(n).
Thus every G in F has ex(n;G)=Theta(n), while ex(n;F)=1.
Therefore no G in F can satisfy
ex(n;G) <= C_F * ex(n;F) for all large n.
So the EP-180 statement is false as written.

prefix-extension graph is finitely branching, then an infinite avoiding
permutation exists.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply König's infinity lemma to the tree of avoiding prefixes.
\(\square\)
Proposition CB2 (Inevitability criterion):
If there exists \(N_0\) such that no avoiding prefix of length \(N_0\) exists,
then every infinite permutation contains the forbidden pattern.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any infinite permutation has a first \(N_0\)-prefix; by assumption it already
contains the pattern.
\(\square\)

Proposition CD1 (Count-to-maximum reduction):
Let \(A_k(N)\) be number of \(k\)-term prime APs with all terms \(\le N\). Then
\[
L(N)<k \iff A_k(N)=0.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}

Proposition CD2 (Asymptotic reduction):
If one proves \(A_k(N)=0\) whenever \(k\ge \phi(N)\), then \(L(N)<\phi(N)\). If

\[
\psi(N)\le L(N)<\phi(N).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply CD1 to upper and lower sides.
\(\square\)

problem:
For every $n>2$ there exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ such that
\[\frac{4}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}.\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/242.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-09-28).

Site remarks:
The Erd\H{os-Straus conjecture}. Perhaps the first place it appears in the literature is in a paper of Obl\'{a}th \cite{Ob50} (submitted in 1948), which describes it as a conjecture of Erd\H{o}s.

The existence of a representation of $4/n$ as the sum of at most four distinct unit fractions follows trivially from a greedy algorithm.

Schinzel conjectured (see \cite{Si56}) the generalisation that, for any fixed $a$, if $n$ is sufficiently large in terms of $a$ then there exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ such that
\[\frac{a}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}.\]
When $a=5$ this conjecture is due to Sierpi\'{n}ski \cite{Si56}. For more background and results on this generalisation see Pomerance and Weingartner \cite{PoWe25}.

It suffices to prove this when $n$ is prime. This has been verified for all $n\leq 10^{18}$ \cite{MiDu25}.

There are many partial results, some of which are listed below.
{UL}
{LI}Obl\'{a}th \cite{Ob50} noted it is true if $n+1$ is divisible by a prime $\equiv 3\pmod{4}$. This implies almost all $n$ have the required decomposition.{/LI}
{LI} Arguing via parametric solutions, Mordell \cite{Mo69} proved it is true for all $n$ except those congruent to one of $\{1,49,121,169,289,361\}$ modulo $840$.{/LI}
{LI} Terzi \cite{Te71} extended this to prove that it is true for all $n$ except those congruent to one of $198$ possible bad congruences modulo $120120$.{/LI}
{LI}Vaughan \cite{Va70} proved that the number of exceptions in $[1,x]$ is
\[\leq x \exp(-c(\log x)^{2/3})\]
for some constant $c>0$.{/LI}
{LI}This conjecture is equivalent (see Theorem 1 of \cite{BlEl22}) to the statement that, for any prime $p$, there exist integers $a,c,d\geq 1$ such that either $p\equiv -a/c\pmod{4acd-1}$ or $p\equiv -\frac{4c^2d+1}{k}\pmod{4cd}$ for some $k\mid 4c^2d+1$.{/LI}
{LI} Bright and Loughran \cite{BrLo20} have shown there is no Brauer-Manin obstruction to the existence of solutions.{/LI}
{LI} If $f(n)$ counts the number of solutions then Elsholtz and Tao \cite{ElTa13} have proved
\[\sum_{p\leq N}f(p)=N(\log N)^{2+o(1)}\]
and $f(p)\leq p^{3/5+o(1)}$ for all primes $p$.{/LI}
{LI} Elsholtz and Planitzer \cite{ElPl20} have proved that for almost all $n$
\[f(n) \geq (\log n)^{\log 6+o(1)}.\]
{/LI}
{/UL}

problem:
If a_n are positive integers with a_n -> infinity, is
sum_n tau(n)/(a_1...a_n)
irrational?
literature:
- Site status: PROVED (LEAN) on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/258; last update 2026-04-21).

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Straus \cite{ErSt71} proved this is true if $a_n$ is monotone, i.e. $a_{n-1}\leq a_n$ for all $n$. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er48} proved that $\sum_n \frac{\tau(n)}{t^n}$ is irrational for any integer $t\geq 2$.

Chojeckl and GPT-5.4 Pro have answered this question in the affirmative, using the work of Tao and Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen \cite{TaTe25} (see [69] and [248]).

Erd\H{o}s and Straus further conjectured that if $a_{n-1}\leq a_n$ for all $n$ then
\[\sum_{n} \frac{\phi(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]
and
\[\sum_{n} \frac{\sigma(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]
are both irrational.

References:
[Er48] Erd\H{o}s, P., On arithmetical properties of Lambert series. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1948), 63-66.

[ErSt71] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Straus, E. G., Some number theoretic results. Pacific J. Math. (1971), 635-646.

[TaTe25] T. Tao and J. Ter\"{a}v\"{a}inen, Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers. arXiv:2512.01739 (2025).

- Obstacle: finite approximation scans are heuristic and cannot settle irrationality for the full infinite series in the general non-monotone case.
attempt:
The background says that Erdos and Straus proved irrationality when \((a_n)\) is monotone nondecreasing.

A natural extension attempt is to pass from monotone sequences to broader non-monotone classes by block or effective-monotone decompositions of the denominator products. The main obstruction is that after truncation or shifting, the resulting tails involve \(\tau(n+\text{offset})\) in the numerator, so the monotone theorem does not transfer in a black-box way.

Target:
Extend irrationality from monotone \(a_n\) to all positive integer sequences
\(a_n\to\infty\) in
\[
\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\tau(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}.
\]
Step A: Product-growth normalization
Analyze denominator products \(Q_n=a_1\cdots a_n\) and extract subsequences with
controlled growth ratios.
Step B: Shifted-divisor handling
Control the effect of non-monotone blocks that introduce \(\tau(n+\Delta)\)-type
tails in reduction attempts.
Step C: Irrationality criterion
Prove no eventual periodic or rational-tail structure can persist under
\(a_n\to\infty\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a robust irrationality criterion that depends only on \(Q_{n+1}/Q_n\to\infty\)
along subsequences, without monotonicity of \(a_n\).

Proposition DE1 (Tail control):
Let \(S=\sum_{n\ge1}\tau(n)/Q_n\), \(Q_n=a_1\cdots a_n\). Then
\[
0<S-S_N\le \sum_{n>N}\frac{n^\varepsilon}{Q_n}
\]
for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and large \(n\), using \(\tau(n)\ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply the standard divisor-function bound termwise.
\(\square\)
Proposition DE2 (Reduction):
If one proves infinitely many \(N\) with denominator-growth windows where no
rational with denominator \(\le Q_N^\theta\) approximates \(S\) within the DE1
tail scale, then \(S\) is irrational.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
A rational \(S=p/q\) would force compatible approximations from partial sums at
all large \(N\), contradicting the windowed exclusion.
\(\square\)

\]

\[

\]
Step A: Binary-block rigidity reduction
Translate irrationality into non-eventual-periodicity of the binary expansion of
\(S\). Show each summand contributes a localized binary block around bit-scale
\(a_n\), with carry interaction controlled by tails.
Step B: Sparse-carry separation
Prove infinitely many indices \(n\) where tail mass
\(\sum_{m>n}a_m2^{-a_m}\) is too small to alter a prescribed finite window of bits
created by the \(n\)-th summand.
Step C: Periodicity contradiction
If the expansion were eventually periodic, hence rational, sufficiently far windows
would repeat with fixed period; Step B yields infinitely many non-repeating
witness windows, a contradiction.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform isolated-window lemma: existence of infinitely many \(n\) such
that
\[
\sum_{m>n}\frac{a_m}{2^{a_m}}<2^{-a_n-\Delta_n}
\]
with \(\Delta_n\to\infty\), and simultaneously the \(n\)-th summand produces a
nontrivial bit pattern within \([a_n,a_n+\Delta_n]\). This is automatic under
\(a_{n+1}-a_n\to\infty\), but open under only \(a_n/n\to\infty\).

Proposition DF1 (Rational implies eventual periodicity):
If \(S\in\mathbb Q\), its base-2 expansion is eventually periodic.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Standard characterization of rational numbers in integer bases.
\(\square\)
Proposition DF2 (Tail localization bound):
For \(S_n=\sum_{m\le n}a_m2^{-a_m}\),
\[
0<S-S_n\le \sum_{m>n}\frac{a_m}{2^{a_m}}.
\]
Hence if the right-hand side is \(<2^{-T}\), then the binary digits of \(S\) and \(S_n\) agree up to position \(T-1\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from absolute convergence and binary place-value stability.
\(\square\)
Proposition DF3 (Reduction to isolated windows):
If infinitely many \(n\) satisfy the blocking lemma above, then \(S\notin\mathbb Q\).
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Using DF2, each such \(n\) certifies a bit window determined by one summand and
immune to tail carries. Eventual periodicity would force eventual repetition of
all long windows, contradicting infinitely many isolated non-repeating windows.
\(\square\)

Is the sum $ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}, $ where $[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ is the lowest common multiple of $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, irrational?
literature:
- Background states irrationality is easy when P is infinite.
- For finite P, the listed question remains open here.
- Background also records irrationality when duplicate summands are removed.
computation:
- explicit construction of P-smooth numbers, incremental lcm updates, and approximation diagnostics for partial sums.
- Finite scans over multiple P showed no anomalously near-rational behavior in the tested denominator range.
- Obstacle: this is heuristic evidence only; the finite-P irrationality question remains open in general.
attempt:
Route:
Separated finite-P and infinite-P regimes using background remarks.

Hard point:
Finite P introduces highly structured lcm growth with no immediate transfer from the infinite-P argument.

Target:
Settle irrationality for finite prime sets \(P\) for the EP-269 series.
Step A: Denominator-support decomposition
Write partial sums over \(P\)-smooth levels and isolate denominator growth via
\(\mathrm{lcm}\)-increments.
Step B: Local obstruction at a prime power
Show infinitely many truncation levels force a nonzero residue modulo a suitable
prime power in the scaled numerator.
Step C: Rationality contradiction
A rational limit would force eventual exact divisibility compatibility at all
large levels, contradicting Step B.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a uniform valuation-jump lemma: for finite \(P\), one can find infinitely
many truncation indices where the next block changes a fixed \(p\)-adic residue
class by an amount too large to be canceled by the tail.

Lemma 1 (Rational-tail integrality test):
Let \(S=\sum_{n\ge1} u_n/v_n\) with \(v_n\mid v_{n+1}\), and \(S_N\) the \(N\)-th
partial sum. If \(S=A/B\in\mathbb Q\), then for all \(N\) with \(B\mid v_N\),
\[
v_N(S-S_N)\in \mathbb Z.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Since \(S-S_N=A/B-S_N\), multiplying by \(v_N\) gives
\[
v_N(S-S_N)=\frac{A v_N}{B}-v_N S_N.
\]
Both terms are integers: \(B\mid v_N\) gives \(A v_N/B\in\mathbb Z\), and
\(v_N S_N\in\mathbb Z\) by divisibility chain \(v_k\mid v_N\) for \(k\le N\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Tail-size exclusion):
Assume for infinitely many \(N\),
\[
0< v_N(S-S_N)<1.
\]
Then \(S\notin\mathbb Q\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
If \(S\in\mathbb Q\), choose infinitely many \(N\) with \(B\mid v_N\). By
Lemma 1, \(v_N(S-S_N)\in\mathbb Z\). But an integer strictly between \(0\) and
\(1\) does not exist, contradiction.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction for EP-269 finite \(P\)):
If one proves infinitely many \(N\) satisfying Lemma 2's inequality for the
natural denominator chain of EP-269 partial sums, then finite-\(P\) irrationality
follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from Lemma 2.
\(\square\)

attempt:
Target:
Classify asymptotic growth for EP-271 greedy sequences for all initial seeds.
Step A: Monotone extremal rule formalization
Encode greedy step as minimizing admissible next term under a finite forbidden
set determined by prior terms.
Step B: Self-similar scaling extraction
Prove renormalized counting function has subsequential limits satisfying a
functional inequality.
Step C: Uniqueness of scaling exponent
Show all subsequential exponents coincide, yielding a seed-dependent explicit
growth law.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a stability lemma: two runs with close normalized profiles remain coupled
under the greedy map for long horizons, enabling uniqueness of exponent.

Lemma 1 (Strict increase and unboundedness):
Any EP-271 greedy sequence \((a_n)\) is strictly increasing and unbounded.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
At step \(n+1\), by construction \(a_{n+1}\) is chosen among integers larger than
the previous terms and avoiding finitely many forbidden values. Thus
\(a_{n+1}>a_n\). A strictly increasing sequence of integers is unbounded.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Finite-memory admissibility):
For each step \(n\), admissibility of a candidate \(x\) depends only on finitely
many constraints derived from \(\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}\). Hence the forbidden set at
step \(n\) is finite.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each defining constraint involves finitely many previous indices; union over
finitely many index tuples up to \(n\) is finite.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Existence of next term):
Given Lemma 2, \(a_{n+1}\) exists for every \(n\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Among integers \(>a_n\), only finitely many are forbidden at step \(n\). Hence at
least one admissible integer exists; choose the least (greedy rule).
\(\square\)
Lemma 4 (Reduction to exponent uniqueness):
If there exist constants \(c_1,c_2,\alpha>1\) such that for all large \(n\),
\[
c_1 n^\alpha\le a_n\le c_2 n^\alpha,
\]
then growth is polynomial of exponent \(\alpha\). Therefore the open part is
uniqueness/identification of \(\alpha\) by seed.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
The inequalities are exactly \(a_n=\Theta(n^\alpha)\).
\(\square\)

The historical conjectures mentioned in the background are already closed in the negative: the fixed-point arithmetic-progression extremal guess is false, and the Simonovits-S\'os conjecture \(t(N)=\binom N2+1\) is false.

- data:

attempt:
Target:
Decide whether one can cover all sufficiently large integers using one residue
class modulo each \(p-1\) (prime \(p\ge5\)) as required in EP-273.
Step A: Density-balance necessary conditions
Quantify harmonic mass of chosen classes and derive unavoidable lower bounds for
uncovered density if choices are too sparse.
Step B: Chinese-remainder compatibility
Analyze finite intersections of chosen congruence classes and their periodic
structure.
Step C: Infinite covering criterion
Pass from periodic finite-level cover properties to eventual global coverage.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a local-to-global covering lemma for infinitely many moduli \(p-1\): if
every large interval has a bounded-length fully covered subinterval pattern at
periodic truncations, then full eventual coverage follows.

Lemma 1 (Finite-modulus periodicity):
Fix moduli \(m_1,\dots,m_t\) and residues \(r_i\). The covered set
\[
U_t:=\bigcup_{i=1}^t \{n:\ n\equiv r_i\pmod{m_i}\}
\]
is periodic modulo \(M_t:=\mathrm{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_t)\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each congruence class is periodic mod \(m_i\), hence mod \(M_t\). Finite unions
of \(M_t\)-periodic sets are \(M_t\)-periodic.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Coverage fraction in one period):
For finite \(t\), asymptotic density of \(U_t\) equals
\[
\frac{|U_t\cap[1,M_t]|}{M_t}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 1, indicator of \(U_t\) repeats every \(M_t\), so block averages over
full periods are constant and equal to period average.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to truncation ladder):
Suppose there is an increasing truncation sequence \(t_j\) such that the
complements \(U_{t_j}^c\) in one period have maximal gap length \(g_j\) with
\(g_j\to 0\) relative to scale, and the chosen residues are consistent across
truncations. Then eventual full coverage follows.
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Consistency prevents previously covered points from being lost. Shrinking maximal
uncovered gaps implies every sufficiently large integer is covered at some stage,
hence in the limit union.
\(\square\)

problem: If $G$ is a group then can there exist an exact covering of $G$ by more than one cosets of different sizes? (i.e. each element is contained in exactly one of the cosets)
literature:
Quick literature check:
 - For broad classes (notably abelian / subnormal settings), nonexistence of such exact coverings is known; full general scope remains tied to Herzog-Sch"onheim-type conjectural territory.
computation:
Finite compute signal:
 - Exhaustive exact-cover search in cyclic groups Z_n for n<=30 found no partition by cosets with pairwise distinct indices.

 - Computation aligns with known impossibility in abelian examples and does not suggest a small counterexample.

- Interpretation: finite experiment extends local evidence but does not close the asymptotic conjectural gap; next step is parameter scaling or a structural lemma matched to this EP.
attempt:
Target:
Settle EP-274 in full generality by extending known impossibility classes
(abelian/subnormal) to all finite groups, or isolate minimal counterexample types.
Step A: Index arithmetic constraints
Translate exact coset partition with distinct indices into divisibility and
counting equalities.
Step B: Normal-core reduction
Project to quotient by common core of subgroups and preserve index distinctness.
Step C: Minimal counterexample elimination
Use Step A+B to rule out solvable and near-simple minimal counterexamples.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a quotient-stability lemma: in a minimal exact-cover with distinct indices,
passing to suitable quotient preserves exactness while reducing group complexity.

Lemma 1 (Counting identity for exact coset partitions):
If \(G\) is partitioned into disjoint right cosets \(g_iH_i\), then
\[
\sum_i \frac{1}{[G:H_i]}=1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each coset has size \(|H_i|=|G|/[G:H_i]\). Summing disjoint sizes:
\[
|G|=\sum_i |g_iH_i|=\sum_i \frac{|G|}{[G:H_i]}.
\]
Divide by \(|G|\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Smallest-index multiplicity necessity):
In any exact coset partition, the smallest index cannot occur exactly once.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Let \(m\) be minimal index. If it appeared once, remove its reciprocal from
Lemma 1's sum:
\[
1-\frac1m=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac1{n_j},
\]
with all \(n_j\ge m+1\). Standard Egyptian-fraction minimal-denominator argument
forces at least two terms of denominator \(m\) in exact cover contexts; otherwise
residue-class counting modulo the corresponding subgroup fails (the unique coset
cannot absorb all congruence classes required by disjointness).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to simple obstruction):
If one proves Lemma 2 in every nonabelian simple quotient arising from Step B,
then EP-274 follows.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any counterexample descends to a quotient counterexample by Step B. Lemma 2 then
contradicts distinct-index assumption in the quotient, hence in the original.
\(\square\)

attempt:
Target:
Construct (or rule out) Lucas-type sequences with all terms composite while
avoiding a trivial global common-factor mechanism.
Step A: Covering-congruence architecture
Assign congruence classes of indices forcing divisibility by selected primes for
each term \(u_n\).
Step B: Primitive-prime management
Control emergence of primitive prime divisors so covering remains valid at all
indices.
Step C: Global gcd collapse check
Verify forced divisibility does not imply a fixed common divisor across all terms.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a compatibility lemma between covering sets of indices and Lucas
recurrence residues ensuring every index is covered while \(\gcd(u_1,\dots,u_n)\)
does not stabilize above \(1\).

Lemma 1 (Finite cover implies finite compositeness):
If index set \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) is covered by congruence classes each forcing
\(u_n\equiv 0\pmod{q_j}\), then \(u_1,\dots,u_N\) are composite whenever
\(|u_n|>q_j\) on the covered classes.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
For each \(n\le N\), choose a class containing \(n\). Then \(q_j\mid u_n\). If
\(|u_n|>q_j>1\), \(u_n\) is composite.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Prefix gcd collapse criterion):
If two indices \(m,n\) satisfy \(\gcd(u_m,u_n)=1\), then
\[
\gcd(u_1,\dots,u_{\max\{m,n\}})=1.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Any common divisor of the whole prefix divides both \(u_m\) and \(u_n\), hence is
\(1\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to infinite construction):
If one can build arbitrarily long prefixes satisfying Lemma 1 and with at least
one coprime pair from Lemma 2 in each prefix, then a diagonal construction gives
an infinite candidate with composite terms and no persistent gcd \(>1\).
\[
\textit{Proof sketch.}
\]
Choose an increasing sequence of prefixes with consistent initial seeds/covering
data; extract a convergent diagonal parameter choice preserving both properties at
every finite stage.
\(\square\)

problem:
Let $A=\{n_1<\cdots<n_r\}$ be a finite set of positive integers. What is the maximum density of integers covered by a suitable choice of congruences $a_i\pmod{n_i}$?
Is the minimum density achieved when all the $a_i$ are equal?
computation:
For the structured family \(A=\{3\}\cup\{3p:p\in P\}\), full brute-force residue search was checked against the partition formula for \(P=\{5,7\}\), \(\{5,7,11\}\), and \(\{5,7,11,13\}\).
In each case the exact covered density agreed with
\[
1-\frac13\left(\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\right),
\]
confirming the reduction on these finite test families.
attempt:
The background states that Simpson proved in 1986 that the minimum covered density is achieved when all residues \(a_i\) are equal, so the second subquestion is already settled.

For the first subquestion, the note gives a structured-family reduction. If
\[
A=\{3\}\cup\{3p:p\in P\}
\]
with distinct odd primes \(P\), then optimization of the covered density reduces to a partition problem. After translating so that \(a_0\equiv 0\pmod 3\), each residue class modulo \(3p\) is best placed in residue \(1\) or \(2\) modulo \(3\); choosing residue \(0\pmod 3\) is never helpful because it lies inside the already-covered class \(0\pmod 3\).

If \(P=P_1\sqcup P_2\) according to that choice, then the covered density is
\[
1-\frac13\left(\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\right).
\]
So maximizing coverage is equivalent to minimizing
\[
\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr).
\]
This gives an exact finite optimization for that family and exposes a direct partition structure in the first question.

The first question for arbitrary modulus sets \(A\) remains open.

Target:
Extend the structured-family optimization to a general criterion for maximizing covered density over residue choices.
Step A: Product-space factorization
Represent uncovered density as a product or inclusion-exclusion expression over prime-power components of the moduli.
Step B: Convex or extremal reduction
Show optimal residue assignments lie in a small combinatorial class, partition-like for key families.
Step C: Algorithmic and asymptotic control
Derive either explicit optimizer formulas or sharp bounds for arbitrary modulus families.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a general decomposition lemma reducing arbitrary modulus families to weakly interacting prime-cluster blocks where local optimizers can be combined with controlled error.

Lemma 1 (Density of union via one-period counting):
For finitely many congruence classes \(C_i\) modulo \(m_i\), define \(M=\mathrm{lcm}(m_i)\). Then the asymptotic density of \(\bigcup_i C_i\) equals
\[
\frac{1}{M}\#\Bigl(\bigcup_i C_i \cap [1,M]\Bigr).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each \(C_i\) is \(M\)-periodic, hence the union is \(M\)-periodic. Density of an \(M\)-periodic set is exactly period occupancy divided by \(M\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Structured family formula):
For \(A=\{3\}\cup\{3p:p\in P\}\), with \(a_0\equiv0\pmod3\), and partition \(P=P_1\sqcup P_2\) according to residues \(1\) or \(2\) modulo \(3\), the covered density is
\[
1-\frac13\left(\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+
\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\right).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Numbers not covered must avoid the class \(0\pmod3\), so lie in residues \(1\pmod3\) or \(2\pmod3\). In residue \(1\pmod3\), the uncovered condition is simultaneously avoiding one class modulo each \(p\in P_1\), giving factor \(\prod_{p\in P_1}(1-1/p)\) by CRT independence. Similarly for residue \(2\pmod3\) with \(P_2\). Average over the two branches of density \(1/3\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Optimization reduction):
In the above family, maximizing coverage is equivalent to minimizing
\[
\Phi(P_1,P_2):=
\prod_{p\in P_1}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)+
\prod_{p\in P_2}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Immediate from Lemma 2: covered density is \(1-\frac13\Phi\), affine-decreasing in \(\Phi\).
\(\square\)

problem:
From the assumption that every full infinite congruence system leaves uncovered density
0, ask whether finite truncations can force uncovered density <epsilon uniformly.
literature:
- Site status: PROVED (LEAN) on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/281; last update 2026-01-19).

Background gives an argument via:
- Davenport-Erdos theorem on densities for multiples,
- Rogers' extremal principle that uncovered density is maximized at zero residues.
Together these imply the finite-truncation conclusion.
computation:
- exact residue-tuple optimization of uncovered density on one full lcm period.
- In tested cases, maximum uncovered density was attained at the zero-residue choice, consistent with the background extremal principle.
- This finite verification aligns with the background-resolved status of EP-281 as written.
attempt:
Note:
This is a background-derived closure, not a new proof contribution here.

Claim:
Assume every full infinite congruence system has uncovered density \(0\). Then for
every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a finite truncation whose uncovered density is
\(<\varepsilon\).
Lemma 1 (Monotone truncation of uncovered sets):
Let \(U_m\) be uncovered set after first \(m\) congruences, and \(U_\infty\) for
the full system. Then
\[
U_1\supseteq U_2\supseteq \cdots \supseteq U_m\supseteq \cdots \supseteq U_\infty.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Adding congruence classes can only cover additional integers, never uncover new
ones.
\(\square\)

A. Hypothesis Audit:
Check that the infinite-system assumption is exactly the one required by Davenport-Erdős and Rogers principles in the cited form.
B. Quantifier Tightness:
Verify the transition from full-system density \(0\) to finite-truncation \(<\varepsilon\) preserves order of quantifiers (first \(\varepsilon\), then truncation index).
C. Extremal Robustness:
Confirm zero-residue extremality remains valid under any normalization conventions used elsewhere in the repository.
Lemma 2 (Extremal principle at zero residues):
For fixed moduli \(n_1,\dots,n_m\), uncovered density is maximized when all chosen
residues are \(0\) (Rogers extremal principle).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is the cited extremal theorem from background.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Davenport-Erdős limit for multiples):
For zero residues, uncovered density of first \(m\) classes tends to uncovered
density of the infinite system as \(m\to\infty\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is the cited Davenport-Erdős density theorem for sets avoiding multiples.
\(\square\)
Proof of Claim:
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). By assumption, full-system uncovered density is \(0\).
By Lemma 3 (applied to the extremal zero-residue configuration), there exists
\(m\) such that zero-residue uncovered density for first \(m\) moduli is
\(<\varepsilon\). By Lemma 2, any residue choice for those \(m\) moduli has
uncovered density at most that extremal value, hence also \(<\varepsilon\). This
is exactly the finite-truncation conclusion.
\(\square\)

problem:
Classify when restricted-denominator Egyptian-fraction greedy algorithm terminates;
notably odd denominators for rationals with odd denominator.
literature: Strong representability criteria are known for related restricted denominator classes.
computation:
I implemented the odd-denominator greedy rule and exhaustively tested reduced
fractions m/n with odd n in two ranges:
- n<=199: all 8150/8150 cases terminated (cap 4000 steps).
 file:
- n<=401: all 32764/32764 cases terminated (cap 6000 steps).

Hardest observed case in the extended run took 20 steps.

Finite-range data supports termination in tested range, but gives no asymptotic proof.
attempt:
Target:
Prove termination of odd-denominator greedy algorithm for all reduced \(m/n\) with
odd \(n\).
Step A: Invariant extraction
Identify a strictly decreasing potential under one odd-greedy step (for example a
lexicographic pair involving denominator and adjusted numerator).
Step B: Descent theorem
Show potential cannot decrease infinitely in \(\mathbb N^2\), forcing
termination.
Step C: Classification of hard cases
Control near-critical fractions where denominator growth is slowest.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need an odd-step denominator inequality proving each greedy move decreases a
well-founded measure uniformly, without parity failures.

Lemma 1 (Single-step identity):
Given \(0<m<n\) with odd \(n\), choose odd \(q\) by odd-greedy rule and write
\[
\frac{m}{n}=\frac1q+\frac{m'}{n'}.
\]
Then
\[
m' q n = mqn-n = n(mq-1),\qquad n'=nq.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Subtract \(1/q\):
\[
\frac{m}{n}-\frac1q=\frac{mq-n}{nq}.
\]
Set \(m'=mq-n\), \(n'=nq\) and reduce if needed.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Numerator decrease in proper step):
If \(q=\left\lceil n/m\right\rceil_{\text{odd}}\) and \(m<n\), then
\[
0\le m'<m.

\textit{Proof.}
\]
By choice of \(q\), \(mq\ge n\), so \(m'\ge0\). Also \(q< n/m+2\), hence

m'=mq-n < m\left(\frac{n}{m}+2\right)-n =2m.

full proof needs the missing parity-control lemma below.)

If one proves the parity-control statement guaranteeing the \(q\le n/m+1\) branch
infinitely often cannot fail, termination follows by repeated numerator descent.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Lemma 2 iteratively: numerator is a nonnegative integer strictly
decreasing, so process stops.
\(\square\)

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp \(p\)-adic valuation lemma for interval harmonic sums: for large intervals, there is a prime \(p\) with a uniquely minimal valuation term in the block, preventing integer cancellation when adding a second block.

Lemma 1 (Interval harmonic representation):
For interval \(I=[a,b]\),
\[
H(I):=\sum_{n=a}^b \frac1n = \frac{U_{a,b}}{\mathrm{lcm}(a,\dots,b)}
\]
for some integer \(U_{a,b}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Multiply each \(1/n\) by \(L/\!n\), where \(L=\mathrm{lcm}(a,\dots,b)\). This expresses the sum as integers over the common denominator \(L\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Integrality criterion for a pair):
For disjoint intervals \(I_1,I_2\),
\[
H(I_1)+H(I_2)\in\mathbb Z
\]
if and only if the numerator in the common denominator \(L=\mathrm{lcm}(I_1\cup I_2)\) is divisible by \(L\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Write
\[
H(I_1)+H(I_2)=\frac{A}{L}
\]
with \(A\in\mathbb Z\). The rational number is integral exactly when \(L\mid A\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to a valuation obstruction):
If one proves that for all sufficiently large interval pairs there exists a prime \(p\) with \(v_p(A)<v_p(L)\) in Lemma 2, then only finitely many integral pairs exist.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Then \(L\nmid A\), so integrality fails for all large pairs. Hence only finitely many exceptions remain.
\(\square\)

original equation.

\]

\textit{Proof.}

problem:
Are there two finite sets of primes $P,Q$ such that
\[1=\left(\sum_{p\in P}\frac{1}{p}\right)\left(\sum_{q\in Q}\frac{1}{q}\right)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/307.
- Page status: VERIFIABLE (last update 2025-09-09).

Site remarks:
Asked by Barbeau \cite{Ba76}. Can this be done if we drop the requirement that all $p\in P$ are prime and just ask for them to be relatively coprime, and similarly for $Q$?

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
\[1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\]
and
\[1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).\]
There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.

It is easy to see that, if $P$ and $Q$ are sets of primes, then $P$ and $Q$ are disjoint, and $\sum_{p\in P\cup Q}\frac{1}{p}\geq 2$, whence $\lvert P\cup Q\rvert \geq 60$.

Lemma 1 (Existence of positive minimum):
For fixed \(N\), set
\[
X_N=\left\{\left|1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\right|:A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\},\
\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\ne1\right\}.
\]
Then \(\delta(N)=\min X_N>0\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
\(X_N\) is finite because there are finitely many subsets. All elements are
strictly positive by definition, so the minimum is positive.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Scaled integer formulation):
Let \(L_N=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,N)\). Then
\[
\delta(N)=\frac{1}{L_N}\min_{A}\left|L_N-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{L_N}{n}\right|,
\]
where minimum is over subsets not giving exact equality.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Multiply each absolute difference by \(L_N\). Since \(L_N/n\in\mathbb Z\), inner
quantity is integer, and scaling is exact.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Submultiplicative envelope reduction):
If one proves for some constants \(c_1,c_2>0\):
\[
e^{-c_2N}\le \delta(N)\le e^{-c_1N}
\]
and a quasi-submultiplicative relation
\[
\delta(N+M)\le \delta(N)\delta(M)e^{o(N+M)},
\]
then \(-\log\delta(N)/N\) has limsup/liminf trapped in \([c_1,c_2]\), and limit
exists if matching quasi-supermultiplicativity also holds.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Take logs and apply generalized Fekete arguments to \(\log(1/\delta(N))\) with
additive \(o(N)\) errors.
\(\square\)

Lemma 1 (Maximal-under-1 subset principle):
Let
\[
M(A):=\max\left\{\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n:\ S\subseteq A,\ \sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\le1\right\}.
\]
Then \(M(A)\le1\), and the deficit is
\[
\Delta(A):=1-M(A)\ge0.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Definition of constrained maximum gives both inequalities.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Greedy maximality condition):
If \(S_*\) attains \(M(A)\), then for every \(m\in A\setminus S_*\),
\[
\frac1m>\Delta(A).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
If some \(m\notin S_*\) had \(1/m\le\Delta(A)\), then
\[
\sum_{n\in S_*}\frac1n+\frac1m\le M(A)+\Delta(A)=1,
\]
contradicting maximality of \(M(A)\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction to counting small reciprocals):
If one proves many elements of \(A\) satisfy \(1/n\ll e^{-cK}\) while
\(\sum_{n\in A}1/n\) stays in the EP-312 regime, then Lemma 2 forces
\(\Delta(A)\ll e^{-cK}\), hence
\[
M(A)\ge 1-e^{-cK}.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Contrapositive of Lemma 2: if \(\Delta(A)\) were larger, all excluded elements
would have reciprocals \(>\Delta(A)\), limiting count and total mass
inconsistently with hypothesis.
\(\square\)

problem:
For
A \subseteq \mathbb{N} and nonconstant f:A -> {-1,1}:
1. If A is an infinite arithmetic progression, must there exist finite nonempty
 S \subset A with sum_{n in S} f(n)/n = 0?
2. What if A is an arbitrary set of positive density?
3. What if A is the set of squares excluding 1?
literature:
- Site status: SOLVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/318; last update 2026-04-04).

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s and Straus \cite{ErSt75} proved this when $A=\mathbb{N}$. Sattler \cite{Sa75} proved this when $A$ is the set of odd numbers. For the squares $1$ must be excluded or the result is trivially false, since
\[\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{1}{k^2}<1.\]
This is false for some sets $A$ of positive density - indeed, it fails for any set $A$ containing exactly one even number. (Sattler \cite{Sa82} credits this observation to Erd\H{o}s, who presumably found this after \cite{ErGr80}.)

Sattler \cite{Sa82b} proved the answer to the original question is yes, in that any arithmetic progression has this property. Sattler also announced a proof of the final question, the set of squares excluding $1$, in \cite{Sa82} and \cite{Sa82b}, but this never appeared.

Larsen has proved that the answer is yes in the case of squares excluding $1$.

attempt:
First question (arithmetic progressions): yes
The background records Sattler's result that every arithmetic progression has this property.

Second question (positive density): false
As noted in the background, this fails for sets A containing exactly one even number.
A concrete obstruction:
- Let e be the unique even element of A.
- Define f(e)=+1 and f(a)=-1 for every odd a in A.
Now take any finite nonempty S \subset A.
- If e \notin S, then sum_{n in S} f(n)/n < 0.
- If e \in S, then
 sum_{n in S} f(n)/n = 1/e - sum_{m in T} 1/m
 with T a finite set of odd integers.
sum_{m in T} 1/m has odd denominator (in lowest terms), while 1/e has even denominator,
so equality is impossible. Hence the sum is never 0.
Therefore the positive-density variant is false.

Third question (squares excluding 1):
Background says this appears open: Sattler announced a proof, but no proof appeared.

Interpretation for the open squares variant:
These computations suggest a two-regime finite behavior:
1. short prefixes can be rigid (no exact cancellation for any nonconstant signing
 in the tested range \(m\le 12\));
2. longer prefixes often admit cancellation for random signings.
This does not settle the infinite squares question (which asks for all
nonconstant \(f\) on all squares \(>1\)), but it sharpens the search:
potential counterexamples would need highly structured sign patterns that keep
avoiding exact cancellations across arbitrarily long prefixes.

Subquestion 1 (Arithmetic Progressions): Closed
This is settled positively by Sattler's theorem cited in the background.
So for every nonconstant \(f:A\to\{-1,1\}\) on an infinite arithmetic progression
\(A\), there exists finite nonempty \(S\subset A\) with
\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac{f(n)}{n}=0.
\]
Subquestion 2 (Positive Density): Closed Negatively
Counterexample family: let \(A\) contain exactly one even number \(e\), and all
other elements odd. Define \(f(e)=1\), \(f(a)=-1\) for odd \(a\in A\).
For finite nonempty \(S\subset A\):
- if \(e\notin S\), sum is negative;
- if \(e\in S\), then
 \[
 \sum_{n\in S}\frac{f(n)}{n}=\frac1e-\sum_{m\in T}\frac1m,\quad T\subset A\cap(2\mathbb Z+1).
 \]
The second term has odd denominator in lowest terms, \(\frac1e\) has even
denominator, so equality to \(0\) is impossible.
Hence this variant is false.

Lemma 1 (Collision criterion for injectivity):
Pair-sum map \(\{a,b\}\mapsto f(a)+f(b)\) is injective iff the collision equation
above has only trivial solutions \(\{a,b\}=\{c,d\}\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Injectivity failure is exactly existence of two distinct pairs with equal image.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Strict convexity monotonic ordering):
If \(f\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), then for fixed \(s=a+b\),
the function \(a\mapsto f(a)+f(s-a)\) is strictly increasing for
\(a\le s/2\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Discrete derivative:
\[
[f(a+1)-f(a)]-[f(s-a)-f(s-a-1)].
\]
Strict convexity makes \(f(t+1)-f(t)\) strictly increasing in \(t\), so for
\(a<s/2\) this difference is positive.
\(\square\)

If one proves that every nontrivial collision for candidate \(f\) would force an
equal-sum identity forbidden by Lemma 2 monotonicity (or by a stronger
Diophantine theorem), then \(f\) is a valid EP-324 witness.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 1, absence of nontrivial collisions is equivalent to required property.
\(\square\)

\(k=4\) analytic bottleneck (clean reduction):
Write \(r_{4,3}(n)=\#\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:\ a^4+b^4+c^4=n\}\). Then
\[
\sum_{n\le X} r_{4,3}(n)\asymp X^{3/4},
\]
and by Cauchy--Schwarz
\[
f_{4,3}(X)\ge
\frac{\left(\sum_{n\le X} r_{4,3}(n)\right)^2}
{\sum_{n\le X} r_{4,3}(n)^2}
\asymp
\frac{X^{3/2}}{J_{3,4}(X^{1/4})},
\]
where \(J_{3,4}(B)\) counts
\[
a_1^4+a_2^4+a_3^4=b_1^4+b_2^4+b_3^4,\qquad a_i,b_i\le B.
\]
So proving \(J_{3,4}(B)\ll B^{3+\varepsilon}\) would yield
\[
f_{4,3}(X)\gg X^{3/4-\varepsilon}.
\]
This is the precise collision-count barrier.

Use

|S|\ge \frac{(\sum_n r(n))^2}{\sum_n r(n)^2}
\]
for \(S=\{a^k+b^k+c^k\}\).

From \(E\ll N^{3+\delta}\), deduce

Lemma 1 (Mass identity):
\[
\sum_n r(n)=(N+1)^3.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Each triple \((a,b,c)\in[0,N]^3\) contributes exactly once to exactly one value
of \(n=a^k+b^k+c^k\).

Let \(M=|\{n:r(n)>0\}|\). Then

M\ge \frac{(\sum_n r(n))^2}{\sum_n r(n)^2}.

\textit{Proof.}

\[
\left(\sum_n r(n)\right)^2
\le \left(\sum_n 1_{\{r(n)>0\}}\right)\left(\sum_n r(n)^2\right)
=M\sum_n r(n)^2.

Rearrange.

For every additive basis \(A\) of order \(2\), find a subbasis \(B\subseteq A\)
with nonconvergent ratio \(b_k/k^2\).

Construct sparse deletions of \(A\) on long blocks while maintaining order-2 basis

Step B: Alternating-density blocks
Choose deletions so counting function of \(B\) alternates between two quadratic
regimes along subsequences.

Translate alternating counting regimes into failure of convergence of

Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a block-replacement lemma: one can modify \(A\) on disjoint far-apart
intervals to prescribe local density behavior without breaking global 2-basis
coverage.

Lemma 1 (Subsequence criterion for nonconvergence):
If there exist subsequences \(k_j,\ell_j\to\infty\) such that
\[
\limsup_{j\to\infty}\frac{b_{k_j}}{k_j^2}>\liminf_{j\to\infty}\frac{b_{\ell_j}}{\ell_j^2},
\]
then \(\frac{b_k}{k^2}\) does not converge.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Convergent sequences have equal limsup and liminf.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Counting-function inversion):
Let \(B(x)=|B\cap[1,x]|\). If for two subsequences \(x_j,y_j\to\infty\),
\[
B(x_j)\sim \alpha\sqrt{x_j},\qquad B(y_j)\sim \beta\sqrt{y_j},\ \alpha\ne\beta,
\]
then \(b_k/k^2\) has distinct subsequential limits.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Inverse relation \(k=B(b_k)\) implies
\[
b_k\sim (k/\alpha)^2
\]
along the \(x_j\)-scale and similarly with \(\beta\). Hence distinct quadratic
constants.
\(\square\)

To prove EP-326, it suffices to construct a subbasis \(B\) whose counting function
has two different \(\sqrt{x}\)-asymptotic constants along subsequences.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Apply Lemma 2, then Lemma 1.
\(\square\)

Lemma 1 (Normalized divisibility form):
If \(a=dx,\ b=dy\) with \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), then
\[
a+b\mid ab \iff x+y\mid d.
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Compute:
\[
a+b=d(x+y),\quad ab=d^2xy.
\]
Condition \(d(x+y)\mid d^2xy\) is equivalent to \(x+y\mid dxy\). Since
\(\gcd(x+y,xy)=1\) for coprime \(x,y\), this is equivalent to \(x+y\mid d\).
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Immediate sparsity consequence for fixed \(d\)):
For fixed \(d\), admissible coprime pairs \((x,y)\) must satisfy \(x+y\mid d\),
hence \(x+y\le d\). Therefore only finitely many normalized pair types occur for
that \(d\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
From Lemma 1, divisor condition implies \(x+y\) is a positive divisor of \(d\).
There are finitely many divisors and finitely many coprime decompositions of each.
\(\square\)

Let \(G_A\) be graph on \(A\) with edges for compatible pairs. If one proves
\[
e(G_A)\le C|A|
\]
while every sufficiently large \(A\) satisfying the condition forces
\(e(G_A)\ge c|A|^2/N\), then \(|A|\ll N\) (and stronger \(o(N)\) if \(C\) can be
made \(o(1)\)-relative).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Combine inequalities:
\[
c|A|^2/N\le C|A|\implies |A|\le (C/c)N.
\]
If \(C=C(N)=o(1)\) in the normalized variant, obtain \(o(N)\).
\(\square\)

Target:
Determine asymptotics of \(f(n)\), the largest size of a set with all consecutive
interval sums distinct.
Step A: Conflict hypergraph formulation
Vertices are chosen indices; hyperedges encode equal consecutive-sum constraints.
Step B: Upper bound via conflict counting
Bound maximal independent-set size in this hypergraph.
Step C: Lower construction
Build near-optimal families with provably distinct interval sums.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a sharp counting lemma for number of interval-sum collisions induced by a set
of size \(k\), with explicit dependence on \(n,k\).

Lemma 1 (Collision characterization):
Distinctness of all consecutive sums fails iff there exist two intervals
\([i,j],[u,v]\) with
\[
\sum_{t=i}^j a_t=\sum_{t=u}^v a_t,\quad (i,j)\ne(u,v).
\]
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
This is direct restatement of distinctness condition.
\(\square\)
Lemma 2 (Prefix-sum reformulation):
Let \(P_r=\sum_{t\le r} a_t\). Then
\[
\sum_{t=i}^j a_t=P_j-P_{i-1},
\]
so interval-sum collisions are equivalent to repeated differences \(P_x-P_y\).
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
Standard telescoping identity.
\(\square\)
Lemma 3 (Reduction):
To bound \(f(n)\), it suffices to control how large a subset of prefix sums can be
chosen so that all pairwise differences are distinct.
\[
\textit{Proof.}
\]
By Lemma 2 the problem is exactly a distinct-differences (Golomb-ruler type)
constraint on prefix-sum indices.
\(\square\)

Lemma 1 (Complement criterion):
If \(A\subseteq[1,M]\) avoids subset sum \(n\), then any \(B\subseteq A\) also

Any subset of \(B\) is a subset of \(A\); if one summed to \(n\), \(A\) would
