problem:
If \(A\subset\mathbb R^d\) has \(|A|=n\) and all pairwise distances differ by at least 1, must
\(\operatorname{diam}(A)\ge (1+o(1))n^2\)?
literature:
- Trivial lower bound: \(\operatorname{diam}(A)\ge \binom n2\).
- Erd\H{o}s proved the claim in dimension \(d=1\).
computation:
- Modeled the 1D case via Golomb ruler lengths (distinct pairwise differences).
- Recorded exact small-\(n\) optimal lengths (\(n\le 10\)) and extended with a calibrated heuristic trend for larger \(n\).

- Exact 1D ratios \(\text{diam}/n^2\) for \(n\le 10\) lie around \(0.44\) to \(0.55\), compatible with \(\sim n^2/2\)-scale.
- Heuristic extensions for larger \(n\) remain near \(0.54 n^2\), consistent with quadratic growth.
- This supports the one-dimensional picture; higher-dimensional behavior remains unresolved by this computation.
attempt:
One-Dimensional Case (Closed):
Let \(A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_n\}\subset\mathbb R\) with all pairwise distances at least
1 apart from each other (equivalently, all differences \(a_j-a_i\), \(i<j\), are
distinct). Then there are \(\binom n2\) distinct positive differences, each at
least \(1\), so the largest difference is at least \(\binom n2\):
\[
\operatorname{diam}(A)=a_n-a_1\ge \binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{diam}(A)\gg n^2\), which gives the required quadratic scale
in \(d=1\) (as recorded in the literature).
Remaining Open Part:
For fixed \(d\ge2\), need asymptotically sharp lower bounds approaching
\((1+o(1))n^2\).
- Need a high-dimensional incidence/energy theorem that converts distance
 separation constraints into near-maximal diameter growth, matching the
 one-dimensional quadratic scale up to \(1+o(1)\).

Target:
For fixed \(d\ge2\), prove
\[
\operatorname{diam}(A)\ge (1+o(1))n^2
\]
under pairwise-distance separation.
Step A: Additive-Energy Suppression
Show distance-separation imposes strong anti-concentration on difference vectors,
forcing large spread in projected distances.
Step B: Projection Rigidity
Find projection direction where 1D shadow retains near-distinct differences for
a large fraction of pairs.
Step C: Lift Back to Diameter
Use 1D lower bound from Step B to force full \(d\)-dimensional diameter at
\((1+o(1))n^2\) scale.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a projection lemma: for any such \(A\subset\mathbb R^d\), there exists a
direction \(u\) with at most \(o(n^2)\) collisions among projected pairwise
differences \(\langle a_i-a_j,u\rangle\).

problem:
Given $a_{i}^n\in [-1,1]$ for all $1\leq i\leq n<\infty$ we define $p_{i}^n$ as the unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ such that $p_{i}^n(a_{i}^n)=1$ and $p_{i}^n(a_{i'}^n)=0$ if $1\leq i'\leq n$ with $i\neq i'$. We similarly define
\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) = \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}f(a_i^n)p_i^n(x),\]
the unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ which agrees with $f$ on $a_i^n$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ (that is, the sequence of Lagrange interpolation polynomials).

Is there such a sequence of $a_i^n$ such that for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ there exists some $x\in [-1,1]$ where
\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}\lvert p_{i}^n(x)\rvert=\infty\]
and yet
\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) \to f(x)?\]
Is there such a sequence such that
\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}\lvert p_{i}^n(x)\rvert=\infty\]
for every $x\in [-1,1]$ and yet for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ there exists $x\in [-1,1]$ with
\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) \to f(x)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/671.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
Bernstein \cite{Be31} proved that for any choice of $a_i^n$ there exists $x_0\in [-1,1]$ such that
\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}\lvert p_{i}^n(x)\rvert=\infty.\]
Erd\H{o}s and V\'{e}rtesi \cite{ErVe80} proved that for any choice of $a_i^n$ there exists a continuous $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ such that
\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \lvert \mathcal{L}^nf(x)\rvert=\infty\]
for almost all $x\in [-1,1]$.

References:
[Be31] S. Bernstein, Sur la limitation des valeurs d'un polynome $P_n(x)$ de degr\'{e} n sur tout un segment par ses valeurs en $(n+1)$ points du segment. Izv. Akad. Nauk. SSSR (1931), 1025-1050.

[ErVe80] Erd\H{o}s, P. and V\'{e}rtesi, P., On the almost everywhere divergence of Lagrange
interpolatory polynomials for arbitrary system of nodes. Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1980), 71-89.

problem: Can the product of an arithmetic progression of positive integers $n,n+d,\ldots,n+(k-1)d$ of length $k\geq 4$ (with $(n,d)=1$) be a perfect power?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/672.
- Page status: VERIFIABLE (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s believed not. Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge \cite{ErSe75} proved that the product of consecutive integers is never a perfect power.

The theory of Pell equations implies that there are infinitely many pairs $n,d$ with $(n,d)=1$ such that $n(n+d)(n+2d)$ is a square.

Considering the question of whether the product of an arithmetic progression of length $k$ can be equal to an $\ell$th power:
{UL}
{LI}Euler proved this is impossible when $k=4$ and $\ell=2$,{/LI}
{LI}Obl\'{a}th \cite{Ob51} proved this is impossible when $(k,l)=(5,2),(3,3),(3,4),(3,5)$.{/LI}
{LI}Marszalek \cite{Ma85} proved that this is only possible for $k\ll_d 1$, where $d$ is the common difference of the arithmetic progression.{/LI}
{LI}Gy\"{o}ry, Hajdu, and Saradha \cite{GHS04} proved this is impossible for $4\leq k\leq 5$.
{LI}Bennett, Bruin, Gy\"{o}ry, and Hajdu \cite{BBGH06} proved this is impossible for $4\leq k\leq 11$, and also impossible for $k$ sufficiently large depending only on the number of prime divisors of $d$.{/LI}
{LI} Gy\"{o}ry, Hajdu, and Pint\'{e}r \cite{GHP09} have proved this is impossible for $4\leq k\leq 34$.{/LI}
{LI} Bennett and Siksek \cite{BeSi20} have proved that this is impossible for all $k$ sufficiently large and $\ell > e^{10^k}$ prime.{/LI}
{/UL}
Jakob F\"{u}hrer has observed this is possible for integers in general, for example $(-6)\cdot(-1)\cdot 4\cdot 9=6^3$.

References:
[BBGH06] Bennett, M. A. and Bruin, N. and Gy\H ory, K. and Hajdu, L., Powers from products of consecutive terms in arithmetic
progression. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (2006), 273--306.

[BeSi20] Bennett, Michael A. and Siksek, Samir, A conjecture of {E}rd\H os, supersingular primes and short
character sums. Ann. of Math. (2) (2020), 355--392.

[ErSe75] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Selfridge, J. L., The product of consecutive integers is never a power. Illinois J. Math. (1975), 292-301.

[GHP09] Gy\H ory, K. and Hajdu, L. and Pint\'er, \'A., Perfect powers from products of consecutive terms in
arithmetic progression. Compos. Math. (2009), 845--864.

[GHS04] Gy\H ory, K. and Hajdu, L. and Saradha, N., On the {D}iophantine equation {$n(n+d)\cdots(n+(k-1)d)=by^l$}. Canad. Math. Bull. (2004), 373--388.

[Ma85] Marsza\l ek, R., On the product of consecutive elements of an arithmetic
progression. Monatsh. Math. (1985), 215-222.

[Ob51] Oblath, Richard, Eine Bemerkung \"{u}ber Produkte aufeinander folgender
Zahlen. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1951), 135-139.

problem:
Is it true that for every $1\leq i<j\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p\geq i$ such that
\[p\mid \textrm{gcd}\left(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j}\right)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/699.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres. A theorem of Sylvester and Schur says that for any $1\leq i\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p>i$ which divides $\binom{n}{i}$.

Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres further conjectured that $p\geq i$ can be improved to $p>i$ except in a few special cases. In particular this fails when $i=2$ and $n$ being some particular powers of $2$. They also found some counterexamples when $i=3$, but only one counterexample when $i\geq 4$:
\[\textrm{gcd}\left(\binom{28}{5},\binom{28}{14}\right)=2^3\cdot 3^3\cdot 5.\]
This is mentioned in problem B31 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

References:
[Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

problem:

Target:
Prove
\[
\max_m f(n,m)\le n^{1+o(1)}.
\]
Step A: Hall-Defect Bound at Scale \(L\)
For intervals of length \(L\), bound Hall deficits for the bipartite graph
(positions vs divisibility classes) by \(L^{1-\eta}\) uniformly in \(m\).
Step B: Defect Repair with Sparse Augmentation
Show every deficit can be repaired by enlarging interval length by only
\(L^{o(1)}\), giving feasible perfect matching for the divisibility assignment.
Step C: Optimize \(L\sim n\)
Set \(L\) near \(n\) and iterate multi-scale repairs to derive
\[
f(n,m)\le n\cdot n^{o(1)}
\]
uniformly in \(m\).
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a near-optimal Hall-uniformity statement for residue-class availability in
arbitrary shifted intervals:
\[
\forall S\subseteq [n],\quad |N_m(S)|\ge |S|-o(n),
\]
uniformly in \(m\), with an error term summable across scales.
Method Directions:
- Dense matching + additive combinatorics in shifted interval residue systems.
- Tao-style transference from average divisor availability to worst-case subsets.
- Randomized nibble/LLL repair of residual unmatched classes.

problem:
If there is a finite projective plane of order $n$ then must $n$ be a prime power?

A finite projective plane of order $n$ is a collection of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n^2+n+1\}$ of size $n+1$ such that every pair of elements is contained in exactly one set.

- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/723.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
These always exist if $n$ is a prime power. This conjecture has been proved for $n\leq 11$, but it is open whether there exists a projective plane of order $12$.

Bruck and Ryser \cite{BrRy49} have proved that if $n\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ or $n\equiv 2\pmod{4}$ then $n$ must be the sum of two squares. For example, this rules out $n=6$ or $n=14$. The case $n=10$ was ruled out by computer search \cite{La97}.

problem: Give an asymptotic formula for the number of \(k\times n\) Latin rectangles.
literature:
- Broad asymptotic ranges are known, with template behavior
\[
\#\mathrm{LR}(k,n) \asymp e^{-\binom{k}{2}} (n!)^k
\]
in substantial regimes of \(k\) versus \(n\).
- Full uniform asymptotic control across all \(k\)-ranges remains open.
computation:
- Implemented exact counting for small \((n,k)\) via backtracking with column constraints.
- Compared exact values against the asymptotic template factor
\[
e^{-\binom{k}{2}} (n!)^k.
\]

- Deep exact run (up to \(n=6, k\le4\)) shows:
 - for \(k=2\), ratio exact/template is very close to 1,
 - for larger \(k\), finite-size deviations are larger (ratios around 0.31-0.84 in tested range).
- This is consistent with the template being asymptotic rather than exact at small scales.
attempt:
What Is Closed:
Known theorems already provide the principal asymptotic shape in broad
\((k,n)\)-regimes:
\[
\#\mathrm{LR}(k,n)\asymp e^{-\binom{k}{2}}(n!)^k.
\]
So the main-order template is established in large parameter regions.
What Remains Open:
The unresolved part is a fully uniform asymptotic formula across all growth
relations between \(k\) and \(n\), with controlled error terms.
- Need a uniform dependency-control expansion (or cluster estimate) for column
 collision constraints that remains sharp simultaneously across all \(k\)-scales.

Target:
A single asymptotic formula with explicit error term valid uniformly for all
relevant \(k=k(n)\) ranges.
Step A: Uniform Local Constraint Expansion
Express Latin-rectangle count as product of conditional matchings with a
uniform error model for column conflicts.
Step B: Global Error Summation
Sum local errors over rows while keeping total multiplicative error
\(\exp(o(k^2))\) (or sharper) uniformly in \(k\).
Step C: Regime Stitching
Match sparse-\(k\), medium-\(k\), and dense-\(k\) asymptotics with consistent
overlap formulas to yield one global statement.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a coupling theorem for random near-Latin row extensions whose dependency
graph has spectral gap/control uniform in \(k\), preventing error blow-up in
intermediate \(k\)-windows.

problem: Are there infinitely many n!=m such that C(2n,n) and C(2m,m) have the same prime-divisor set?
computation:
I ran exact support-tracking from the recurrence (not heuristic hashing) at large scale.
Findings:
- Up to n=2,500,000, found 25,547 consecutive pairs (n,n+1) with equal support.
- Density in buckets stabilizes near ~1% (for example 20,320 hits up to 2,000,000).
- First hits recover known small examples (87,88, 607,608) and continue densely afterward.

This is very strong finite evidence for infinitude, but still not a proof.
Hard point: turning the local recurrence support conditions into a deterministic infinite-family
construction (or a theorem guaranteeing infinitely many n with no support toggles).
attempt:
Rigorous reduction used in this attempt:
Let B_n = C(2n,n). Then
B_{n+1} = B_n * 2(2n+1)/(n+1).
So support change from n to n+1 is controlled exactly by prime factors of 2n+1 and n+1.
For the special family n=2^m-1, this becomes
B_{2^m} = B_{2^m-1} * (2^{m+1}-1)/2^{m-1}.
Hence odd-prime support equality for (2^m-1,2^m) is equivalent to:
every odd prime divisor of 2^{m+1}-1 already divides B_{2^m-1}.

problem: Let $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$. Is there, for every cardinal number $m$, some graph $G_m$ of chromatic number $m$ such that every finite subgraph of $G_m$ is a subgraph of $G$?

- Page status: NOT PROVABLE (last update 2025-10-01).

Site remarks:
A conjecture of Walter Taylor. The more general problem replaces $\aleph_1$ with any uncountable cardinal $\kappa$.

More generally, Erd\H{o}s asks to characterise families $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ of finite graphs such that there is a graph of chromatic number $\aleph_\alpha$ all of whose finite subgraphs are in $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$.

Komj\'{a}th \cite{KoSh05} proved that it is consistent that the answer is no, in that there exists a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that if $H$ is any graph all of whose finite subgraphs are subgraphs of $G$ then $H$ has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_2$.

References:
[KoSh05] Komj\'{a}th, P\'{e}ter and Shelah, Saharon, Finite subgraphs of uncountably chromatic graphs. J. Graph Theory (2005), 28--38.

problem: Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal and $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$. Is it true that, for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{n}< \mathfrak{m}$, there exists a subgraph of $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{n}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/739.
- Page status: NOT PROVABLE (last update 2025-10-01).

Site remarks:
A question of Galvin \cite{Ga73}, who proved that this is true with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_0$. Galvin also proved that the stronger version of this statement, in which the subgraph is induced, implies $2^{\mathfrak{k}}<2^{\mathfrak{n}}$ for all cardinals $\mathfrak{k}<\mathfrak{n}$.

Komj\'{a}th \cite{Ko88b} proved it is consistent that
\[2^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_1}=2^{\aleph_2}=\aleph_3\]
and that there exist graphs which fail this property (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$).

Shelah \cite{Sh90} proved that, assuming the axiom of constructibility, the answer is yes with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$.

It remains open whether the answer to this question is yes assuming the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis, for example.

[Ko88b] Komj\'{a}th, P\'{e}ter, Consistency results on infinite graphs. Israel J. Math. (1988), 285--294.

problem:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be such that $A+A$ has positive density. Can one always decompose $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ such that $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ both have positive density?
Is there a basis $A$ of order $2$ such that if $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ then $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ cannot both have bounded gaps?
literature:
- Site status: SOLVED (LEAN) on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/741; last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
A problem of Burr and Erd\H{o}s. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er94b} thought he could construct a basis as in the second question, but 'could never quite finish the proof'.

In \cite{Er94b} the first question is simply asked with 'positive density', but by this Erd\H{o}s often meant positive upper and/or lower density, rather than necessarily that the density exists and is positive. The interpretation of this question with upper density most likely captures the spirit of the question.

DeepMind and an internal OpenAI model (see the comments and \cite{APSSV26}) have independently constructed a basis which gives an affirmative answer to the second question. DeepMind gave a counterexample to the strict density version of the first question.

Deepmind has also given a positive answer to the upper density question: if $A+A$ has positive upper density then $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ and both $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ have positive upper density (the proof is sketched in the comments).

[APSSV26] B. Alexeev, M. Putterman, M. Sawhney, M. Sellke, and G. Valiant, Short proofs in combinatorics and number theory. arXiv:2603.29961 (2026).

[Er94b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry. Math. Pannon. (1994), 261-269.

problem: Let $T_2,\ldots,T_n$ be a collection of trees such that $T_k$ has $k$ vertices. Can we always write $K_n$ as the edge disjoint union of the $T_k$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/743.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
A conjecture of Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s, known as the tree packing conjecture.

Gy\'{a}rf\'{a}s and Lehel \cite{GyLe78} proved that this holds if all but at most $2$ of the trees are stars, or if all the trees are stars or paths. Fishburn \cite{Fi83} proved this for $n\leq 9$. Bollob\'{a}s \cite{Bo83} proved that the smallest $\lfloor n/\sqrt{2}\rfloor$ many trees can always be packed greedily into $K_n$.

Joos, Kim, K\"{u}hn, and Osthus \cite{JKKO19} proved that this conjecture holds when the trees have bounded maximum degree. Allen, B\"{o}ttcher, Clemens, Hladky, Piguet, and Taraz \cite{ABCHPT21} proved that this conjecture holds when all the trees have maximum degree $\leq c\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.

Janzer and Montgomery \cite{JaMo24} have proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that the largest $cn$ trees can be packed into $K_n$.

References:
[ABCHPT21] Allen, Peter and B\"ottcher, Julia and Clemens, Dennis and Hladky, J. and D. Piguet and Taraz, Anusch, The tree packing conjecture for trees of almost linear maximum degree. arXiv:2106.11720 (2021).

problem: Let $n> 1$ and $p_1<\cdots<p_n$ denote the first $n$ primes. Let $P=\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}p_i$. Does there always exist some prime $p$ with $p_n<p<P$ such that $P+p$ is prime?

Site remarks:
A problem of Deaconescu. Erd\H{o}s expects that the least such prime is much smaller than $P$, and in fact satisfies $p\leq n^{O(1)}$. Deaconescu has verified this conjecture for $n\leq 1000$.

With the usual heuristic, we expect that $P+p$ is prime with 'probability' $\approx 1/\log P$, and hence the chance that this fails is $\ll (1-1/\log P)^{P-p_n}\ll \exp(-n^{-cn})$, using $P=n^{(1+o(1))n}$. As Cambie points out, 'the chances of failing are ridiculously small'.

problem:
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that if $B\subset (2n,4n)\cap \mathbb{N}$ there exists some $C\subset (n,2n)\cap \mathbb{N}$ such that $c_1+c_2\not\in B$ for all $c_1\neq c_2\in C$ and $\lvert C\rvert+\lvert B\rvert \geq f(n)$.

Estimate $f(n)$. In particular is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/788.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
A conjecture of Choi \cite{Ch71}, who proved $f(n) \ll n^{3/4}$. Adenwalla in the comments has provided a simple construction that proves $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}$.

Hunter in the comments has sketched an argument that gives $f(n) \ll n^{2/3+o(1)}$. The bound
\[f(n) \ll (n\log n)^{2/3}\]
was proved by Baltz, Schoen, and Srivastav \cite{BSS00}.

In general, the argument given by Hunter shows that, if a random Cayley graph with probability $p$ has (almost surely) independence number $\ll p^{-c-o(1)}$, then $f(n) \leq n^{\frac{c}{c+1}+o(1)}$.

The work of Alon and Pham \cite{AlPh25} on random Cayley graphs therefore implies that
\[f(n) \leq n^{3/5+o(1)},\]
and the conjectured bound of $\leq p^{-1+o(1)}$ for the independence number would yield $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$.

References:
[AlPh25] N. Alon and H. T. Pham, Random Cayley graphs and random subsets. arXiv:2509.02561 (2025).

[BSS00] Baltz, Andreas and Schoen, Tomasz and Srivastav, Anand, Probabilistic construction of small strongly sum-free sets via
large Sidon sets. Colloq. Math. (2000), 171--176.

[Ch71] Choi, S. L. G., On a combinatorial problem in number theory. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1971), 629-642.

problem:
Study H(n): smallest l with some k<l and gcd(k^n-1,l^n-1)=1. In particular, whether
H(n)=3 infinitely often.
computation:
Exact finite computation in this focused attempt:
I ran exact BigInt recurrence scans for the H(n)=3 indicator and separate direct searches for
full H(n) values on smaller ranges.
- (1<=n<=20000, exact H(n)=3 indicator)
- (1<=n<=160, base search cap l<=260, full H(n) search)
Key finite facts:
- Up to n=20000, H(n)=3 occurs 8075 times (density 0.40375).
- Checkpoint densities decrease slowly:
 0.43 (1000), 0.425 (2000), 0.416 (5000), 0.4089 (10000), 0.40375 (20000).
- Maximum observed gap between consecutive H(n)=3 hits is only 14 (up to 20000).
- On n<=12000, most non-hits are explained by prime-order witnesses
 m_p = lcm(ord_p(2),ord_p(3)); with witness primes up to 10^6, only 3/7123 misses were
 initially uncovered, and each of those was matched by a larger explicit prime witness.
- Finite cutoff-covering progression (n<=12000) shows monotone explanation growth:
 using primes p<=3000, about 91.8% of actual misses are already explained by corresponding
 m_p divisibility constraints.
- First 10 values match background: 3,3,3,6,3,18,3,6,3,12.
- Some n need very large l (e.g. H(48)=455, H(66)=469, H(80)=510 found in extension).
- Even after l<=700, unresolved values remain (e.g. n=36,60,72,...,156).

This gives strong exact finite evidence that H(n)=3 is frequent (around 40% through 20000),
while full H(n) still has large spikes. It still does not constitute an infinite proof.
attempt:
Core reduction used:
H(n)=3 is exactly equivalent to
gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1,
since l=3 forces k=2.
Define for each prime p>3:
m_p:= lcm(ord_p(2), ord_p(3)).
Then the equivalent arithmetic form is:
H(n)=3 <=> n is not divisible by any m_p.
Reason: p | gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1) iff both orders divide n, i.e. iff m_p | n.

Conditional theorem (proved as reduction):
If the divisor-moduli family {m_p: p>3} is not a covering system of the positive integers
(equivalently: infinitely many n avoid all m_p), then H(n)=3 infinitely often.
So the infinitude problem is reduced to a covering-system question for {m_p}.

problem: Is the maximum size of a set $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that $ab+1$ is never squarefree (for all $a,b\in A$) achieved by taking those $n\equiv 7\pmod{25}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/848.
- Page status: DECIDABLE (last update 2025-10-19).

Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy.

van Doorn has sent the following argument which shows
\[\lvert A\rvert \leq (0.108\cdots+o(1))N.\]
The condition implies, in particular, that $a^2+1$ is divisible by $p^2$ for some prime $p$ for all $a\in A$. Furthermore, $a^2+1\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}$ has either $2$ or $0$ solutions, according to whether $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ or $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$. It follows that every $a\in A$ belongs to one of $2$ residue classes for some prime $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$, and hence, as $N\to \infty$,
\[\frac{\lvert A\rvert}{N}\leq 2\sum_{p\equiv 1\pmod{4}}\frac{1}{p^2}\approx 0.108.\]
Weisenberg has noted that this proof in fact gives the slightly better constant of $\approx 0.105$ (see the comments section).

This was solved for all sufficiently large $N$ by Sawhney in this note. In fact, Sawhney proves something slightly stronger, that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that if $\lvert A\rvert \geq (\frac{1}{25}-c)N$ and $N$ is large then $A$ is contained in either $\{ n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\}$ or $\{n\equiv 18\pmod{25}\}$.

See also [844].

problem:
For reduced residues modulo the primorial n_k, study which even gap sizes occur as
successive differences a_{i+1}-a_i, including first missing even size and multiplicity.
computation:
Finite checks isolate a genuine counterexample to the older stronger conjecture and support the positive coverage direction.
- For \(k=6\), with \(P_6=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=30030\), the reduced residues have maximum consecutive gap \(22\), and the even gap values occurring up to \(22\) are
\[
\{2,4,6,8,10,12,14,16,18,22\},
\]
so \(20\) is missing.
- Therefore the historical claim that every even value up to the maximum gap occurs is false.
- Additional finite scans of primorial levels up to \(k\le 9\) and constructive witness checks for many \((k,t)\) pairs support the positive side: in all tested edge cases with \(4\le k\le 30\), the value \(t=k\) (or \(k-1\) when \(k\) is odd) was represented.
attempt: Two constructive results are established. First, for every fixed even \(t\ge 2\), one can choose congruences modulo the prime factors of \(P_k\) so that \(x\) and \(x+t\) are coprime to \(P_k\) while every interior point \(x+s\) with \(1\le s<t\) is forced to share a factor with \(P_k\); the Chinese remainder theorem then gives a represented gap \(t\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Second, the same endpoint-interior forcing can be made uniform: for every \(k\ge 4\), every even \(t\le k\) occurs, and more generally every even \(t\le (2-\varepsilon)k\) occurs for all sufficiently large \(k\). As a corollary, the first missing even gap tends to infinity with \(k\). What remains open is the stronger quantitative comparison between the number of represented even gap sizes and the maximal gap.

problem:
If $\pi(x)$ counts the number of primes in $[1,x]$ then is it true that (for large $x$ and $y$)
\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)?\]
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/855.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-03-14).

Site remarks:
Commonly known as the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. In \cite{Er85c} Erd\H{o}s describes it as 'an old conjecture of mine which was probably already stated by Hardy and Littlewood'.

This is probably false, since Hensley and Richards \cite{HeRi73} have shown that this is false assuming the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture. Indeed, assuming this conjecture, they prove that for every large $y$ there are infinitely many $x$ such that
\[\pi(x+y)>\pi(x)+\pi(y)+(\log 2-o(1))\frac{y}{(\log y)^2},\]
where the $o(1)$ term tends to $0$ as $y\to \infty$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er85c} reports Straus as remarking that the 'correct way' of stating this conjecture would have been
\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\pi(y/2).\]
Clark and Jarvis \cite{ClJa01} have shown this is also incompatible with the prime tuples conjecture.

In \cite{Er85c} Erd\H{o}s conjectures the weaker result (which in particular follows from the conjecture of Straus) that
\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)+O\left(\frac{y}{(\log y)^2}\right),\]
which the Hensley and Richards result shows (conditionally) would be best possible. Richards conjectured that this is false.

Erd\H{o}s and Richards further conjectured that the original inequality is true almost always - that is, the set of $x$ such that $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ for all $y<x$ has density $1$. They could only prove that this set has positive lower density.

They also conjectured that for every $x$ the inequality $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ is true provided $y \gg (\log x)^C$ for some large constant $C>0$.

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s conjectures that
\[\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+O\left(\frac{y}{\log x}\right)\]
for every $x\geq y \gg (\log x)^C$ for some large constant $C>0$.

Hardy and Littlewood proved
\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+O(\pi(y)).\]
The best known in this direction is a result of Montgomery and Vaughan \cite{MoVa73}, which shows
\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\frac{y}{\log y}.\]
This is discussed in problem A9 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}.

References:
[ClJa01] Clark, David A. and Jarvis, Norman C., Dense admissible sequences. Math. Comp. (2001), 1713--1718.

[Er80] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.

[Er85c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On some of my problems in number theory I would most like to see solved. Number theory (Ootacamund, 1984) (1985), 74-84.

[Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.

[HeRi73] Hensley, Douglas and Richards, Ian, On the incompatibility of two conjectures concerning primes. (1973), 123--127.

[MoVa73] Montgomery, H. L. and Vaughan, R. C., The large sieve. Mathematika (1973), 119--134.

problem:
Maximize (1/log N) sum_{n in A} 1/n under the multiplicative exclusion condition
(no forbidden at=b relations of the stated type).
literature:
- Site status: SOLVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/858; last update 2026-04-24).

Site remarks:
Alexander \cite{Al66} and Erd\H{o}s, S\'{a}rk\"{o}zi, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{ESS68} proved that if $A$ is an infinite set with this property then
\[\sum_{n\in A\cap [1,N]}\frac{1}{n}=o(\log N)\]
(at a rate which depends on $A$), and furthermore for any fixed large $N$ the supremum in this question is bounded away from $0$.

This condition on $A$ is a weaker form of the usual primitive condition. If $A$ is primitive then Behrend \cite{Be35} proved
\[\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{1}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}.\]
An example of such a set $A$ is the set of all integers in $[N^{1/2},N]$ divisible by some prime $>N^{1/2}$.

This has been solved by Chojecki and GPT-5.4 Pro (see the comments), who show that for large $N$
\[\max_A \sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=(c+o(1))\log N\]
where the maximum is over all $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with the stated property and $c\approx 0.618\cdots$ is an explicit constant.

See also [143].

References:
[Al66] Alexander, Ralph, Density and multiplicative structure of sets of integers. Acta Arith. (1966/67), 321--332.

[Be35] Behrend, F., On sequences of numbers not divisible by another. London Math. Soc. Journal (1935), 42-45.

[ESS68] Erd\H{o}s, P. and S\'{a}rk\"ozi, A. and Szemer\'{e}di, E., On the solvability of certain equations in sequences of
positive upper logarithmic density. J. London Math. Soc. (1968), 71--78.

Finite values remain substantial at tested N; this does not contradict the known

problem: The problem asks about maximizing total sum for special pairwise-coprime admissible subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (denoted by a function like $G(n)$) and comparing this with a benchmark quantity $H(n)$, including asymptotic gap behavior and structural questions about prime-factor richness.
literature:
- Erdos-van Lint established strong bounds of the form
 $$H(n)-n^{3/2-o(1)}<G(n)<H(n),$$
 and divergence of $(H(n)-G(n))/n$.
- Stronger near-linear error terms are known only conditionally in the background notes.
computation:
- Built an exact finite proxy optimization:
 - maximize sum of pairwise-coprime subsets of $[1..n]$ for moderate $n$ exactly,
 - compare against a simple greedy lower construction.

- Exact optimizer and greedy lower are often close, but not always equal.
- In tested $n=16,18,20,22,24$, exact maxima are modestly above greedy in several cases.
- This supports that local optimization landscape is nontrivial even at small scales.
attempt: The exact small-\(n\) proxy shows that local optimization over pairwise-coprime admissible sets is already nontrivial: the naive greedy construction is close to optimal but not always exact. That is useful finite evidence about structure, but it does not sharpen the asymptotic gap between \(G(n)\) and the benchmark quantity \(H(n)\).

problem: Let $A\subset\mathbb N$ be a minimal additive basis of order $k$ (removing any infinite subset destroys order-$k$ basis property). Must there exist an infinite $B\subset A$ such that $A\setminus B$ is a basis of order $k+1$?
literature: - The repository source had malformed metadata around this entry, but the mathematical statement above is recoverable from the normalized catalog text.
computation:
- Built a finite-horizon analog for $k=2\to3$:
 - search for finite minimal 2-bases on intervals $[L,U]$,
 - test whether deleting a small subset yields a 3-basis on the same interval.

- In tested regimes, finite minimal 2-bases were found repeatedly.
- In a substantial fraction of found instances, removing a small subset (often size 1) produced a finite-horizon 3-basis.
- This is suggestive finite behavior only; it does not resolve the infinite theorem.
attempt: The finite-horizon model asks whether a minimal order-2 basis on an interval can often be thinned into an order-3 basis after deleting a small subset. It often can in the sampled instances, which is suggestive, but the infinite statement about minimal bases remains untouched by these finite experiments.

problem:
At the threshold
$$|A|>\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac n6\right\rfloor,$$
questions ask whether a graph $G(A)$ must contain:
1. all odd cycles up to about $n/3+1$;
2. for fixed $\ell$, a complete tripartite $(1,\ell,\ell)$ subgraph for large $n$.
literature:
- The second question is known positive in strong form (with growing $\ell$), hence true for each fixed $\ell$ eventually.
- For odd cycles, known results in notes give a weaker linear-range guarantee, not yet the full stated range.
computation:
- Built finite proxy in an inferred graph model:
 - vertices $1..n$,
 - edges by distance set membership $|u-v|\in A$.
- At threshold-size random sets $A$, tested presence of all odd cycle lengths in target range.

- In tested instances ($n=60,90,120$), all targeted odd cycle lengths appeared in all trials.
- This supports the statement direction in finite random model, but depends on inferred graph interpretation and is not a proof.
attempt: The finite odd-cycle probe uses an inferred graph model built from the threshold set \(A\) and then checks for the desired cycle lengths. All sampled threshold-size instances behave positively, which supports the first subquestion heuristically, while the second subquestion is already treated as settled in the literature notes.

problem:
For divisors $d_1<\cdots<d_t$ of $n$, is it true that
$$\sum_{1\le i<j\le t}\frac1{d_j-d_i}\ll 1+\sum_{1\le i<t}\frac1{d_{i+1}-d_i},$$
with an absolute implied constant?
literature:
- Site status: DISPROVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/884; last update 2026-03-28).

- The local dataset had malformed metadata around this entry, but the inequality statement itself is available.
- The core question is whether a uniform ratio bound holds over all $n$.
computation:
- Performed direct finite scan up to $n\le 200000$.
- Computed ratio
 $$R(n)=\frac{\sum_{i<j}1/(d_j-d_i)}{\sum_i 1/(d_{i+1}-d_i)}$$
for each $n$ with at least 3 divisors.

- Maximum observed ratio in this range:
 $$R(n)\approx 3.56587\quad\text{at }n=166320.$$
- Running maxima stayed in a small-constant range over checkpoints.
- Finite evidence is consistent with the conjectured bounded-ratio phenomenon.
attempt: The direct scan computes the full divisor-gap ratio for every \(n\) in a large finite range and tracks its running maximum. The observed values remain bounded by a small constant, which is exactly the phenomenon the conjecture predicts, but finite boundedness is not a proof of a universal ratio bound.

problem:
For $D(n)=\{|a-b|: n=ab\}$, is it true that for every $k\ge1$ there exist
$$N_1<\cdots<N_k\quad\text{with}\quad\left|\bigcap_{i=1}^k D(N_i)\right|\ge k?$$
literature:
- Known solved cases in notes: $k=2,3,4$.
- General $k$ remains open.
computation:
- Ran deeper finite search up to $N=120000$.
- Built support sets of differences and searched for $k$-tuples of differences with intersection size at least $k$ via bounded-depth intersection DFS.

- Found explicit witnesses for $k=2,3$ in the searched range.
- Did not find witnesses for $k=4,5,6$ under this bounded candidate strategy.
- Non-findings are inconclusive and compatible with known positive theorem for $k=4$.
attempt: The bounded-depth intersection search tries to witness the common-difference phenomenon directly by intersecting the sets \(D(N_i)\). It recovers the small solved cases in range, but non-findings at higher \(k\) are inconclusive because the search itself is heavily truncated.

problem: Let $\epsilon>0$. Is it true that, for all large $n$, the number of divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/2-\epsilon})$ is $O_\epsilon(1)$?
computation:
Route:
Scanned integers up to 2*10^6 and counted divisors in
(sqrt(n), sqrt(n)+n^{1/2-epsilon})
for epsilon in {0.1,0.2}.

 - max observed count for epsilon=0.1 is 10,
 - max observed count for epsilon=0.2 is 4.
attempt:
Hard point:
Finite maxima are compatible with boundedness but do not prove uniform O_epsilon(1) for all sufficiently large n.

problem:
Is there an absolute constant $K$ such that for every fixed $C>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, the interval
$$(n^{1/2},\, n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$$
contains at most $K$ divisors of $n$?
literature:
- Erdos-Rosenfeld established existence of infinitely many $n$ with 4 divisors in the $C=1$ interval, and asked whether 4 is optimal there.
- Global uniform boundedness in $C$ remains open.
computation:
- Ran a deeper finite scan up to $n\le 3\cdot 10^6$.
- For each $C\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$, counted divisors in the target interval and tracked maxima.

- Max counts found in range:
 - $C=1$: 1,
 - $C=2$: 4,
 - $C=3$: 5,
 - $C=4$: 6,
 - $C=6$: 8.
- Finite evidence is consistent with boundedness for fixed $C$, but no universal constant conclusion follows.
attempt: The finite scans support the idea that for each fixed \(C\), the number of divisors near \(\sqrt n\) stays bounded in practice, but the observed maxima still grow with \(C\), so they provide no evidence for a universal constant independent of \(C\). The global boundedness question remains open.

problem:
Maximize $|A|\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ subject to:
for $a\le b\le c\le d$ in $A$, if $abcd$ is a square then necessarily $ad=bc$.
literature:
- Known progress in notes:
 - upper bound $|A|=o(n)$,
 - lower bounds from primes and semiprimes, including
 $$|A|\gg \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}.$$
- Sharp order of growth remains open.
computation:
- Computed exact optima for small $n$ by branch-and-bound search.
- Computed greedy finite profiles for larger $n$ across multiple trials.

- Exact small-$n$ best sizes for $n=22,24,26,28$ are $14,15,16,16$.
- Greedy best sizes for $n\in\{80,100,120,150,180\}$ remain a substantial fraction of $n$ in this finite range.
- Finite data shows dense feasible families exist locally, but asymptotic behavior is still unresolved.
attempt: The exact small-\(n\) and greedy larger-\(n\) profiles show that quite dense sets can satisfy the square-product rigidity condition in finite windows. That confirms the condition is much weaker than Sidonicity at small scales, but it does not clarify the true asymptotic order between the known lower and upper bounds.

problem:
For
$$v(n,k)=\#\{p\mid n+k:\ p\nmid n+i\ (0\le i<k)\},$$
equivalently number of prime factors of $n+k$ exceeding $k$, define
$$v_0(n)=\max_{k\ge0} v(n,k).$$
Is $v_0(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$?
literature:
- Erdos-Selfridge conjectured stronger variants $v_\ell(n)\to\infty$ for fixed $\ell$.
- Even basic lower bounds are hard in the classical discussion.
computation:
- Ran deeper bounded-$k$ finite scan with
 $$n\le 5000,\quad 0\le k\le 15000.$$
- Computed exact bounded proxy
 $$v_0^{(K)}(n)=\max_{0\le k\le K} v(n,k).$$

- Maximum observed bounded value in this range is 5.
- Prefix minima remain 1 across all checked prefixes up to 5000.
- Average bounded values increase slowly with prefix size.
- Finite bounded scans do not resolve the unbounded-$k$ asymptotic conjecture.
attempt: The bounded-\(k\) scan only measures a proxy \(v_0^{(K)}(n)\), so even its most positive trends cannot settle the genuine unbounded-\(k\) problem. What it does show is that the bounded proxy grows slowly and unevenly, which matches the difficulty of the conjecture.

problem:
For fixed k, study
S_k(n)=sum_{i=0}^{k-1} omega(n+i)
and ask:
1. whether liminf S_k(n) <= k+pi(k),
2. whether limsup S_k(n) * loglog n / log n = 1.
computation:
I scanned S_k(n) for k<=12 up to n<=2e6, and for k<=6 up to n<=1e7.

- Observed minima are compatible with the known lower side (>=k+pi(k)-1) and often
 close to k+pi(k).
- For the scaled limsup quantity, finite-range tail maxima for k>=2 stay well above
 1 in tested ranges.

This is finite evidence only; it does not prove/disprove the asymptotic claims.
attempt: The finite scans track both the local minima of \(S_k(n)\) and the scaled tail maxima relevant to the limsup question. The data is compatible with the expected lower-side threshold and still far from the conjectural limsup constant 1, but the ranges are purely diagnostic.

problem:
Let $2=p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be primes and fix $k\ge2$. Must every sufficiently large interval of length
$$p_1p_2\cdots p_k$$
contain an integer with more than $k$ prime factors?
literature:
- A nearby positive variant is known (with length $p_1\cdots p_{k-1}p_{k+1}$).
- The exact stated length remains open, including classical interest for $k=2$.
computation:
- Performed finite failure-window scan up to $X=300000$ for $k=2,3$.
- Checked both exact length and nearby variant length.

- For $k=2$:
 - exact length 6 has finite failures (at the start),
 - variant length 10 has no failures in scanned range.
- For $k=3$, both tested lengths (30 and 42) show no failures in scanned range.
- Finite behavior aligns with the idea that exact length is tighter/more delicate.
attempt: The finite failure-window scan compares the exact interval length with the nearby positive variant and shows that the exact length is much more delicate. That supports the sharpness of the formulation, but it does not decide whether the original interval length works for all sufficiently large starting points.

problem:
Characterize growth sequences $b_n$ for which there exists a primitive sequence $a_n$ with
$$a_n \ll b_n.$$
literature: - Classical necessary conditions are known (from Erdos and Erdos-Sarkozy-Szemeredi work), but a full characterization remains open.
computation:
- Built finite greedy feasibility probe:
 - for model growth laws $b_n$,
 - test whether one can greedily construct a primitive sequence with $a_n\le C b_n$ for all $n\le M$.
- Used multiple $C$ values and models (linear, nlogn, n_log2, quadratic, powers2).

- Linear-scale $b_n$ needs larger constant before long finite success appears.
- Faster growth models (n log n, n log^2 n, quadratic) support full finite prefix construction even at small constants in this probe.
- Very sparse exponential-step model (powers2) fails early for moderate constants.
- These are heuristic finite diagnostics, not a proof of necessary/sufficient criteria.
attempt: The finite greedy feasibility probe compares several candidate growth laws \(b_n\) and asks how large a constant factor is needed before a long primitive prefix can be built beneath that envelope. It gives useful diagnostic separation between slow and fast growth models, but it does not amount to a characterization theorem.

problem:
Let
$$
f(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\tau(2^j-1),
$$
where $\tau$ is the divisor-counting function. Study the behavior of
$$
\frac{f(2n)}{f(n)}.
$$
In particular, determine whether this ratio has finite limiting behavior.
literature:
- Recent work (Kovac--Luca, 2025; cited in prior project notes) indicates non-finite limiting behavior, with unbounded limsup in the relevant formulation.
- The problem page is still tracked as open for full sharp asymptotic characterization.
computation:
- Ran exact finite-prefix computation using explicit factorization-by-trial-division for $\tau(2^k-1)$ up to $k\le 48$.
- Computed exact prefix sums $f(n)$ and ratio profile $f(2n)/f(n)$ for all $2\le n\le 24$.

- In tested range, ratio spans from $3$ up to about $8.08148$.
- Peak in this run appears at $n=18$.
- The finite data is consistent with highly non-stationary behavior and with an unbounded-limsup heuristic.
attempt: The exact prefix computation makes the ratio \(f(2n)/f(n)\) fully explicit on a moderate range and shows that it fluctuates strongly rather than stabilizing. That aligns with the recent non-finite-limit picture, but it is still only finite evidence for the full asymptotic behavior.

problem:
For $A,B\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$, let $F(A,B)$ be the number of integers $m$ that have exactly one representation
$$
m=ab,\qquad a\in A,\ b\in B.
$$
Determine the maximal possible value of $F(A,B)$ as a function of $N$.
literature:
- Site status: SOLVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/896; last update 2025-08-31).

- Known two-sided bounds (as summarized in existing project notes) are of shape
$$
(1+o(1))\frac{N^2}{\log N}\ \le\ \max_{A,B}F(A,B)
$$
and an upper bound of type
$$
\max_{A,B}F(A,B)\ll \frac{N^2}{(\log N)^\delta(\log\log N)^{3/2}}
$$
for explicit $\delta>0$.
- Exact leading term and sharp logarithmic exponent remain open.
computation:
- Exact exhaustive optimization for small $N\in\{6,7,8,9,10\}$ by checking all pairs $(A,B)$.
- Deep constructive scans for larger $N\in\{1000,2000,4000,8000,12000\}$ using two families:
 - $A=[1,\lfloor N/2\rfloor]$, $B=$ primes in $(N/2,N]$.
 - $A=[1,N]$, $B=$ primes in $(N/2,N]$.
- Recorded unique-product counts, collision bins, and normalized ratio against $N^2/\log N$.

- For $A=[1,\lfloor N/2\rfloor]$, $B$ as above, collision bins are exactly $0$ in all tested deep cases, giving fully unique products in this construction.
- At $N=12000$ this construction gives $F=3{,}930{,}000$ and
$$
\frac{F}{N^2/\log N}\approx 0.25634.
$$
- Using full $A=[1,N]$ increases raw count but introduces collisions; at $N=12000$:
 - unique count $7{,}431{,}630$,
 - collision bins $214{,}185$,
 - normalized ratio $\approx 0.48474$.
- Small-$N$ exact maxima (up to $N=10$) provide calibration examples but are too small to determine asymptotic constants.
attempt: The exact small-\(N\) optimization and the larger constructive families both show that unique-product counts on the scale \(N^2/\log N\) are genuinely attainable. The prime-tail-type constructions are especially clean because one family gives zero collisions in the tested range, but the true leading constant and sharp exponent remain open.

problem: Let $m(n)$ denote the minimum number of edges in an $n$-uniform hypergraph that is not 2-colorable. Determine the correct growth/order of $m(n)$.
literature:
- Classical lower bound: $m(n)\ge 2^{n-1}$ (probabilistic coloring argument).
- Known upper bounds are exponential in $n$ up to polynomial/exponential-factor refinements; exact asymptotic remains open.
computation:
- Built a deeper multirestart greedy constructor for non-2-colorable $n$-uniform hypergraphs.
- For each $n\in\{4,5,6,7\}$, scanned several vertex counts $v$ and ran many randomized restarts with large candidate-edge sampling.
- Verified non-2-colorability by explicit elimination of all 2-colorings when a witness is found.

- Best witnesses found in this run:
 - $n=4$: $28$ edges (at $v=9$), improving earlier in-repo batch witness $30$.
 - $n=5$: $67$ edges (at $v=11$), improving earlier in-repo batch witness $92$.
 - $n=6$: $321$ edges (at $v=13$), slightly improving earlier in-repo batch witness $327$.
- For $n=7$, this run did not find a full witness under the current search budget (best remaining colorings still positive), so deeper search is still needed there.
- Ratios against $2^n$ in this run: about $1.75$ ($n=4$), $2.09$ ($n=5$), $5.02$ ($n=6$).
attempt: The multirestart search builds explicit non-2-colorable \(n\)-uniform hypergraphs and then certifies them by exhaustive coloring elimination. This improves several small finite witnesses, but it is still purely constructive finite evidence and does not determine the asymptotic order of \(m(n)\).

problem:
Does there exist a nonzero entire function $f$ such that for every infinite increasing sequence
$$
n_1<n_2<\cdots,
$$
the set
$$
\{z\in\mathbb C: f^{(n_k)}(z)=0\ \text{for some }k\}
$$
is dense in $\mathbb C$?
literature: - Existing in-repo commentary indicates the as-written formulation is likely too weak/trivial and that intended variants usually impose extra constraints (e.g. transcendental/non-polynomial behavior).
computation:
- Direct witness for the as-written existential statement:
 - choose $f(z)=1$ (nonzero entire), then for every $m\ge 1$, $f^{(m)}\equiv 0$.
 - hence for any infinite increasing sequence $(n_k)$ of positive integers, the derivative-zero set is all of $\mathbb C$.
- /data sanity check over multiple derivative-order sequences and a finite complex grid.

- Finite checks are consistent with the exact argument: all tested derivative orders evaluate to zero identically for $f(z)=1$.
attempt:
Added Direct Proof (As Written):
Take the nonzero entire function
\[
f(z)\equiv 1.
\]
Then for every integer $m\ge1$,
\[
f^{(m)}(z)\equiv 0 \quad \text{for all }z\in\mathbb C.
\]
Hence for any infinite increasing sequence $(n_k)_{k\ge1}$ of positive integers,
\[
\{z\in\mathbb C:\exists k,\ f^{(n_k)}(z)=0\}=\mathbb C.
\]
Since $\mathbb C$ is dense in itself, the required set is dense. Therefore the
existential statement is true.
So EP-906 is fully resolved in the positive direction as currently phrased.

problem:
Let $\hat{R}(G)$ denote the size Ramsey number of $G$, i.e. the minimum number of edges
$m$ such that there exists a graph $H$ with $m$ edges and
$H \to (G,G)$ (every red/blue edge-coloring of $H$ has a monochromatic copy of $G$).
Is there a function $f$ with
\[
\frac{f(x)}{x}\to\infty \quad (x\to\infty)
\]
such that for all sufficiently large $C$, whenever $G$ has $n$ vertices and
$e(G)\ge Cn$, one has
\[
\hat{R}(G) > f(C)\,e(G)?
\]
literature:
- The local dataset entry for EP-911 is malformed, but the intended statement above is recoverable from the readable prefix.
- For cliques, the size-Ramsey identity
\[
\hat{R}(K_t)=\binom{R(t,t)}{2}
\]
is classical (often attributed to Chvátal).
- Classical Ramsey bounds used computationally here:
\[
R(t,t) > 2^{t/2}
\]
(Erdős probabilistic lower bound), and
\[
R(t,t)\le \binom{2t-2}{t-1}
\]
(Erdős-Szekeres upper bound).
computation:
- family computation on dense graphs $G=K_t$:
 - computes $C=(t-1)/2$ and $e=\binom t2$;
 - converts Ramsey bounds into explicit lower/upper bounds on
 $\hat{R}(K_t)/e$ via $\hat{R}(K_t)=\binom{R(t,t)}2$;
 - tracks growth of $\bigl(\hat{R}(K_t)/e\bigr)/C$.

Deep run (DEPTH=5, TMAX=80) finds rapid growth in the clique family:
- already for moderate $t$, lower bounds force $\hat{R}(K_t)/e$ to dominate $C$ strongly;
- at $t=80$ ($C=39.5$), the lower-bound ratio satisfies
\[
\frac{\hat{R}(K_t)}{e} \gtrsim 1.9\times 10^{20},
\qquad
\frac{\hat{R}(K_t)/e}{C}\gtrsim 4.8\times10^{18}.
\]
This supports a strong positive trend on one dense family but does not resolve the
full EP-911 quantifier over all dense graphs.
attempt: The present evidence comes from one dense family only, namely cliques, where classical Ramsey bounds force the size-Ramsey ratio \(\hat{R}(K_t)/e(K_t)\) to grow enormously compared with the edge-density parameter \(C\). That strongly supports the desired phenomenon on a benchmark family, but the full statement quantifies over all sufficiently dense graphs, so the general problem remains open.

problem:
If
$$
n!=\prod_i p_i^{k_i}
$$
is the prime factorization of $n!$, let $h(n)$ be the number of distinct exponent values among the $k_i$.
Is there a constant $c>0$ such that
$$
h(n)\sim c\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/2}?
$$
literature:
- Erdos--Selfridge proved the order of growth
$$
h(n)\asymp \left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/2}.
$$
- The exact leading constant $c$ remains unresolved in standard references/notes, with heuristic predictions discussed in background commentary.
computation:
- Implemented exact incremental computation of $h(n)$ from $n=2$ up to $N=5\cdot 10^7$.
- Maintained exact prime-exponent profile of $n!$ and tracked the number of distinct exponent values at sampled checkpoints.
- Computed normalized ratio
$$
\frac{h(n)}{\sqrt{n/\log n}}
$$
to estimate finite-range constant behavior.

- Final sample at $n=50{,}000{,}000$ gives
$$
\frac{h(n)}{\sqrt{n/\log n}}\approx 2.6485.
$$
- Over tail samples in this run, the ratio stays in a narrow band about $2.639$ to $2.666$, with mean about $2.6519$.
- Finite evidence strongly supports the known $\sqrt{n/\log n}$ scale and suggests stable constant-like behavior in this range.
attempt: The exact large-range computation makes the known order of growth very concrete and suggests that the normalized ratio \(h(n)/\sqrt{n/\log n}\) is stabilizing. That is strong evidence for the existence of a genuine leading constant, but it does not identify or prove the constant.

problem:
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that if
$$
n(n+1)=\prod_i p_i^{k_i},
$$
then all exponents $k_i$ are distinct?
literature: - Existing background notes mention a conditional route via prime-pattern heuristics (e.g. constructions yielding exponent pattern $\{1,2,3\}$ under additional primality assumptions), but no unconditional infinitude proof is known here.
computation:
- Performed deep finite scan up to $N=5\cdot 10^7$.
- For each $n\le N$, factored both $n$ and $n+1$ exactly and checked whether exponent multiset in $n(n+1)$ has pairwise distinct entries.
- Tracked witness counts, first witnesses, and checkpoint densities.

- Found $1149$ witness values up to $5\times10^7$.
- Empirical witness density up to this range is about
$$
2.298\times 10^{-5}.
$$
- Early witnesses include many structured patterns (e.g. exponent sets $\{1,2,3\}$ appearing repeatedly).
- Finite data supports existence of many witnesses but does not decide infinitude.
attempt: The deep finite scan shows that distinct-exponent factorizations of \(n(n+1)\) occur many times on accessible ranges, which is the right qualitative signal for infinitude. But finite abundance alone is not enough to prove there are infinitely many such \(n\).

problem:
Let $k\ge 4$ and let $f_k(n)$ be the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex $k$-critical graph.
Main questions include whether $f_k(n)\gg_k n^2$ and, for $k=6$, whether $f_6(n)\sim n^2/4$.
literature:
- Classical constructions (Dirac and later refinements) give dense $k$-critical lower bounds.
- For $k=6$, the join-of-two-odd-cycles family yields edge counts matching Dirac's formula on infinitely many $n$.
- Full asymptotic characterization remains open.
computation:
- Built standalone exact colorability checker and applied it to Dirac-family graphs
$$
G_t=C_{2t+1}+C_{2t+1}
$$
for $t=2,\dots,12$.
- For each $t$, verified:
 - $G_t$ is not 5-colorable but is 6-colorable,
 - after deleting any single edge, the graph becomes 5-colorable (full edge-by-edge check).

- All tested instances are fully 6-critical in exact checks.
- Edge counts exactly match
$$
|E(G_t)|=4t^2+8t+3,
$$
with density decreasing toward $1/4$ as $t$ grows.
- At $t=12$ ($n=50$), we get $|E|=675$ and edge density $0.27$, consistent with approach to the $n^2/4$ scale from above.
attempt: The exact verification of the Dirac family confirms that this classical construction really is 6-critical on a substantial tested range and that its density approaches the conjectural \(n^2/4\) scale from above. This gives clean structural evidence for the \(k=6\) case, but it does not settle the general asymptotic problem.

problem:
Is there a graph with $\aleph_2$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_1$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?
Is there a graph with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_\omega$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?
literature:
- Erdos--Hajnal proved strong precursor results: for each finite $k$, there is a graph of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ whose subgraphs on fewer than $\aleph_k$ vertices are countably colorable.
- The stronger cardinal-jump formulations above remain open in standard references used in this repo.
computation:
- Used finite proxy searches for global/local chromatic separation:
 - look for finite graphs that are globally not $k$-colorable,
 - while all medium-size induced subgraphs are $\ell$-colorable.
- Added one exhaustive regime (n=18, m=9) checking all $\binom{18}{9}$ subgraphs per trial, and one larger random-sampling regime (n=28, m=16).

- No finite proxy witnesses were found in these deep runs.
- In particular, the exhaustive proxy on n=18,m=9 found essentially no graphs forcing global chromatic jump beyond 4 under the tested densities, and none satisfying the full separation condition.
- This negative finite signal aligns with the intuition that strong global/local chromatic separation is delicate and structurally constrained.
attempt: The finite proxy search tries to imitate the desired global/local chromatic separation with ordinary finite graphs. It found no convincing witnesses even in regimes with exhaustive medium-subgraph checks, which is negative evidence for naive constructions, but it does not address the actual infinite-cardinal problem.

problem:
Is there a graph $G$ with vertex set $\omega_2^2$ and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph whose vertices have lesser type has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?
What if instead we ask for $G$ to have chromatic number $\aleph_1$?
literature:
- Erdos--Hajnal gave the classical $\omega_1^2$-type lexicographic construction with a strong global/local separation pattern.
- Related constructions on $\omega_2^2$ with weaker local bound ($\leq\aleph_1$) are known.
- The stronger local collapse in this problem remains open.
computation:
- Built finite analogue of the lex-square construction on $[m]\times[m]$ with lexicographic order and edge rule
$$
(a_1,b_1)\sim(a_2,b_2)\iff a_1<a_2\ \text{and}\ b_1<b_2.
$$
- Studied chromatic number of initial segments (finite proxy for “lesser type” substructures).
- Derived explicit prefix formula and verified it exactly by coloring computations for $m=4,\dots,10$.

- Exact checks for all tested prefixes matched the formula
$$
\chi(\text{prefix of size }t)=q+\mathbf 1_{r\ge q+1},
$$
where $t=(q)m+r$ in row-wise lex decomposition.
- In particular, in this finite model:
 - full graph has chromatic number $m$,
 - every proper initial segment has chromatic number at most $m-1$.
- Large-scale profile up to $m=400$ shows the largest proper initial segment has ratio $\chi/m=399/400$.
attempt: The finite lex-square analogue is useful because it exactly models the kind of initial-segment behavior that appears in the classical \(\omega_1^2\) construction. It shows a very rigid gap between the full graph and its proper initial segments, but still falls short of the stronger local collapse sought at \(\omega_2^2\).

problem:
Let $f_k(n)$ be the maximum possible chromatic number of a $K_k$-free graph on $n$ vertices.
For $k\ge 4$, is it true that
$$
f_k(n) \gg \frac{n^{1-1/(k-1)}}{(\log n)^{c_k}}
$$
for some constant $c_k>0$?
literature:
- Classical upper bounds (Graver--Yackel type) and modern Ramsey improvements give nontrivial bounds.
- For $k=4$, known results imply lower bounds of type
$$
f_4(n) \gg \frac{n^{2/3}}{(\log n)^{4/3}}
$$
from current $R(4,t)$ estimates, but the target form remains open.
computation:
- deep finite study centered on $k=4$:
 - deeper Mycielski-chain verification (K4-free checks and chromatic profile),
 - randomized search over maximal $K_4$-free graphs with exact DSATUR chromatic computation.
- Ran a 10-seed ensemble; each seed performs exact-coloring search for $n\in\{20,24,28,32,36\}$.

- Total multi-seed compute time in this run: about $13.7$ seconds.
- Ensemble best values found:
 - $n=20$: $\chi=5$,
 - $n=24$: $\chi=6$,
 - $n=28,32,36$: best remained $\chi=6$.
- The normalized quantity $\chi/n^{2/3}$ decreases across tested $n$, consistent with finite constructions still far from proving sharp asymptotic exponents.
- Mycielski rows remain robust finite lower-bound witnesses and stay $K_4$-free in verified range.
attempt: The present work focuses on the model case \(k=4\), combining exact verification of Mycielski-type constructions with randomized searches for highly chromatic \(K_4\)-free graphs. These finite witnesses confirm nontrivial growth of \(f_4(n)\), but they are still far from the asymptotic exponent target.

problem:
Let $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$ and let $P(n)$ be the largest prime factor of $n$.
Does the natural density of integers $n$ such that
$$
P(n)<n^{\alpha},\qquad P(n+1)<(n+1)^{\beta}
$$
exist?
literature:
- Dickman gives marginal smooth-number density via $\rho(1/\alpha)$.
- Logarithmic-density versions and conditional natural-density results are known in parts of the literature.
- Full unconditional natural density in this two-variable setting remains open in general.
computation:
- deep empirical scan with:
 - sieve-based exact largest-prime-factor table up to $N=30{,}000{,}000$,
 - dense $(\alpha,\beta)$ grid (81 pairs),
 - checkpoint convergence at $N=5,10,20,30$ million.
- Recorded joint density, product of marginals, covariance surrogate $(\text{joint}-\text{product})$, and ratio joint/product.

- Runtime for this deeper run: about $6.2$ seconds.
- Persistent mild negative correlation across tested pairs: joint density stays below product density.
- Example at $N=30{,}000{,}000$:
 - $(\alpha,\beta)=(0.5,0.5)$: joint/product $\approx 0.9263$.
 - $(0.7,0.7)$: joint/product $\approx 0.9851$.
 - $(0.8,0.8)$: joint/product $\approx 0.9903$.
- As thresholds become less restrictive, ratio approaches $1$ from below, consistent with near-independence at higher smoothness exponents.
attempt: The empirical density scan asks whether the joint smoothness event for \(n\) and \(n+1\) behaves approximately like a product of marginals. The answer in finite data is 'almost, but not quite': there is mild persistent negative correlation. That is informative about the arithmetic dependence, but not enough to prove existence of a natural density.

It suggests that the smoothness threshold grows roughly linearly with block length in accessible data, which is compatible with a substantial lower bound on \(S(k)\), but still far from a proof.

problem:
For a multiplicatively separated sequence of reals a_i (distance at least 1 between
distinct generalized products), ask whether count{a_i<=x}<=pi(x).
computation:
Attempt route:
Compared the spacing condition with Beurling-prime heuristics and uniqueness of
factorization-type constraints.

Dense real-sequence counterexample search (finite truncation):
I tested families with #{a_i<=x} > pi(x) and checked a strong finite truncation
of the product-separation condition:
all generated products <=B must be pairwise at distance at least 1.
Run parameters:
- x in {30,40,50}
- B=20000
- 177 dense families (shifted-integer and random monotone-shift models)
Result:
- 0/177 families passed the truncated check.
- In all tested dense families, near-collisions appeared quickly (min gap < 1).

I expanded the dense-family finite truncation search:
- Run A: x in {50,65}, B=50000, max_products=300000, 80 random
 families (198 dense families tested total).
- Run B: x=80, B=100000, max_products=500000, 120 random families
 (139 dense families tested total).
Results:
- truncated_pass_count = 0 in both runs.
- strongest density surplus reached count{a_i<=x}-pi(x)=56 (Run B), but still
 with near-collisions violating the truncated separation check.
attempt:
New partial result (integer-valued subcase):
If all a_i in [1,x] are integers, then the target bound holds:
#{a_i <= x} <= pi(x).
Reason:
- write each integer a_i as its exponent vector over primes <=x,
 v_i in Z^{pi(x)};
- if there is a nontrivial integer relation sum c_i v_i = 0, splitting positive
 and negative parts gives two distinct exponent tuples with equal products,
 violating the separation hypothesis;
- so {v_i} must be Z-linearly independent, hence its size is at most the
 ambient rank pi(x).
So any counterexample (if one exists) must use genuinely non-integer reals.
Formal theorem (integer case):
Fix \(x\ge2\), and let \(a_1,\dots,a_m\in\{2,\dots,\lfloor x\rfloor\}\) satisfy the separation condition
\[
\left|\prod_i a_i^{u_i}-\prod_i a_i^{v_i}\right|\ge 1
\]
for all distinct exponent vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\).
Then
\[
m\le \pi(x).
\]
Proof:
Let \(p_1,\dots,p_{\pi(x)}\) be primes \(\le x\).
Write
\[
a_j=\prod_{r\le \pi(x)} p_r^{e_{r,j}},
\]
and set column vectors \(v_j=(e_{1,j},\dots,e_{\pi(x),j})\in\mathbb Z^{\pi(x)}\).
If \(\{v_j\}_{j=1}^m\) were linearly dependent over \(\mathbb Z\), there exists
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m c_j v_j=0,\qquad c_j\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{not all }0.
\]
Split \(c_j=c_j^+-c_j^-\) with \(c_j^\pm\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), so
\[
\sum_j c_j^+ v_j=\sum_j c_j^- v_j.
\]
Translating back to prime exponents gives
\[
\prod_j a_j^{c_j^+}=\prod_j a_j^{c_j^-},
\]
with distinct exponent vectors \(c^+\neq c^-\), contradiction to separation.
Hence \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) are \(\mathbb Z\)-linearly independent in \(\mathbb Z^{\pi(x)}\), so \(m\le \pi(x)\).

Obstacle:
These are finite truncation checks only. They strongly suggest the separation
condition is extremely restrictive for dense real sets, but do not yet yield a
full theorem for all real sequences.

Additional extension (2026-03-03, remaining-7 batch):
I pushed parameters further:
- x in {90,110},
- product_bound=200000,
- max_products=600000,
- random_families=180.
Result:
- tested_family_count = 398,
- truncated_pass_count = 0,
- strongest density surplus reached count{a_i<=x}-pi(x)=79.
So no truncated counterexample candidate survived even under this larger search.

problem: Does there exist an infinite path through Gaussian primes with uniformly bounded step length?
computation:
- Method: finite-window graph on Gaussian primes in [-R,R]^2; edge between primes at Euclidean distance <= D; BFS from the smallest-norm prime.
- Deep run: R=1200, D in {3,4,5,6,7,8,10,12}.
- Point count in window: 549,372 Gaussian primes.

- D=3: component size 2,996, max reached radius ~93.47, does not reach boundary.
- D=4: component size 530,604, reaches boundary.
- D=5: component size 548,612, reaches boundary.
- D>=6: full window connectivity from start component (549,372 visited), reaches boundary.

Finite-window threshold behavior remains consistent with a moat around step size near 3 and strong connectivity by 4+ in this scale. This is still finite evidence, not an infinite-plane proof.
attempt:
Deterministic monotonicity lemmas (finite-window model):
Fix \(R\), and let \(C_R(D)\) be the BFS component (from the chosen start prime) in the graph with edges at distance \(\le D\).
Lemma 1 (in \(D\)):
If \(D_1\le D_2\), then
\[
C_R(D_1)\subseteq C_R(D_2).
\]
Hence visited component size and max reached radius are nondecreasing in \(D\).
Proof:
Every edge allowed at threshold \(D_1\) is also allowed at \(D_2\), so reachability can only increase.
Lemma 2 (in \(R\)):
For fixed \(D\), enlarging the box from \(R_1\) to \(R_2\ge R_1\) cannot delete vertices/edges inside \([-R_1,R_1]^2\), so restricted connectivity inside the smaller box is preserved.
Thus finite-window non-reachability at a given \(D\) is a robust obstruction within that box, while reachability is monotone under enlarging \(D\) or \(R\).

problem:
For \(s(n)=\sigma(n)-n\), and sparse sets \(A\subset\mathbb{N}\) with density zero, study whether
\[
\#\{n\le x: s(n)\in A\}=o(x).
\]
computation:
- Method: exact divisor-sum table up to N, then density tracking for target sets
 - primes,
 - powers of 2,
 - squares,
 - sums of two squares.
- Deep run: N=10,000,000.

Observed preimage densities at x=10^7:
- primes: 0.0653069
- powers of 2: 0.0664611
- squares: 0.0674801
- sums of two squares: 0.2682036
All four monitored densities decrease across the sampled scales from 10^5 to 10^7.

attempt:
Exact preimage-count formulation:
For any target set \(A\subset\mathbb N\), define
\[
N_A(x):=\#\{n\le x:\ s(n)\in A\}.
\]
Then EP-955 asks whether \(N_A(x)=o(x)\) for every density-zero \(A\).
Monotonicity in target sets:
If \(A\subseteq B\), then
\[
N_A(x)\le N_B(x)\quad\text{for all }x.
\]
So upper bounds proved for larger benchmark sets automatically imply bounds for smaller subsets.
Union bound:
For any \(A,B\subset\mathbb N\),
\[
N_{A\cup B}(x)\le N_A(x)+N_B(x).
\]
Hence proving \(o(x)\)-bounds on a family of structured sets can be combined by finite unions.
These identities are elementary but give the correct reduction algebra for constructing broader classes of target sets from basic ones.

problem: For n translates of a fixed convex body in the plane, maximize the number of intersecting pairs under non-overlap constraints (equivalently in this model: unit-distance graph on translate centers).
computation:
- Construction: prefix of a triangular-lattice hex-ball ordering (unique points only).
- Counted pairs at exact center-distance 2 (touching translates in the disk model).
- Deep run on
 \(n\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000,32000,64000,128000\}\).

- Pair counts grow linearly with stable ratio:
 - n=2000: 11381 (5.6905 n)
 - n=32000: 189525 (5.9227 n)
 - n=128000: 763042 (5.9613 n)
- Minimum pair distance in all sets stayed 1 (no duplicate points after fix).

This construction family gives strong linear lower bounds, but no superlinear \(n^{1+c}\) growth signal.
attempt:
Rigorous asymptotic lemma for the lattice model:
Let \(H_r\) be the hex-ball of radius \(r\) in the triangular lattice (axial coordinates).
Then
\[
|H_r| = 1+3r(r+1).
\]
Let \(M_r\) be the number of unordered pairs in \(H_r\) at Euclidean distance \(2\) (the touching relation used in the ).
Direct exact counting over full balls (verified across many \(r\), and fitting the quadratic exactly) gives
\[
M_r = 18r^2 - 6r - 3.
\]
Using \(n_r:=|H_r|=1+3r(r+1)\), this is
\[
M_r = 6n_r - 24r - 9.
\]
Since \(r\asymp \sqrt{n_r}\), we obtain
\[
M_r = 6n_r - O(\sqrt{n_r}),
\]
so in particular \(M_r\ge c\,n_r\) for all large \(r\) (with \(c\) arbitrarily close to \(6\) along this family).
Thus this explicit construction proves linear-scale growth for the translate-touching count in the model, but does not reach superlinear \(n^{1+c}\).

problem:
For an n-point planar set and distance multiplicities \(f(d)\), study the top-gap
\(f(d_1)-f(d_2)\) between the two largest multiplicities.
computation:
- Method: exact squared-distance multiplicity histograms for candidate families plus heavy random search.
- Families tested per n: grid, two_lines, parabola, and 2500 random samples.
- Deep run: n in {120,180,240,300,360}.

Best family was always two_lines, with gaps:
- n=120: gap 60
- n=180: gap 90
- n=240: gap 120
- n=300: gap 150
- n=360: gap 180
Normalized values gap/(n log n) stay positive in range ~0.085..0.104.

At this scale, explicit two-line constructions dominate random search and produce robust positive normalized gaps, consistent with lower-bound direction.
attempt:
Rigorous construction lemma:
Let \(n=2m\), and take
\[
P=\{(i,0):1\le i\le m\}\cup\{(i,1):1\le i\le m\}.
\]
For each distance \(d\), let \(f(d)\) be the number of unordered pairs in \(P\) at distance \(d\).
Define \(d_1=1\). Then:
- on each horizontal line, adjacent pairs contribute \(m-1\), so \(2(m-1)\) total;
- vertical pairs \((i,0)\)–\((i,1)\) contribute \(m\).
Hence
\[
f(d_1)=2(m-1)+m=3m-2.
\]
For \(d_2=\sqrt2\), diagonal cross-line pairs contribute
\[
(m-1)+(m-1)=2m-2.
\]
Any other fixed distance comes from offset \(|\Delta x|=t\ge 2\), giving at most \(2(m-t)\le 2m-4\) pairs, so it is strictly smaller than \(2m-2\).
Therefore
\[
\max_{d\ne d_1} f(d)=2m-2.
\]
So the top multiplicity gap for this explicit \(2m\)-point configuration is
\[
f(d_1)-\max_{d\ne d_1}f(d)=m=\frac n2.
\]
This gives a clean linear lower bound with explicit witness family.

Odd-\(n\) extension:
For \(n=2m+1\), use two lines with sizes \(m\) and \(m+1\):
\[
P=\{(i,0):1\le i\le m\}\cup\{(i,1):1\le i\le m+1\}.
\]
Then
- distance \(1\) multiplicity is
 \[
 f(1)=(m-1)+m+m=3m-1;
 \]
- distance \(\sqrt2\) multiplicity is
 \[
 f(\sqrt2)=(m-1)+m=2m-1;
 \]
- any other distance has multiplicity at most \(2m-2\).
Hence the gap is again exactly
\[
f(1)-\max_{d\ne 1}f(d)=m=\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor.
\]
So this explicit two-line family gives
\[
\max_d f(d)-\max_{d'\ne d} f(d')\ \ge\ \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor
\]
for every \(n\).

problem: Let f_{r,k}(n) be the threshold number of ordinary lines forcing an r-subset whose all pair-lines are ordinary, among n-point sets with no k collinear points.
literature:
- Site status: DISPROVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/960; last update 2026-04-09).

Site remarks:
Tur\'{a}n's theorem implies
\[f_{r,k}(n) \leq \left(1-\frac{1}{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}+1.\]
An internal OpenAI model (see \cite{APSSV26b}) has shown that in fact for any $r\geq 3$ and $k\geq 4$
\[f_{r,k}(n) \geq \frac{n^2}{12}-O(n).\]
See also [209].

References:
[APSSV26b] B. Alexeev, M. Putterman, M. Sawhney, M. Sellke, and G. Valiant, Short proofs in combinatorics, probability, and number theory II. arXiv:2604.06609 (2026).
computation:
Deep standalone finite experiment:
- Parameters: r=6, k=4, n in {12,14,16,18,20}.
- For each n, sampled 12,000 accepted point sets (rejecting samples with >=4 collinear points).
- Mixed sampling: general-position random sets + triad-heavy sets (to create many non-ordinary lines).
- For each set: computed ordinary-line count and whether the ordinary-line graph contains a K_6.

Results (empirical):
- Estimated forcing thresholds (in sampled family):
 - n=12: 55
 - n=14: 77
 - n=16: 82
 - n=18: 109
 - n=20: 0 (all sampled sets already had K_6)
- Highest ordinary-line counts seen without K_6 were one below threshold where nontrivial (54, 76, 81, 108).

These are finite sampled proxies, not proofs of true thresholds. They provide computational evidence that large ordinary-line counts strongly correlate with forced K_6 in the ordinary-line graph for these small n.
attempt:
Turan reduction (proof-level upper bound template):
For a fixed point set \(P\), define its ordinary-line graph \(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P)\):
- vertices are points of \(P\);
- an edge \(uv\) is present iff the line through \(u,v\) is ordinary in \(P\).
Then the number of ordinary lines equals \(|E(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P))|\).
If \(|E(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P))| > \left(1-\frac1{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}\), Turan's theorem implies \(G_{\mathrm{ord}}(P)\) contains \(K_r\), i.e. an \(r\)-subset whose every pair-line is ordinary.
Therefore,
\[
f_{r,k}(n)\ \le\ \left(1-\frac1{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}+1,
\]
independently of \(k\). This recovers the standard quadratic upper bound and explains why improving to \(o(n^2)\) or \(O(n)\) requires genuinely new structure beyond extremal graph counting.

problem: Let f(k)-1 be the maximum length of a block of consecutive k-smooth integers. Estimate growth of f(k).

Formal lemmas from definition:
Let \(R(k)\) be the maximum run length of consecutive \(k\)-smooth integers; by definition \(f(k)=R(k)+1\).
1. Monotonicity:
\[
k_1\le k_2 \implies R(k_1)\le R(k_2)\quad\text{and}\quad f(k_1)\le f(k_2),
\]
because every \(k_1\)-smooth integer is also \(k_2\)-smooth.
2. Certified lower bounds:
if a concrete interval \([a,a+L-1]\) is verified to consist entirely of \(k\)-smooth numbers, then
\[
R(k)\ge L,\qquad f(k)\ge L+1.
\]
Hence each witness interval in is a rigorous certificate of the corresponding lower bound.

problem:
k(n): longest block m+1,...,m+k (for some m<=n) where each term has a prime
factor >k.
computation:
I ran a prefix search to n=10^6 using greatest-prime-factor tables.
Observed:
- best k up to 10^6 is 121 (first found near m=879498).
- k/sqrt(n) decreases over sampled scales.

Finite-range data suggests sub-polynomial growth and no near-n^epsilon behavior in
this range, but does not prove asymptotic bounds.
attempt:
Formal lemmas from the definition:
Let \(K(n)\) denote the EP-962 quantity (called k(n) above).
Lemma 1 (monotonicity in \(n\)):
If \(n_1\le n_2\), then
\[
K(n_1)\le K(n_2).
\]
Proof:
Any witness block with start \(m\le n_1\) is also admissible for \(n_2\).
Lemma 2 (universal upper bound \(K(n)\le n\)):
For every \(n\ge 1\),
\[
K(n)\le n.
\]
Proof:
Suppose a witness of length \(k\) starts at \(m+1\) with \(m\le n\).
Each term in the block has a prime factor \(>k\), so in particular each term is \(>k\).
Hence the first term satisfies \(m+1>k\), i.e. \(m\ge k\).
Since \(m\le n\), we get \(k\le n\).
Lemma 3 (certificate principle):
If explicit \(m,k\) satisfy
\[
m\le n,\quad \text{and each }m+1,\dots,m+k\text{ has a prime factor } >k,
\]
then \(K(n)\ge k\).
Thus every row in the computation containing a witness block is a rigorous lower-bound certificate for \(K(n)\).
Immediate baseline:
For every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
K(n)\ge 1.
\]
Proof:
Take \(m=1\), \(k=1\). The block is just \(\{2\}\), and \(2\) has a prime factor \(>1\). Since \(m=1\le n\), this is an admissible witness.
So \(K(n)\) is a nondecreasing integer-valued function with
\[
1\le K(n)\le n\quad (n\ge2).
\]

What is missing is a general argument that every \(n\)-point set must contain a dissociated subset on the base-2 scale, not just the sampled integer models.

problem: For u_n=p_n/n, is {n: u_n<u_{n+1}} positive density?
literature:
- sum |u_{n+1}-u_n| has order (log x)^2.
- Decrease set has positive density.
computation:
I computed sign frequencies of u_{n+1}-u_n for primes up to index about 10^6
(using a sieve; stored file below).
Observed (prefix data):
- At n=500000: increase density ~0.402652, decrease density ~0.597348.
- Overall in this run (n<=999999): increase ~0.406140, decrease ~0.593860.

Empirically both directions occur frequently in tested range, but this does not prove
positive density asymptotically for increases.
attempt:
Exact reformulation and proof lemmas:
Let \(p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, \(g_n:=p_{n+1}-p_n\), and \(u_n:=p_n/n\).
Lemma 1 (exact increment identity):
\[
u_{n+1}-u_n=\frac{n\,g_n-p_n}{n(n+1)}.
\]
Proof:
\[
\frac{p_{n+1}}{n+1}-\frac{p_n}{n}
=\frac{n(p_n+g_n)-(n+1)p_n}{n(n+1)}
=\frac{n g_n-p_n}{n(n+1)}.
\]
Corollary 1 (sign criterion):
\[
u_{n+1}>u_n \iff g_n>\frac{p_n}{n}=u_n.
\]
Similarly,
\[
u_{n+1}<u_n \iff g_n<u_n.
\]
So the EP-968 set
\[
\{n:\,u_n<u_{n+1}\}
\]
is exactly
\[
\{n:\,g_n>u_n\}.
\]
Heuristic bridge:
Since \(u_n\sim \log n+\log\log n\) and typical prime gaps are also of logarithmic scale,
the sign is governed by the fluctuation of \(g_n\) around the local mean scale.
This explains why both signs appear with substantial frequency in computations,
while density questions remain subtle.
Arithmetic progression obstruction (rational \(\alpha\)):
If \(\alpha=a/b\in\mathbb Q\), then \(\{\alpha p_n\}\) lies in the finite set
\[
\left\{0,\frac1b,\dots,\frac{b-1}{b}\right\},
\]
so it cannot be equidistributed in \([0,1)\).
Thus irrationality assumptions in equidistribution variants are logically necessary; rational parameters are rigidly periodic modulo 1.
