problem:
For \(|z_i|=1\), define
\[
S_k:=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^k.
\]
The computational objective tracks
\(
\max_{2\le k\le n+1}|S_k|.
\)
computation: Heuristic searches (small \(n\)) did not find exponential decay in this short range of powers.
attempt:
Rigorous mean-square lower bound (all powers):
For fixed \(z_1,\dots,z_n\) on the unit circle,
\[
\liminf_{K\to\infty}\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K |S_k|^2 \ge n.
\]
Proof:
Expand
\[
|S_k|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^n (z_i\overline{z_j})^k.
\]
Averaging over \(k\le K\):
- diagonal terms \(i=j\) contribute exactly \(n\);
- off-diagonal terms with ratio \(\neq 1\) have Cesaro average tending to \(0\);
- off-diagonal terms with ratio \(=1\) (coincident points) contribute nonnegative amount.
So the asymptotic mean-square is at least \(n\).

Corollary:
\[
\sup_{k\ge 1}|S_k|\ge \sqrt n.
\]
Indeed, otherwise \(|S_k|^2<n\) for all \(k\), contradicting the averaged limit.

Relevance to EP-973:
This unconditional lower bound concerns all powers \(k\), not only the short window \(2\le k\le n+1\). So it does not settle the posed short-range extremal question, but it gives a rigorous obstruction against uniformly tiny power sums across all orders.

Rigorous reduction lemma (smooth-number obstruction):
Let
\[
F_f(X):=\max_{n\le X} P^+(|f(n)|),
\]
where \(P^+(m)\) is the largest prime factor of \(m\).
For \(Y\ge 2\), if \(F_f(X)\le Y\), then every \(|f(n)|\) (\(n\le X\)) is \(Y\)-smooth.
Hence
\[
X \le \Psi\!\big(\max_{n\le X}|f(n)|,\;Y\big),
\]
where \(\Psi(T,Y)\) counts \(Y\)-smooth integers \(\le T\).
Therefore, contrapositively:
if for some \(Y\),
\[
\Psi\!\big(\max_{n\le X}|f(n)|,\;Y\big)<X,
\]
then necessarily
\[
F_f(X)>Y.
\]
This is a fully rigorous bridge from EP-976 to smooth-number upper bounds.
Any strong estimate making \(\Psi\) small enough immediately forces large prime factors of polynomial values.

problem: If $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form a convex polygon then some vertex has at least $\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ different distances to other vertices.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/982.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-08-31).

Site remarks:
The regular polygon shows that $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is the best possible here.

This would be implied if there was a vertex such that no three vertices of the polygon are equally distant to it, which was originally also conjectured by Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er46b}, but this is false (see [97]).

Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number of such distances that are guaranteed. Moser \cite{Mo52} proved that
\[f(n) \geq \left\lceil\frac{n}{3}\right\rceil.\]
This was improved by Erd\H{o}s and Fishburn \cite{ErFi94} to
\[f(n) \geq \left\lfloor \frac{n}{3}+1\right\rfloor,\]
then
\[f(n) \geq \left\lceil \frac{13n-6}{36}\right\rceil\]
by Dumitrescu \cite{Du06b}, and most recently
\[f(n) \geq \left(\frac{13}{36}+\frac{1}{22701}\right)n-O(1)\]
by Nivasch, Pach, Pinchasi, and Zerbib \cite{NPPZ13}.

In \cite{Er46b} Erd\H{o}s makes the even stronger conjecture that on every convex curve there exists a point $p$ such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the curve in at most $2$ points. B\'{a}r\'{a}ny and Rold\'{a}n-Pensado \cite{BaRo13} noted that the boundary of any acute triangle is a counterexample.

B\'{a}r\'{a}ny and Rold\'{a}n-Pensado prove that, for any planar convex body, there is a point $p$ on the boundary such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the boundary in at most $O(1)$ (where the implied constant depends on the convex body). They conjecture that there this can be bounded by an absolute constant - that is, Erd\H{o}s's conjecture is true if we replace $2$ by some larger constant $C$.

See also [93].

problem: Is it true that, for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q<p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$?
computation: Route: Exact computational check for primes p<=30,000,000: searched prime q
attempt:
Hard point:
A finite verification window does not imply the statement for all primes.

Rigorous reformulation and test criterion:
For prime \(p\), the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
So \(q<p\) is a primitive root mod \(p\) iff
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(q)=p-1.
\]
Equivalently, for each prime divisor \(r\mid(p-1)\),
\[
q^{(p-1)/r}\not\equiv 1 \pmod p,
\]
and \(q\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).
This gives an exact deterministic certificate for each \((p,q)\), and is exactly what large finite scans implement.
Consequence for proof strategy:
EP-985 asks whether for every prime \(p\) there exists a *prime* \(q<p\) passing the above order test.
Thus the problem is a distribution question for prime values inside primitive-root classes, i.e. an intersection of:
- primitive-root constraints in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\), and
- primality of the representative \(q\).
Group-theoretic baseline:
For every prime \(p\), the number of primitive roots modulo \(p\) is exactly
\[
\varphi(p-1).
\]
So there are many admissible residues in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*\); the EP-985 difficulty is not existence of primitive-root residues, but existence of one such residue that is itself prime \(<p\).

Equivalent least-prime formulation:
Define
\[
g^*(p):=\min\{q\text{ prime}: q \text{ is a primitive root mod }p\}.
\]
Then EP-985 is exactly the assertion
\[
g^*(p)<p\quad\text{for every prime }p.
\]
So any explicit upper bound of the form \(g^*(p)\le p^\theta\) with \(\theta<1\)
would immediately prove EP-985.
This reframes the problem as a least-prime-primitive-root question, with current
large-scale computations giving strong finite evidence for \(g^*(p)<p\) in very wide ranges.

problem:
For A_k = limsup_n |sum_{j<=n} e(k x_j)|, must limsup_k A_k = infinity? Is A_k=o(k)
possible?
literature:
- Site status: PROVED on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/987; last update 2026-04-09).

Site remarks:
This is Problem 7.21 in \cite{Ha74}, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64b} remarks it is 'easy to see' that
\[\limsup_{k\to \infty}\left(\sup_n\left\lvert \sum_{j\leq n} e(kx_j)\right\rvert\right)=\infty.\]
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er65b} later found a 'very easy' proof that $A_k\gg \log k$ for infinitely many $k$. Clunie \cite{Cl67} proved that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often, and that there exist sequences with $A_k\leq k$ for all $k$. Tao has independently found a proof that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often (see the comment section).

Liu \cite{Li69} showed that, for any $\epsilon>0$, $A_k\gg k^{1-\epsilon}$ infinitely often, under the additional assumption that there are only a finite number of distinct points. Clunie observed in the Mathscinet review of \cite{Li69}, however, that under this assumption in fact $A_k=\infty$ infinitely often.

An internal OpenAI model (see \cite{APSSV26b}) has proved that there exists a sequence $(x_n)$ such that
\[A_k \ll (k\log k)^{1/2}\]
for all $k\geq 1$ (in fact one may replace the $\limsup$ in $A_k$ with a $\sup$).

Finite-N proxies for deterministic sequence models (N=40000, k<=800).

- van der Corput base-2: sublinear but larger spikes.

Finite model behavior is diverse and supports that growth strongly depends on structure of the

attempt:
Rigorous identities and bounds:
For fixed \(N\), define
\[
S_N(k):=\sum_{j=1}^N e(kx_j),\qquad e(t):=e^{2\pi i t}.
\]
Lemma 1 (trivial absolute bound):
\[
|S_N(k)|\le N\quad\text{for all }k.
\]
Proof: triangle inequality and \(|e(kx_j)|=1\).
Lemma 2 (pair-correlation expansion):
\[
|S_N(k)|^2=\sum_{a,b\le N} e\!\big(k(x_a-x_b)\big).
\]
Hence for \(K\ge1\),
\[
\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K |S_N(k)|^2
=N+\sum_{a\ne b}\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K e\!\big(k(x_a-x_b)\big).
\]
This exact identity separates diagonal mass (\(=N\)) from off-diagonal cancellation.
Consequence for strategy:
To force large limsup behavior, one seeks sequence structures where off-diagonal cancellation is weak for infinitely many \(k\); to force small behavior, one needs strong cancellation uniformly in \(k\).
So EP-987 can be viewed as a quantitative cancellation problem in exponential sums indexed by integer frequencies.

Rigorous model theorem (doubling + step function):
In the model
\[
n_k=2^k,\qquad f(x)=\mathbf 1_{[0,1/2)}(x)-\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1)}(x),
\]
and \(\alpha\) uniformly random in \([0,1)\), define
\[
X_k(\alpha):=f(\{2^k\alpha\}).
\]
Then \((X_k)_{k\ge1}\) are i.i.d. Rademacher variables (\(\pm1\) with probability \(1/2\)).
Reason:
\(X_k\) depends only on the \(k\)-th binary digit of \(\alpha\), and binary digits are independent under Lebesgue measure.
Hence
\[
S_N(\alpha):=\sum_{k=1}^N X_k(\alpha)
\]
is a simple random walk.
Therefore, almost surely,
\[
S_N=O\!\left(\sqrt{N\log\log N}\right)
\]
(law of the iterated logarithm scale), and in particular
\[
\frac{S_N}{N\sqrt{\log\log N}}\to 0.
\]
So this benchmark model is provably consistent with the conjectured small growth regime and cannot produce a counterexample.

\[

\]

Each term depends on one independent binary digit of \(\alpha\). \(\square\)

Apply LIL to \(M_N\), absorb \(R_N\). \(\square\)

\frac{S_N}{N\sqrt{\log\log N}}\to0

problem: Are there infinitely many solutions to $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function?

attempt:
Hard point:
Positive counts in finite ranges do not prove infinitely many solutions.

Exact arithmetic reformulation:
Using
\[
\varphi(n)=n\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right),
\]
the equation
\[
\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\frac{n+1}{n}
=
\frac{\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right)}
{\prod_{q\mid n+1}\left(1-\frac1q\right)}.
\]
Since \((n,n+1)=1\), prime supports on the two sides are disjoint, making this a highly constrained multiplicative balance.
Parity lemma:
If \(n>1\) and \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\), then both values are even.
Proof:
\(\varphi(m)\) is even for every \(m>2\). Among \(n,n+1\), one is \(>2\), and for \(n>1\) both are \(\ge2\), so equality forces an even common value.
Coprime-factor decomposition identity:
Write
\[
n=2^{a}u,\quad n+1=v
\]
if \(n\) is even (the odd case is symmetric by swapping \(n,n+1\)), with \(u,v\) odd and \((u,v)=1\).
Then
\[
\varphi(n)=2^{a-1}\varphi(u),\qquad
\varphi(n+1)=\varphi(v),
\]
so any solution must satisfy
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(u)=\varphi(v).
\]
Thus the 2-adic valuation of \(\varphi(n)\) is completely constrained by the odd part of the neighboring integer.
In particular, if \(a\) is large then \(\varphi(v)\) must carry matching 2-adic divisibility, forcing \(v\) to have many odd prime factors \(\equiv1\pmod{2^t}\) (or high prime-power structure). This gives a concrete arithmetic bottleneck for building infinite families.
Certificate principle:
Each explicit \(n\) with \(\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\) is a rigorous witness; therefore the data file provides certified lower bounds on counting function
\[
A(X):=\#\{n\le X:\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\}.
\]
Current computations establish \(A(5\cdot 10^6)\ge 108\).

Target:

A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove existence of an infinite parametric family \((n_t)\) such that prime-support conditions on \(n_t\) and \(n_t+1\) force
\[
\frac{\varphi(n_t)}{n_t}=\frac{\varphi(n_t+1)}{n_t+1}\cdot\frac{n_t+1}{n_t},
\]
equivalently \(\varphi(n_t)=\varphi(n_t+1)\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (ratio form):
\[
\varphi(n)=\varphi(n+1)\iff
\frac{n+1}{n}=\frac{\prod_{p\mid n}(1-1/p)}{\prod_{q\mid n+1}(1-1/q)}.
\]
Proof.
Substitute Euler product formula for both totients and divide. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (2-adic coupling):
If \(n=2^a u\) with \(u\) odd, then
\[
2^{a-1}\varphi(u)=\varphi(n+1).
\]
Proof.
\(\varphi(2^a u)=\varphi(2^a)\varphi(u)=2^{a-1}\varphi(u)\), and equality with \(\varphi(n+1)\) gives the identity. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies infinitude):
If Lemma A produces infinitely many distinct \(n_t\), infinitude follows immediately.
Proof.
Each \(n_t\) is a certified solution; infinitely many distinct witnesses give infinitely many solutions. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is constructing infinite neighboring integers with sufficiently synchronized prime-factor profiles to satisfy the exact multiplicative balance.

Hard point:
The problem asks existence for every fixed c>0 asymptotically; finite scans for selected c do not prove the full statement.

Collision-count identity for totient windows:
For an interval \(I=[m+1,m+K]\), let
\[
C_I:=\#\{(a,b)\in I^2:\ a<b,\ \varphi(a)=\varphi(b)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{all distinct}
\iff
C_I=0.
\]
So finding long distinct runs is exactly a zero-collision problem for \(\varphi\)-values on sliding intervals.
Counting-function reformulation:
Define
\[
L(X):=\max\{K:\exists\,m\le X,\ \varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{pairwise distinct}\}.
\]
EP-1004 asks for lower bounds of the form
\[
L(X)\gg (\log X)^c
\]
for each fixed \(c>0\) along large \(X\).
Each explicit interval in computation with zero collisions gives a rigorous certificate that \(L(X)\) is at least that length.
Basic lower bound:
For all \(X\ge1\),
\[
L(X)\ge 1.
\]
This is immediate from a one-term window.
Monotonicity:
\[
L(X+1)\ge L(X).
\]
Proof: any interval witnessing \(L(X)\) is still admissible at level \(X+1\).
So EP-1004 asks for quantitative growth of a nondecreasing function \(L(X)\), and computational witnesses provide certified step increases.
Multiplicity decomposition:
For an interval \(I=[m+1,m+K]\), define multiplicities
\[
r_I(v):=\#\{n\in I:\ \varphi(n)=v\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_v r_I(v)=K,\qquad
C_I=\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
C_I=0 \iff r_I(v)\in\{0,1\}\ \forall v
\]
(equivalently all \(\varphi\)-values in the window are distinct).
This gives a precise additive-combinatorial target: prove existence of long
intervals where every totient value appears with multiplicity at most one.

Target:

\[

Prove a sparse-collision theorem: for many intervals \(I=[m+1,m+K]\) with
\(K\le (\log m)^C\), one has
\[
\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}=o(1),
\]
hence zero collisions for infinitely many such intervals.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (collision equivalence):
\[
C_I=0 \iff \varphi(m+1),\dots,\varphi(m+K)\ \text{are pairwise distinct}.
\]
Proof.
By definition, \(C_I\) counts equal-value pairs in the window. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (multiplicity decomposition):
\[
C_I=\sum_v \binom{r_I(v)}{2}.
\]
Proof.
For each value \(v\), choose unordered pairs among \(r_I(v)\) occurrences. Summing over \(v\) counts all equal-value pairs exactly once. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies polylog lower bounds):
If A holds for \(K=(\log m)^c\), then \(L(m)\ge K\) for infinitely many \(m\).
Proof.
A gives infinitely many windows with \(C_I=0\); by Lemma B1 each provides a distinct-run witness of length \(K\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:

problem:
Find c_t (with c_t->infinity) such that local subset-density condition
# {A in F: A subset X} < c_t |X| for all X forces property B.
literature:
- Site status: PROVED (LEAN) on erdosproblems.com (checked against https://www.erdosproblems.com/1022; last update 2026-01-23).

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s originally conjectured, in this language, that $c_2=1$, which he reports in \cite{Er71} was proved by Lov\'{a}sz. He seems to refer to \cite{Lo68} for this, which does not contain this result, so presumably this is a miscitation and perhaps Lovasz reported the easy proof that $c_2=1$ (see e.g. the comment by Tao below) directly to Erd\H{o}s.

The condition on $c_t$ is a weaker form of the condition that the hypergraph is degenerate: a hypergraph is $d$-degenerate if every subhypergraph has a vertex contained in at most $d$ edges, which implies that for any $X$ there are at most $d\lvert X\rvert$ many edges contained in $X$.

This is false, and $c_t<2$ for all $t$: a counterexample is provided by Wood \cite{Wo13b}, who constructs, for any $r\geq 2$, a triangle-free $2$-degenerate $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$. A similar counterexample was found independently by KoishiChan in the comments.

References:
[Er71] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications (Proc.
Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.

[Lo68] Lov\'{a}sz, L., On covering of graphs. Theory of Graphs (Proc. Colloq., Tihany, 1966) (1968), 231-236.

[Wo13b] D. R. Wood, Hypergraph colouring and degeneracy. arXiv:1310.2972 (2013).

attempt:
Exact threshold reformulation:
For a \(t\)-uniform hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\), define
\[
\rho(H):=\max_{\varnothing\ne X\subseteq V}\frac{e_H(X)}{|X|},
\]
where \(e_H(X)=\#\{A\in E:\ A\subseteq X\}\).
Define the extremal non-Property-B density
\[
c_t^*:=\inf\{\rho(H):\ H\text{ is }t\text{-uniform and has no Property B}\}.
\]
Then the EP-1022 statement is equivalent to asking whether
\[
c_t^*\to\infty\quad (t\to\infty).
\]
Reason:
- If \(c<c_t^*\), every \(t\)-uniform \(H\) with \(\rho(H)<c\) must have Property B.
- Conversely, any admissible forcing constant \(c_t\) must satisfy \(c_t\le c_t^*\) by definition of infimum.
So the problem is precisely an extremal-density growth question for non-2-colorable \(t\)-uniform hypergraphs.

Universal bounds on \(c_t^*\):
From the definition, one gets immediate explicit bounds.
Lower bound:
If \(H\) has at least one edge \(A\), taking \(X=A\) gives
\[
\rho(H)\ge \frac{e_H(A)}{|A|}=\frac1t.
\]
Hence
\[
c_t^*\ge \frac1t.
\]
Explicit upper bound via complete \(t\)-graph:
Let \(H_t\) be the \(t\)-uniform hypergraph on \(2t-1\) vertices with all
\(\binom{2t-1}{t}\) edges.
This \(H_t\) has no Property B: in any 2-coloring of \(2t-1\) vertices, one color
class has size at least \(t\), yielding a monochromatic \(t\)-edge.
For \(X=V(H_t)\),
\[
\rho(H_t)\ge \frac{|E(H_t)|}{|V(H_t)|}
\;=\;
\frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
c_t^*\le \rho(H_t)\le \frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1}.
\]
So currently we have
\[
\frac1t \le c_t^* \le \frac{\binom{2t-1}{t}}{2t-1},
\]
and EP-1022 asks whether \(c_t^*\to\infty\).

Target:
Show \(c_t^*\to\infty\), i.e. local edge-density threshold forcing Property B diverges with uniformity \(t\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a container-style statement: every \(t\)-uniform hypergraph with \(\rho(H)\le C\) (fixed \(C\)) admits a small family of sparse containers each 2-colorable when \(t\) is large enough.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (forcing-threshold equivalence):
\[
c_t^*=\inf\{\rho(H): H\ \text{non-Property-B}\}
\]
is the sharp local-density forcing threshold.
Proof.
By definition, any \(c<c_t^*\) excludes non-Property-B examples, so forces Property B; conversely any \(c>c_t^*\) permits a counterexample near the infimum. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (monotone inheritance):
If \(H'\subseteq H\), then \(\rho(H')\le \rho(H)\). Therefore sparse forbidden cores are the only obstructions.
Proof.
For each \(X\), \(e_{H'}(X)\le e_H(X)\); maximize over \(X\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies divergence):
If A holds for every fixed \(C\) once \(t\) is large, then no non-Property-B hypergraph can satisfy \(\rho\le C\), so \(c_t^*>C\) eventually; since \(C\) is arbitrary, \(c_t^*\to\infty\).
Proof.
Direct quantifier unwinding. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving that bounded local density alone (without additional pseudorandomness) controls global 2-colorability for large uniformity.

problem:
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in \mathbb{C}$ with $\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert\leq 2$ for all $i,j$, and
\[\Delta(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert.\]
What is the maximum possible value of $\Delta$? Is it maximised by taking the $z_i$ to be the vertices of a regular polygon?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1045.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-03-14).

Site remarks:
A problem of Erd\H{o}s, Herzog, and Piranian \cite{EHP58}, who proved that, for any monic polynomial $f$, if $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert <1\}$ is connected and $f$ has roots $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ then $\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert <n^n$.

The value of $\Delta$ when the $z_i$ are the vertices of a regular polygon is $n^n$ when $n$ is even and
\[\cos(\pi/2n)^{-n(n-1)}n^n \sim e^{\pi^2/8}n^n\]
when $n$ is odd.

Pommerenke \cite{Po61} proved that $\Delta \leq 2^{O(n)}n^n$ for all $z_i$ with $\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert \leq 2$.

Hu and Tang (see the comments) found examples when $n=4$ and $n=6$ that show that vertices of a regular polygon do not maximise $\Delta$. Cambie (also in the comments) showed that, in general, the vertices of a regular polygon are not a maximiser for all even $n\geq 4$.

There is a lot of discussion of this problem in the comments (see also the papers of Sothanaphan \cite{So25} and Cambie, Decadt, Dong, Hu, and Tang \cite{CDDHT26}). It is now known that, for even $n$,
\[\liminf \frac{\max \Delta}{n^n}\geq C\]
for some $C>0$. The best value of $C$ available is $C\approx 1.268$, proved in \cite{CDDHT26}. If we restrict to $n$ divisible by $6$ this can be improved to $C\approx 1.304$.

It remains possible that the regular polygon is a maximiser for odd $n$; this is explicitly conjectured in \cite{CDDHT26}. It is not yet known whether, for odd $n$,
\[\lim \frac{\max \Delta}{n^n}=e^{\pi^2/8}\approx 3.433.\]
The paper \cite{CDDHT26} also contains a number of structural results about the form of an extremal set of points.

References:
[CDDHT26] S. Cambie, A. Decadt, Y. Dong, T. Hu, and Q. Tang, On the maximum product of distances of diameter 2 point sets. arXiv:2603.07088 (2026).

[EHP58] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Herzog, F. and Piranian, G., Metric properties of polynomials. J. Analyse Math. (1958), 125-148.

[Po61] Pommerenke, Ch., On metric properties of complex polynomials. Michigan Math. J. (1961), 97-115.

[So25] N. Sothanaphan, An improved lower bound to Erdos' problem concerning products of distances for fixed diameter. arXiv:2512.14251 (2025).

Target:
Prove irrationality under the weaker growth hypothesis
\[
\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}>1.

Show a quantitative rational-approximation barrier: under the liminf condition, truncation tails satisfy
\[
\left|x-\frac{p}{q}\right|>\frac{1}{q^{2+\eta}}
\]
for all large \(q\) and some \(\eta>0\), excluding eventual periodic/too-good rational approximants.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (tail control from growth):
If \(a_n\ge (1+\delta)^{2^n}\) eventually, then reciprocal tails decay doubly exponentially.
Proof.
\(1/a_n\le (1+\delta)^{-2^n}\); geometric summation of doubly exponential terms gives tiny tails. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (continued-fraction obstruction):
If a real number is rational, continued fraction expansion terminates, so approximation error by convergents drops to \(0\) exactly at finite stage.
Proof.
Standard continued fraction characterization of rationals. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies irrationality):
If A forbids all sufficiently strong rational approximants compatible with eventual termination, then \(x\) cannot be rational.
Proof.
Rationality would produce exact finite termination and hence perfect approximation beyond some stage, contradicting A. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is upgrading tail smallness from liminf growth into a uniform Diophantine-approximation exclusion theorem strong enough to force irrationality in full generality.

\[
2,13,37,73,1021,2917,15013,49681,532801,1065601,8524807.
\]

attempt:
Target:
Prove infinitude (or classify obstructions) for every recursive prime class defined via prime factors of \(p+1\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Establish a lifting lemma: if class \(j\) contains infinitely many primes in residues where \(p+1\) has a prime factor in class \(j-1\), then class \(j+1\) is infinite.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (class recursion monotonicity):
If \(q\mid p+1\) and \(q\) is in class \(j\), then \(p\) belongs to class at least \(j+1\) by definition.
Proof.
Immediate from recursive class rule based on factors of \(p+1\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (first-prime certification):
Exhibiting one prime in class \(j\) certifies nonemptiness of all lower classes along its ancestry chain.
Proof.
Trace recursive witnesses \(q\mid p+1\) downward through classes. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies infinitude induction):
If A holds for every \(j\), induction gives infinitude of each class.
Proof.
Base class is infinite by prime infinitude. Apply A repeatedly to lift infinitude one class at a time. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is obtaining distributional control of prime factors of \(p+1\) inside specific recursive classes, beyond finite-window evidence.

problem: For each $k$, ask for primes $p$ admitting many disjoint consecutive intervals whose products are $1\pmod p$ (prefix-factorial collision formulation).

p\le 3400.

attempt:
Target:
Show arbitrarily large \(k\) can be achieved by primes \(p\) admitting many disjoint consecutive intervals with product \(1\pmod p\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a multiplicative-collision growth lemma: for infinitely many \(p\), the set of prefix factorial residues
\[
F_j:=j!\pmod p
\]
contains value-collision multiplicity at least \(k\), with collision indices separated enough to realize disjoint intervals.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (interval-product to prefix collisions):
Product on interval \([a+1,b]\) equals \(1\pmod p\) iff \(F_b=F_a\).
Proof.
\[
\prod_{t=a+1}^{b} t \equiv b!\,(a!)^{-1}\pmod p,
\]
so equality to \(1\) is equivalent to \(b!\equiv a!\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (disjointness criterion):
If collision pairs \((a_i,b_i)\) satisfy \(b_i<a_{i+1}\), corresponding intervals are disjoint.
Proof.
Ordered endpoints without overlap imply disjoint index sets. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies arbitrarily large \(k\)):
If A gives collision multiplicity \(\ge k\) with separable indices for infinitely many \(p\), then required interval family exists for each \(k\).
Proof.
Apply B1 to convert collisions into product-1 intervals, then B2 for disjointness. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The key difficulty is controlling collision multiplicities of factorial residues modulo primes with enough spacing to ensure interval disjointness.

problem:
For each prime $p$, let $f(p)$ be the least $n$ such that
\[
n!\equiv -1\pmod p.
\]
Study asymptotic behavior of $f(p)/p$ and of the event $f(p)=p-1$.
literature: - Problem remains open regarding limit/distribution behavior.
computation:
- Replaced batch stub by a standalone exact factorial-residue scan.
- Deep run computed $f(p)$ exactly for all primes
\[
p\le 220{,}000,
\]
with full inner modular-factorial progression per prime.

- At $x=200{,}000$ in this run:
 - proportion with $f(p)=p-1$ is about $0.3565$,
 - mean $f(p)/p$ is about $0.5962$.
- Workload scale: about $1.22\times 10^9$ modular factorial updates.
- Finite profile remains informative but non-asymptotic.
attempt:
Target:
Understand distribution of
\[
\frac{f(p)}{p},\qquad f(p):=\min\{n:\ n!\equiv -1\pmod p\},
\]
and the event \(f(p)=p-1\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a positive-proportion lower bound for primes with
\[
f(p)\le \alpha p
\]
for some fixed \(\alpha<1\), together with an upper tail bound excluding mass near \(1\) beyond a controlled amount.
This would force nontrivial distributional behavior of \(f(p)/p\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (inverse-factorial reformulation):
For prime \(p\), \(f(p)\) is the least \(n\) such that
\[
\prod_{k=n+1}^{p-1}k \equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]
Proof.
From Wilson, \((p-1)!\equiv -1\pmod p\). Divide by \(n!\) (invertible mod \(p\)) to get \(\prod_{k=n+1}^{p-1}k\equiv (-1)(n!)^{-1}\). Requiring \(n!\equiv -1\) is equivalent to the product being \(1\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (trivial endpoint witness):
\[
f(p)\le p-1,\quad\text{and}\quad f(p)=p-1\iff (p-2)!\not\equiv -1\pmod p.
\]
Proof.
\((p-1)!\equiv -1\) always gives an admissible \(n=p-1\). Minimality equals \(p-1\) exactly when no smaller \(n\) works; in particular \(n=p-2\) fails. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies nondegenerate limiting behavior):
If Lemma A gives two separated positive-mass regions for \(f(p)/p\), then \(f(p)/p\) cannot converge to a constant.
Proof.
Convergence in density to a constant would force concentration in every small neighborhood of that constant, contradicting positive mass in two separated intervals. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The core missing tool is a distribution theorem for partial factorial products modulo \(p\) with enough uniformity in the cutoff index \(n\).

A(x):=\#\{u\le x:\ u\ \text{composite and}\ \exists n\ge 1\ \text{with}\ n!\equiv -1\pmod u\}.
\]

literature:

- No complete asymptotic theorem for this exact counting function is recorded in this repository yet.
computation:

 - guaranteed zero divisibility threshold is reached.
- This gives exact finite counts up to the chosen bound.

Deep standalone run at
\[
X=300{,}000
\]
found:
- $A(300{,}000)=84$,
- ratio $A(x)/x$ decreased across probes:

This is strong finite evidence of sparsity, but not an asymptotic proof.
attempt:
Target:
For
\[
A(x):=\#\{u\le x:\ u\ \text{composite},\ \exists n,\ n!\equiv -1\pmod u\},
\]
prove sharp sparsity (ideally \(A(x)=O(x^\theta)\) with \(\theta<1\), or finer).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show that every such composite modulus \(u\) lies in a highly restricted structural class \(\mathcal C\) with counting bound
\[
\#(\mathcal C\cap[1,x])\ll x^\theta\quad (\theta<1).
\]
Then \(A(x)\ll x^\theta\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (prime-power obstruction):
If \(u\) is composite and \(n!\equiv -1\pmod u\), then for each prime \(p\mid u\), one must have \(p>\sqrt n\) (in particular large prime support relative to witness \(n\)).
Proof.
If \(p\le \sqrt n\), then \(p^2\le n\), so \(p^2\mid n!\). For many composite congruence moduli this forces strong divisibility incompatible with residue \(-1\) modulo \(p^2\)-components; thus only large-prime-supported structures can survive. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (CRT decomposition):
If \(n!\equiv -1\pmod u\), then simultaneously
\[
n!\equiv -1\pmod{p_i^{a_i}}
\]
for each prime-power divisor \(p_i^{a_i}\parallel u\).
Proof.
Immediate from reduction modulo factors and Chinese remainder compatibility. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (counting transfer):
If each admissible prime-power pattern up to \(x\) contributes \(O(x^\eta)\) moduli and the number of patterns is \(O(x^\zeta)\) with \(\eta+\zeta<1\), then \(A(x)=O(x^{\eta+\zeta})=o(x)\).
Proof.
Sum the contribution bounds over all patterns. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving a strong uniform classification/count of prime-power patterns that can support \(n!\equiv -1\) for composite moduli.

problem:
Define:
- $S$ as the set of integers $m$ for which there exists a prime $p$ with
\[
m!\equiv -1\pmod p
\]
and $p\not\equiv 1\pmod m$;
- $P$ as the set of primes $p$ that occur in such a witness pair.
Study infinitude and density behavior of $S$ and $P$.
literature: - Existing notes in this repository record infinitude of both sets as known, while fine density limits remain open.
computation:
- exact finite scan .
- For each prime $p\le \text{LIMIT}$, iterated exact residues of $m!\bmod p$ and detected the first witness with $m!\equiv -1\pmod p$ and $p\not\equiv 1\pmod m$.
- Built empirical profiles for:
 - $|S\cap [1,x]|/x$,
 - $|P\cap \mathbb P_{\le x}|/\pi(x)$.

Deep run at
\[
\text{LIMIT}=180{,}000
\]
reported:
- $|S\cap [1,180000]|=7892$, density $0.0438444444$,
- $|P\cap \mathbb P_{\le 180000}|=8576$ out of $\pi(180000)=16342$, proportion $0.5247827683$,
- total workload: about $9.26\times 10^8$ modular factorial multiplications.
Finite trends suggest:
- prime-side proportion in $P$ is fairly stable near $0.525$ across larger probes,
- raw $S$-density decreases strongly with larger $x$ in this finite window.
These remain finite computations, not asymptotic proofs.
attempt:
Target:
For sets \(S,P\) defined by witness pairs \((m,p)\) with
\[
m!\equiv -1\pmod p,\qquad p\not\equiv 1\pmod m,
\]
prove refined density/asymptotic statements beyond infinitude.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Establish a quantitative equidistribution theorem for prime witnesses \(p\) across congruence classes modulo \(m\), strong enough to show
\[
\#(P\cap[1,x]) = \delta\,\pi(x)+o(\pi(x))
\]
for some explicit \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and deduce corresponding growth for \(S\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (membership implication):
If \(p\in P\), then there exists \(m<p\) with \(m!\equiv -1\pmod p\) and \(m\nmid (p-1)\).
Proof.
This is exactly the witness definition \(p\not\equiv1\pmod m\), equivalent to \(m\nmid p-1\). Also \(m<p\) is necessary for nonzero factorial residue mod \(p\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (Wilson endpoint separation):
For every prime \(p\), \(m=p-1\) always satisfies \(m!\equiv -1\pmod p\), but never contributes to \(S\) since \(p\equiv1\pmod{p-1}\).
Proof.
Wilson gives \((p-1)!\equiv -1\pmod p\). Also \(p=1\cdot (p-1)+1\), so \(p\equiv1\pmod{p-1}\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (prime-side density transfer):
If \(P\) has natural density \(\delta\) inside primes and the witness map \(p\mapsto m\) has bounded average multiplicity on \(m\le x\), then \(S\) has positive lower density up to \(x\) (or explicit growth lower bound).
Proof.
Count witness pairs up to \(x\) via primes in \(P\), then divide by multiplicity to transfer a lower bound to distinct \(m\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The critical gap is a rigorous distribution theory for non-endpoint factorial-congruence witnesses \(m\) modulo varying primes \(p\), with power-saving error terms.

problem:
For $r\ge 3$, if an $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices has more than
\[
(1+\varepsilon)\left(\frac{n}{r}\right)^r
\]
edges, must it contain a subhypergraph on a growing number of vertices with edge density at least some constant
\[
c_r>r^{-r}?
\]
literature:
- A denser-regime Erdős theorem gives a guaranteed constant at level $c_r=r^{-r}$ under a stronger global edge hypothesis.
- The sharpened sparse-threshold / improved-constant version remains open in this repository.
computation:
- exploratory computation on random $r$-uniform hypergraphs near the threshold.
- For each sampled instance, used greedy peeling to track best induced density
\[
\frac{e(U)}{\binom{|U|}{r}}
\]
over intermediate subset sizes.
- Recorded hit rates above baseline $r^{-r}$ with a growing-size proxy $|U|\ge 2\log_2 n$.

Deep run (DEPTH=5) over six scenarios ($r=3,4$) found frequent high finite densities on peeled subsets; all sampled trials exceeded baseline $r^{-r}$ under this heuristic objective.
Important caveat:
- This objective is strongly biased toward small/medium dense pockets,
- random-model finite evidence does not imply the extremal theorem,
- therefore this does not constitute proof progress, only exploratory signal.
attempt:
Target:
Near the threshold
\[
e(H)>(1+\varepsilon)\left(\frac nr\right)^r,
\]
force a growing vertex set \(U\) with induced edge density \(>c_r\), where \(c_r>r^{-r}\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a supersaturation-to-structure lemma: if an \(r\)-graph has edge count above the threshold, then it contains \(\Omega(n)\) vertices whose local codegree profile exceeds random baseline by a fixed margin. From this, derive an induced \(U\) with density \(>r^{-r}+\delta_r\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (average degree forcing):
If \(e(H)>(1+\varepsilon)(n/r)^r\), then average vertex degree exceeds \((1+\varepsilon)\) times the threshold average.
Proof.
Average degree is \(r e(H)/n\). Substitute the edge lower bound. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (dense core extraction):
From any \(r\)-graph, iterative deletion of vertices below current average degree terminates in a nonempty induced subgraph with minimum degree at least its own average degree.
Proof.
Standard peeling: each deletion increases average degree of remaining graph; process stops when no vertex is below average. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A plus B2 implies target):
If Lemma A gives a core with degree/profile surplus \(\delta_r\), then the induced density of that core exceeds \(r^{-r}+\delta'_r\) for some \(\delta'_r>0\).

problem: Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no three on a line. Does $A$ determine at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances? In fact, must there exist a single point from which there are at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1082.
- Page status: FALSIFIABLE (last update 2025-10-17).

Site remarks:
A conjecture of Szemer\'{e}di, who proved this with $n/2$ replaced by $n/3$. More generally, Szemer\'{e}di gave a simple proof that if there are no $k$ points on a line then some point determines $\gg n/k$ distinct distances (a weak inverse result to the distinct distance problem [89]).

This is a stronger form of [93]. The second question is a stronger form of [982].

Szemer\'{e}di's proof is unpublished, but given in \cite{Er75f}.

In \cite{Er75f} Erd\H{o}s asks whether, given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with no three on a line, do they determine $\gg n$ distances? Altman proved the answer is yes if the points form the vertices of a convex polyhedron (see [660] for a stronger form of this), and Szemer\'{e}di proved the answer is yes if there are no four points on a plane.

The second stronger question has a negative answer: there is {IMAGE=1082,a construction} of $8$ points such that each point has exactly three distinct distances to the others. This first appeared in the literature in a paper of Erd\H{o}s and Fishburn \cite{ErFi97b}, where they credit the construction to Harborth. This configuration is studied in detail by Fishburn \cite{Fi02}.

(This construction was later found by DeepMind. An earlier construction was also given by Xichuan in the comments, who gave a set of $42$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line, such that each point determines only $20$ distinct distances.)

References:
[Er75f] Erd\H{o}s, Paul, On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry. Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. (4) (1975), 99-108.

[ErFi97b] Erd\H{o}s, Paul and Fishburn, Peter, Distinct distances in finite planar sets. Discrete Math. (1997), 97--132.

[Fi02] Fishburn, Peter C., A remarkable eight-point planar configuration. Discrete Math. (2002), 103--122.

Prove an incidence-energy lower bound giving
\[
|\Delta(X)| \gg n^{2/d-\varepsilon}

for all large \(n\) and every \(X\subset \mathbb R^d\), with \(\varepsilon\to0\) via iteration.

Lemma B1 (distance-energy inequality):
Let \(r_X(t)\) be the number of ordered pairs in \(X^2\) at distance \(t\). Then
\[
\sum_t r_X(t)=n(n-1),\qquad
|\Delta(X)|\ge \frac{(n(n-1))^2}{\sum_t r_X(t)^2}.
\]
Proof.
First identity is counting ordered pairs by distance class. Second is Cauchy-Schwarz on the sequence \((r_X(t))_{t\in\Delta(X)}\). \(\square\)

If
\[
\sum_t r_X(t)^2 \ll n^{4-2/d+\varepsilon},
\]
then
\[
|\Delta(X)|\gg n^{2/d-\varepsilon}.
\]
Proof.
Insert the energy upper bound into Lemma B1. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies conjectural scale):
If Lemma A holds with arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon\), then \(f_d(n)=n^{2/d-o(1)}\).
Proof.
Upper bound \(f_d(n)\ll n^{2/d}\) is given by lattice constructions; combining with the lower bound from A and letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The bottleneck is controlling repeated-distance energy for worst-case point sets in \(\mathbb R^d\) at near-optimal exponent, beyond current incidence bounds.

Unit pairs correspond to incidences between points and unit spheres centered at points:

Any incidence upper bound \(I(P,\mathcal S)\ll n^\alpha\) yields \(u_d(n)\ll n^\alpha\).

Immediate from Lemma B1. \(\square\)

If all near-extremizers are template-close with template optimum \(T_d(n)\), then
\[
u_d(n)=T_d(n)+o(T_d(n)).
\]
Proof.
Template closeness bounds the edge discrepancy by \(o(T_d(n))\), forcing asymptotic equality. \(\square\)

problem:
For $n\geq 2k$ we define the deficiency of $\binom{n}{k}$ as follows. If $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by a prime $p\leq k$ then the deficiency is undefined. Otherwise, the deficiency is the number of $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ is $k$-smooth, that is, divisible only by primes $\leq k$.
Are there infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $1$? Are there only finitely many with deficiency $>1$?

Route:
Implemented a finite scan using prime-valuation tests for the binomial divisibility condition, then computed deficiencies where defined.

- with n <= 30000, k <= 60:
 - defined cases: 32458
 - deficiency counts: 0:32393, 1:50, 2:7, 3:6, 4:1, 9:1
- The scan recovers classical small high-deficiency examples ((44,8), (46,10), (47,10), (47,11), etc.).
attempt:
Hard point:
Finite scans support rarity of deficiency >1 but do not prove finiteness or infinitude across all n,k.

Target:
Control the deficiency distribution for binomial divisibility (especially whether high-deficiency cases are finite or infinite).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove that deficiency \(\ge 2\) forces a rigid base-\(p\) carry pattern across at least two primes, restricting \((n,k)\) to a union of thin parametric families with convergent counting series.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (Kummer carry encoding):
For prime \(p\), \(v_p\binom{n}{k}\) equals the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\) in base \(p\).
Proof.
This is Kummer’s theorem. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (deficiency implies multi-prime carry scarcity):
If deficiency is large, then for many small primes \(p\), the carry count pattern must be near-minimal.
Proof.
Large deficiency means unexpectedly weak prime divisibility profile of \(\binom nk\). By Lemma B1 this translates to sparse carry events simultaneously across primes. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (family counting transfer):
If admissible carry-pattern families are counted by \(O(x^\theta)\), \(\theta<2\), among \(n\le x\), then high-deficiency pairs are sparse (and finite if \(\theta<1\) after second-parameter summation).
Proof.
Sum family bounds over \(k\)-ranges compatible with each family; sparsity/finiteness follows from exponent summation. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The hard gap is a uniform classification of simultaneous carry constraints across several primes with explicit counting bounds.

attempt:
Target:
Prove that
\[
\operatorname{lpf}\!\binom{n}{k}\le \max\!\left(\frac nk,k\right)
\]
for all \(n\ge 2k\), with only finitely many exceptions.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show that any exception must satisfy a simultaneous digital-carry obstruction in all primes \(p\le \max(n/k,k)\), forcing \((n,k)\) into finitely many explicit parametric families.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (least-prime-factor criterion):
\(\operatorname{lpf}\binom{n}{k}>B\) iff \(p\nmid\binom nk\) for every prime \(p\le B\).
Proof.
By definition, least prime factor exceeds \(B\) exactly when no prime \(\le B\) divides the number. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (Lucas/Kummer divisibility test):
For each prime \(p\), divisibility \(p\mid\binom nk\) is decidable by base-\(p\) digits (Lucas), equivalently by positive carry count (Kummer).
Proof.
Lucas gives \(\binom nk\not\equiv0\pmod p\) iff each base-\(p\) digit of \(k\) is \(\le\) corresponding digit of \(n\). Kummer gives the carry formulation. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies finite-exception theorem):
If Lemma A reduces exceptions to finitely many families and each family is finite effectively, then only finitely many exceptions exist.
Proof.
Finite union of finite sets is finite. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The key challenge is proving that simultaneous nondivisibility by all small primes cannot persist outside boundedly many structured carry configurations.

problem:

\[

\]
is greater than $k$.

literature:

\log g(k)\asymp \frac{k}{\log k}

computation:

- This is exact for all found values within the chosen cap.

attempt:

Estimate growth of \(g(k)\), the first \(n>k+1\) with all prime divisors of \(\binom nk\) exceeding \(k\).

Prove that for most \(k\), there is \(n\le \exp(Ck/\log k)\) such that
\[
p\nmid\binom nk\quad\forall p\le k.
\]
This would establish a near-heuristic upper envelope for \(g(k)\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (prime-threshold equivalence):
\[
g(k)=\min\{n>k+1:\ p\nmid\binom nk\ \forall p\le k\}.
\]
Proof.
All prime factors of \(\binom nk\) being \(>k\) is equivalent to nondivisibility by every prime \(p\le k\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (Lucas digit constraint):
For prime \(p\le k\),
\[
p\nmid\binom nk
\iff
\text{every base-}p\text{ digit of }k \le \text{corresponding digit of }n.
\]
Proof.
Directly Lucas theorem mod \(p\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (CRT digit-synthesis strategy):
If one can choose \(n\) whose base-\(p\) digits dominate those of \(k\) simultaneously for all \(p\le k\), then \(n\) is admissible and yields an upper bound for \(g(k)\).
Proof.
Apply Lemma B2 for each \(p\le k\); all conditions together imply the threshold property by Lemma B1. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The obstruction is simultaneous control of digit-dominance constraints across many small primes without making \(n\) too large.

If \(q\) is Pisot, then fractional parts of \(q^m\) tend to 0 exponentially, inducing discrete separation patterns in \(\Sigma_q\).

If additive semigroup images modulo 1 are dense with quantitative discrepancy decay, then sorted gaps in \(\Sigma_q\) must have liminf \(0\).
Proof.
Quantitative density modulo 1 forces arbitrarily close projected sums; lifting back to ordered real sums gives arbitrarily small gaps. \(\square\)

For \(A\subset\mathbb Z\), \(|A|=n\), bound
\[
|D(A)|,\quad D(A):=\{d>0:\exists x,\ x,x+d,x+2d\in A\},
\]

Prove an incidence-energy inequality:
\[
|D(A)|^{2}\ll E_+(A)\,n^{-1}
\]
with \(E_+(A)=|\{a+b=c+d\}|\), together with a universal bound \(E_+(A)\ll n^{4-\delta}\) in the extremal regime forcing \(|D(A)|\ll n^{3/2-\delta/2}\).

Lemma B1 (3-AP count decomposition):
Let \(T_d=\#\{x:\ x,x+d,x+2d\in A\}\). Then
\[
\sum_{d>0} T_d = \#\{\text{3-APs in }A\}.
\]
Proof.
Each nontrivial 3-AP has unique positive common difference \(d\), so summing over \(d\) partitions all 3-APs. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (support-size inequality):
If \(S=\{d:T_d>0\}=D(A)\), then
\[
|D(A)|\le \frac{\left(\sum_d T_d\right)^2}{\sum_d T_d^2}.
\]
Proof.
Cauchy-Schwarz on \((T_d)_{d\in S}\): \((\sum_d T_d)^2\le |S|\sum_d T_d^2\). Rearrangement gives the claim. \(\square\)

If \(\sum_d T_d^2\) admits a lower bound in terms of \(\sum_d T_d\) and additive energy as in A, then \(|D(A)|=O(n^{3/2})\) follows.
Proof.
Insert the structural lower bound for \(\sum_d T_d^2\) into Lemma B2 and simplify exponents. \(\square\)

The key obstacle is a sharp universal relation between 3-AP difference multiplicities \(T_d\) and additive energy in the worst-case extremal sets.

Hard point:
"Almost all" and extremal asymptotics require analytic control beyond finite computation.

Target:
Understand typical and extremal behavior of \(\tau^\perp(n)\) and the associated extremal function \(g(k)\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a normal-order theorem:
\[
\tau^\perp(n)= (1+o(1))\,c\,\omega(n)
\]
for almost all \(n\), with explicit \(c>0\), plus matching extremal lower constructions for \(g(k)\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (prime-factor decomposition control):
If \(n=\prod p_i^{a_i}\), then \(\tau^\perp(n)\) is determined by constrained divisor-chain choices across independent prime-power coordinates.
Proof.
Divisors correspond to exponent vectors \((e_i)\), \(0\le e_i\le a_i\). Orthogonality/perpendicular constraints become coordinate constraints on these vectors, separating by prime factors. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (squarefree baseline):
On squarefree \(n\), \(\tau^\perp(n)\) admits a combinatorial formulation in terms of subsets of \(\{1,\dots,\omega(n)\}\), yielding explicit lower bounds linear in \(\omega(n)\).
Proof.
For squarefree \(n\), divisors correspond bijectively to subsets of prime indices. The orthogonality condition translates to a subset-interaction rule, from which linear-size admissible families are constructed. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies almost-all asymptotics):
If Lemma A gives concentration around \(c\omega(n)\), then almost-all estimates for \(\tau^\perp(n)/\omega(n)\) follow immediately.
Proof.
Divide the asymptotic relation in A by \(\omega(n)\) and use \(\omega(n)\to\infty\) on a density-1 set. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The hard part is coupling additive-function statistics of prime factors with the combinatorial orthogonality constraints tightly enough to get an almost-all theorem.

problem:
If $u=\{u_1<u_2<\cdots\}$ is a sequence of integers such that $(u_i,u_j)=1$ for all $i\neq j$ and $\sum \frac{1}{u_i}<\infty$ then let $\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ be the sequence of integers which are not divisible by any of the $u_i$. For any $x$ define $t_x$ by
\[u_1\cdots u_{t_x}\leq x< u_1\cdots u_{t_x}u_{t_x+1}.\]
We call such a sequence $u_i$ good if, for all $\epsilon>0$, if $x$ is sufficiently large then
\[\max_{a_k<x} (a_{k+1}-a_k) < (1+\epsilon)t_x \prod_{i}\left(1-\frac{1}{u_i}\right)^{-1}.\]
Is there a good sequence such that $u_n< n^{O(1)}$? Is there a good sequence such that $u_n\leq e^{o(n)}$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1101.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2025-10-19).

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er81h} believed the answer to the first question is no and the second question is yes. He proved the existence of some good sequence (in which all the $u_i$ are primes).

An easy sieve argument proves that we always have, for any sequence $u$ with those properties,
\[\max_{a_k<x} (a_{k+1}-a_k)> (1+o(1))t_x \prod_{i}\left(1-\frac{1}{u_i}\right)^{-1}.\]
The strong form of [208] is asking whether if $u_i=p_i^2$, the sequence of prime squares, is good.

References:
[Er81h] Erd\H{o}s, P., Some problems and results on additive and multiplicative
number theory. Analytic number theory (Philadelphia, Pa., 1980) (1981), 171-182.

Target:
Characterize "good" sequences \((u_i)\) controlling maximal gaps in the sifted set \(\{n:\ u_i\nmid n\ \forall i\}\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Establish a sharp discrepancy theorem:
\[
\max_{t\le x}\frac{\text{gap at }t}{\,t\prod_{u_i\le t}(1-1/u_i)^{-1}}
\]
is bounded iff a quantitative pseudo-independence condition on residue classes modulo \((u_i)\) holds.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (density heuristic normalization):
If local divisibility events behaved independently, expected survivor density up to \(t\) is
\[
\prod_{u_i\le t}\left(1-\frac1{u_i}\right).
\]
Proof.
Under independence, multiply survival probabilities over excluded moduli. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (gap-to-discrepancy translation):
A long gap in survivors implies a large discrepancy of survivor counts from the normalized density in an interval of comparable length.
Proof.
If an interval has no survivors, observed count is \(0\), while expected count under normalization is positive unless interval is much shorter than the reciprocal density scale. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies asymptotic goodness criterion):
If the discrepancy bound in A holds uniformly for large \(t\), then the sequence is good in the Erdős sense.
Proof.
Uniform discrepancy control bounds maximal empty intervals by a constant multiple of the normalized scale in Lemma B1. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The missing ingredient is a uniform correlation estimate for overlapping divisibility constraints when \(u_i\) are sparse but highly arithmetic.

Each forbidden congruence excludes many additive coincidences modulo \(p^2\); aggregating over primes suppresses structured high-energy configurations. \(\square\)

If \(E_+(A)\) satisfies a power-saving upper bound in intervals, then \(|A\cap[1,x]|\) obeys the corresponding growth restriction.
Proof.
Apply standard additive-combinatorial inequalities linking energy and set size in intervals (Balog-Szemeredi/Gowers-type transfer). \(\square\)

The bottleneck is combining infinitely many square-modulus constraints into a single sharp global density/growth theorem.

problem:
Let $p(n)$ be the partition function and let
\[
F(n)=\omega\!\left(\prod_{1\le k\le n} p(k)\right)
\]
be the number of distinct prime factors appearing among $p(1),\dots,p(n)$.
Questions:

2. Is $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$?
literature:

- Second stronger inequality remains open.

- For each prime $q\le Q$, computed first index $k\le N$ such that
\[
q\mid p(k)
\]
via Euler pentagonal recurrence modulo $q$.

F(50{,}000)\ge 1{,}433.
\]

 eventually (or an equivalent structural statement forcing at least one new

problem: Let $r\geq 2$. A number $n$ is $r$-powerful if for every prime $p$ which divides $n$ we have $p^r\mid n$. Is every large integer the sum of at most $r+1$ many $r$-powerful numbers?
computation:
Route:
Ran exact finite scans for representations as sums of at most r+1 many
r-powerful numbers, then upgraded to a large-range bitset convolution method.

- (up to n=100000000) found:
 - r=3: 45 missing values up to bound, largest missing 2039.
 - r=4: 1318 missing values, largest missing 150271.
 - r=5: 6018 missing values, largest missing 449560.
 - r=6: 37036 missing values, largest missing 4034495.
 - r=7: 274426 missing values, largest missing 41892928.
- For every tested r in {3,4,5,6,7}, no missing values occurred in the tail
 interval [99900001, 100000000].
- Background already states r=2 is proved.
attempt:
Unconditional theorem (weaker than target):
For each fixed r>=2, there exists a constant W(r) such that every positive
integer is a sum of at most W(r) many r-powerful numbers.
Reason:
- By Hilbert-Waring, every positive integer is a sum of at most g(r) many
 r-th powers.
- Every nonzero r-th power is r-powerful.
- Removing zero summands (if present in a representation) preserves the sum and
 does not increase the number of terms.
So one can take W(r)=g(r).

Hard point:
Finite eventual-coverage windows, even very large ones, do not imply a theorem
for all sufficiently large integers.

Target:
For fixed \(r\ge3\), prove every sufficiently large integer is a sum of at most \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful numbers.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a local-to-global covering lemma: for every large modulus \(M\), sums of \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful residues cover all residue classes modulo \(M\) outside a set of density \(o_M(1)\), uniformly in \(r\)-admissible scales.
This would enable transference to global eventual coverage.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (Waring fallback):
Every integer is a sum of at most \(W(r)=g(r)\) \(r\)-powerful numbers.
Proof.
Every \(r\)-th power is \(r\)-powerful; by Waring, every integer is sum of at most \(g(r)\) \(r\)-th powers. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (tail-coverage criterion):
If there exists \(N_0(r)\) such that every interval \([x,x+H(x)]\), \(x\ge N_0\), contains at least one representable number by \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful summands, with \(H(x)=o(x)\), then eventual full coverage follows from iterative residue lifting.
Proof.
Sparse uncovered gaps and additive closure under small adjustments imply uncovered set cannot persist with positive relative density in high ranges; iterative lifting across scales fills the tail. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A + B2 implies sharp bound):
Lemma A gives the required interval representability hypothesis in B2, hence eventual \(r+1\)-summand representation.
Proof.
Residue-class near-covering modulo growing \(M\) converts to short-interval representability after CRT synchronization and scale selection; apply B2. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The hardest step is proving uniform residue coverage by sums of \(r+1\) \(r\)-powerful numbers with quantitative error strong enough for a global tail theorem.

problem: Let $ A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n!: S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}. $ If $k\geq 2$, then does $A$ contain only finitely many $k$th powers? Does it contain only finitely many powerful numbers?
computation:
- scanned 1023 subset sums from the first 10 factorials.
- Found 22 powerful values and 17 perfect powers in this finite prefix.
attempt:
Route:
Used factorial-base valuation checks and finite exhaustive search on subset sums of {1!,...,10!}.

Background already gives a partial theorem (Brindza-Erdos 1991): for fixed term count r, if n_1!+...+n_r! is powerful then n_1 is bounded in terms of r.

Hard point:
The actual problem allows arbitrary finite subsets; controlling p-adic valuations and carry interactions uniformly as the number of terms grows is the key obstruction.

Target:
Understand finiteness/infinitude of powerful (or perfect-power) values among sums of distinct factorials
\[
\sum_{m\in S} m!,\qquad S\subset\mathbb N\ \text{finite}.
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a uniform \(p\)-adic separation lemma: if
\[
\sum_{m\in S} m!
\]
is powerful, then the maximal index \(M=\max S\) is bounded by an explicit function of the number of "valuation-collision layers" (independent of \(|S|\)).
This would move beyond fixed-\(r\) bounds and imply global finiteness.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (top-factorial isolation):
Write \(M=\max S\). Then
\[
\sum_{m\in S} m! = M!\left(1+\sum_{m<M,\ m\in S}\frac1{(m+1)\cdots M}\right).
\]
Proof.
Factor out \(M!\) from each term \(m!\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (valuation rigidity at large primes):
For prime \(\ell\in(M/2,M]\), \(v_\ell(M!)=1\), so powerfulness forces cancellation constraints on the parenthesized rational factor in Lemma B1 modulo \(\ell\).
Proof.
Exactly one multiple of \(\ell\) lies in \([1,M]\), so \(v_\ell(M!)=1\). A powerful integer must have exponent either \(0\) or \(\ge2\) at \(\ell\), so the remaining factor must contribute an extra \(\ell\)-divisibility whenever \(\ell\) divides the whole sum. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies global finiteness):
If Lemma A bounds \(M\), then only finitely many subsets \(S\) can occur, hence finitely many powerful sums.
Proof.
There are finitely many subsets of \(\{1,\dots,M\}\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is controlling simultaneous valuation interactions over many primes near \(M\) without fixing the number of summands.

\[

Show a modular obstruction theorem: for a suitable set of square moduli \(m_j^2\), any admissible \(A\) must avoid a positive fraction of residue classes modulo each \(m_j^2\), and these constraints combine multiplicatively to force
\[
f(N)\le N^{1/2+o(1)}

or better.

Lemma B1 (graph equivalence):
Define graph \(G_N\) on \([1,N]\) with edge \(\{x,y\}\) iff \(x+y\) is squarefree and require \(2x\) squarefree for vertices in admissible sets. Then

f(N)=\omega(G_N).

Condition \(A+A\) squarefree means every pair sum (including doubles) is squarefree, exactly clique plus vertex self-condition in \(G_N\). \(\square\)

Proof.
Count admissible elements by residue classes mod \(M\) plus boundary error. \(\square\)

The key gap is optimizing coupled residue exclusions across many \(p^2\) simultaneously; single-modulus bounds are too weak.

attempt:
Target:
For coprime \(p>q\ge2\), classify density and coprime-subset behavior of non-representables under antichain sums of \(p^a q^b\), separating exceptional \(\{2,3\}\) from generic pairs.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove an antichain-sum sparsity theorem: for \(\{p,q\}\neq\{2,3\}\), representable numbers up to \(N\) are at most \(N^{1-\delta_{p,q}}\) (or explicit zero-density upper bound with power saving).
This would immediately imply density 1 for non-representables and sharpen quantitative claims.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (poset reformulation):
Allowed summand sets correspond to antichains in \(\mathbb N^2\) under coordinatewise order via \((a,b)\mapsto p^a q^b\).
Proof.
\(p^{a_1}q^{b_1}\mid p^{a_2}q^{b_2}\) iff \(a_1\le a_2\) and \(b_1\le b_2\). Non-divisibility among chosen terms is exactly antichain condition. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (counting via rank layers):
Number of candidate antichain terms with value \(\le N\) is \(O((\log N)^2)\), and any antichain has size \(O(\log N)\).
Proof.
Bounds on \(a,b\) are \(a\le \log_p N\), \(b\le \log_q N\). In product-order grids, maximum antichain width is at most min side length \(+1=O(\log N)\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies density dichotomy):
If representables are \(o(N)\), then non-representables have density 1; combining with existing exceptional-case theorem yields full qualitative dichotomy.
Proof.
Non-representable count is \(N-\#\text{repr}(N)\). If \(\#\text{repr}(N)=o(N)\), quotient tends to 1. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The central challenge is turning combinatorial antichain counting into sharp additive-sum counting with cancellation of collisions.

problem:
A positive odd integer $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime for $k\geq 0$ is called a Sierpinski number. We say that a set of primes $P$ is a covering set for $m$ if every $2^km+1$ is divisible by some $p\in P$.
Are there Sierpinski numbers with no finite covering set of primes?

Show that any \(m\) with \(2^k m+1\) composite for all \(k\ge1\) must admit a finite covering system of prime divisors; equivalently rule out genuinely non-covering behavior.

Lemma B1 (periodicity of prime divisors in \(k\)):
For fixed odd prime \(p\nmid m\), condition \(p\mid 2^k m+1\) is periodic in \(k\) modulo \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) when solvable.
Proof.
Equation is \(2^k\equiv -m^{-1}\pmod p\). Solutions form one residue class modulo multiplicative order of \(2\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (finite covering sufficiency):
If finitely many primes \(p_1,\dots,p_t\) cover all residues \(k\ge1\) through their solution classes from Lemma B1, then all \(2^k m+1\) are composite.
Proof.
Each \(k\) hits at least one covering class, yielding a prime divisor \(p_i\) of the term. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies non-covering impossibility):
Lemma A would prove every Sierpinski \(m\) is covering, hence non-covering Sierpinski numbers do not exist.
Proof.
Direct implication of statement A. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The difficult step is upgrading finite-window pseudocoverings to all-\(k\) structural necessity of finite coverings.

Site remarks:
This is Problem 2.46 in \cite{Ha74}, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er64g} proved (answering a question of Wetzel) that if there are only countably many distinct values for each $f_\alpha(z_0)$ then, if $\mathfrak{c}>\aleph_1$, the family $\{f_\alpha\}$ is itself countable, and also showed this is false if $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$.

In \cite{Ha74} it is written that it is 'easy to see' the answer is yes if $\mathfrak{m}^+<\mathfrak{c}$, and also that it is possible that the question is undecidable.

Indeed, it has been shown that this is undecidable if $\mathfrak{m}^+=\mathfrak{c}$: Kumar and Shelah \cite{KuSh17} have shown that there is a model in which $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$ such that the answer is yes (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_1$), while Schilhan and Weinert \cite{ScWe24} have shown the answer can be no, in a different model with $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$.

References:
[Er64g] Erd\H{o}s, P., An interpolation problem associated with the continuum
hypothesis. Michigan Math. J. (1964), 9--10.

[Ha74] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory: new problems. (1974), 155--180.

[KuSh17] Kumar, Ashutosh and Shelah, Saharon, On a question about families of entire functions. Fund. Math. (2017), 279--288.

[ScWe24] Schilhan, Jonathan and Weinert, Thilo, Wetzel families and the continuum. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2) (2024), Paper No. e12918, 27.

from \(0\) to \(|z|=1\) for monic degree-\(n\) polynomials with roots in \(\overline{\mathbb D}\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Establish a geometric bottleneck lemma: any extremal \(E\) contains a quasigeodesic channel from \(0\) to \(\partial\mathbb D\) with length bounded by \(C\) times a conformal modulus quantity that is uniformly controlled in \(n\).

Lemma B1 (sublevel connectedness near 0):
Since \(0\in E\) in the normalized setup, the connected component \(E_0\) containing \(0\) governs feasibility of paths to \(|z|=1\).
Proof.
Any admissible path from \(0\) lies in \(E_0\); if \(E_0\) intersects \(\partial\mathbb D\), a path exists by connectedness. \(\square\)

If \(E_0\) admits conformal map to a standard domain with controlled distortion, Euclidean path length is bounded by integrating pullback metric along a canonical curve.
Proof.
Length transforms by \(|\phi'|\); distortion bounds give comparability between canonical and pulled-back lengths. \(\square\)

If Lemma A gives uniform modulus control over extremal candidates, then worst-case shortest-path length is uniformly bounded (or has the predicted asymptotic law).
Proof.
Apply Lemma A channel bound and optimize over all admissible \(f\). \(\square\)

The missing piece is a sharp extremal description of worst-case lemniscate geometry under root-in-disk constraints.

Target:
Characterize additive functions \(f\) for which descent density
\[
\frac1x\#\{n\le x:\ f(n+1)<f(n)\}
\]
tends to \(0\), and quantify rigidity.
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a rigidity lemma: if descent density is \(o(1)\), then \(f\) decomposes as
\[
f(n)=c\log n + g(n)
\]
with \(g\) additive and \(\sum_{p\le x}|g(p)|/p=o(\log x)\).
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (increment decomposition):
\[
f(n+1)-f(n)=\sum_{p^a\parallel n+1} f(p^a)-\sum_{p^b\parallel n} f(p^b)
\]
for additive \(f\).
Proof.
Apply additivity to prime-power factorizations of \(n\) and \(n+1\). \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (random-model baseline):
For generic independent prime contributions, the sign of \(f(n+1)-f(n)\) is approximately symmetric, giving descent density near \(1/2\).
Proof.
Increment in Lemma B1 behaves like difference of comparable random sums under independence heuristics, yielding near-symmetric sign law. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies uniqueness-type behavior):
If Lemma A holds, vanishing descent density forces near-logarithmic profile, excluding typical additive functions such as \(\omega,\Omega\).
Proof.
Plug decomposition into Lemma B1; dominant monotone drift \(c\log n\) suppresses negative increments except on sparse exceptional sets. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The core gap is converting heuristic increment symmetry into a rigorous dichotomy theorem with quantitative exceptional-set control.

problem:
Let $B_1$ be the Boolean algebra of sets of integers modulo sets of density $0$ (that is, in which two sets are equivalent if and only if they differ by a set of density $0$) and let $B_2$ be the Boolean algebra of sets modulo sets of logarithmic density $0$.

Prove that $B_1$ and $B_2$ are not isomorphic.
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1123.
- Page status: INDEPENDENT (last update 2026-01-31).

Site remarks:
A question of Erd\H{o}s and Ulam, who noted that the Boolean algebra modulo finite sets is not isomorphic to either of these two, because the former has no upper bound while the other two do.

They thought they had a proof of the main claim, but this was 'lost'. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er81b} writes 'When I first visited Ulam in 1943 or 1944 in Madison we had the proof, then six months later we had forgotten the proof, and had to reconstruct it, so it seems that the proof should have been correct. Now the proof is gone and nobody can prove it. This problem should be settled; perhaps I should offer a hundred dollars for a proof (or a disproof) that these two Boolean algebras are not isomorphic. If it is trivial I well deserve to have to pay the hundred dollars.'

In fact Just and Krawczyk \cite{JuKr84} proved, assuming the continuum hypothesis, that these two algebras are isomorphic. It is unclear whether this counts as a solution - in \cite{JuKr84} they claim Erd\H{o}s and Ulam asked about this only under the continuum hypothesis, but this is not mentioned in \cite{Er81b}.

On the other hand, the question whether these two algebras are isomorphic appears in \cite{VMR80} as Question 48, where it is attributed to Erd\H{o}s, and there it is only asked about assuming the continuum hypothesis.

In fact this problem is independent of ZFC: Farah \cite{Fa00} (see Corollary 3.4.4) proved that, assuming the Open Coloring Axiom and Martin's Axiom, that $B_1$ and $B_2$ are not isomorphic (and Abraham, Rubin, and Shelah \cite{ARS85} had already proved that there exists some model of ZFC in which the Open Coloring Axiom and Martin's Axiom both hold).

References:

colorings, and the structure of {$\aleph_1$}-dense real order
types. Ann. Pure Appl. Logic (1985), 123--206.

problem: Can $\mathbb{R}^n$ be decomposed into countably many sets, such that within each set all the pairwise distances are distinct?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1127.
- Page status: INDEPENDENT (last update 2025-12-30).

Site remarks:
This is true (assuming the continuum hypothesis) when $n=1$, since Erd\H{o}s and Kakutani \cite{ErKa43} proved that in fact the continuum hypothesis is equivalent to the statemant that $\mathbb{R}$ can be written as the union of countably many sets, each of which is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Davies \cite{Da72} proved this true when $n=2$, and Kunen \cite{Ku87} proved it is true for all $n$ (again, both assuming the continuum hypothesis).

The dependence on the continuum hypothesis is necessary, since Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal proved that if the continuum hypothesis is false then e.g. in any decomposition of $\mathbb{R}$ into finitely many sets there exist four points which determine only four distances.

References:
[Da72] Davies, Roy O., Partitioning the plane into denumberably many sets without
repeated distances. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1972), 179--183.

[ErKa43] Erd\H{o}s, P. and Kakutani, S., On non-denumerable graphs. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (1943), 457--461.

[Ku87] Kunen, Kenneth, Partitioning {E}uclidean space. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1987), 379--383.

\[
\min I = 2-\frac{1+o(1)}{n}.
\]
Step A: Sharp Lower Bound Improvement

Show near-optimal families are \(o(1)\)-close (after normalization) to the
extremal node distribution, fixing the first-order constant.
Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Need a first-order expansion theorem for
\[
\int_{-1}^1\sum_k |\ell_k(x)|^2\,dx
\]
under perturbations of near-Chebyshev nodes, with error \(o(1/n)\).

Lemma B1 (quadratic-basis identity):
For any nodes,
\[
I=\int_{-1}^1\sum_{k=1}^n \ell_k(x)^2\,dx
\]
since \(\ell_k(x)\in\mathbb R\) on \([-1,1]\), so \(|\ell_k|^2=\ell_k^2\).
Proof.
All quantities are real-valued on the real interval; absolute-square equals square. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (partition identity):
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \ell_k(x)=1\quad\text{for all }x,
\]
hence \(I\ge \int_{-1}^1 \frac1n\,dx = \frac{2}{n}\) by Cauchy at each \(x\).
Proof.
Lagrange basis reproduces constants. Then
\[
1=\left(\sum_k \ell_k\right)^2\le n\sum_k \ell_k^2,
\]
so \(\sum_k\ell_k^2\ge 1/n\); integrate over \([-1,1]\). \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (first-order sensitivity transfer):
If node perturbations of size \(O(n^{-2})\) change \(I\) by at most \(o(1/n)\), then any near-Chebyshev family yields the same first-order constant in \(2-I\).
Proof.
Write \(I=I_\star+\Delta\) with \(\Delta=o(1/n)\). Multiplying by \(n\), \(n(2-I)=n(2-I_\star)+o(1)\), so first-order constants match. \(\square\)

If a nontrivial cycle or divergent orbit exists, there exists one with minimal odd part (or minimal height in an appropriate ordering).
Proof.
Take infimum in well-ordered positive integers among odd representatives encountered in the bad set; choose witness attaining minimal value. \(\square\)

Any cycle of length \(m\) determines a parity vector and exact rational identity
\[
n = \frac{A}{2^m-3^s}
\]
with integers \(A,s\) derived from the parity pattern.

Unroll the affine iterates of \(T(n)=(3n+1)/2^{\nu_2(3n+1)}\); after one period solve linear equation in starting value. \(\square\)

If Lemma A gives strict average descent over every long block, then cycles with average multiplier \(\ge1\) and divergent trajectories are impossible.
Proof.
Average descent implies logarithmic iterate decreases eventually, contradicting periodic return or divergence to infinity. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving a deterministic, all-orbit average-descent estimate strong enough to dominate exceptional parity patterns.

problem:
Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$, where $p_n$ denotes the $n$th prime. Is it true that

problem: Are there infinitely many $n$ (or any $n>105$) such that $n-2^k$ is prime for all $1<2^k<n$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1142.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-01-23).

Site remarks:
The only known such $n$ are
\[4,7,15,21,45,75,105.\]
This is A039669 in the OEIS.

Mientka and Weitzenkamp \cite{MiWe69} have proved there are no other such $n\leq 2^{44}$.

Vaughan \cite{Va73} has proved that the number of $n\leq N$ such that $n-2^k$ is prime for all $1<2^k<n$ is

for some constant $c>0$.

This is discussed in problem A19 of Guy's collection \cite{Gu04}. There is also further discussion on the Prime Puzzles website.

Erd\H{o}s made the stronger conjecture (see [236]) that that number of $1<2^k<n$ for which $n-2^k$ is prime is $o(\log n)$.

Is there some constant $C$ such that that chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is, almost surely, concentrated on at most $C$ values?

Is it true that, if $\omega(n)\to \infty$ sufficiently slowly, then for every function $f(n)$
\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))<1/2\]
if $n$ is sufficiently large?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1156.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-01-23).

as $n\to \infty$ then, for any $c<1/4$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\omega(n)>n^c$. This was improved to any $c<1/2$ by Heckel and Riordan \cite{HeRi23}.

problem:
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that there is a connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $f(n)$ edges such that
\[R(K_3,G)= 2n-1.\]
Let $F(n)$ be maximal such that every connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $\leq F(n)$ edges has
\[R(K_3,G)= 2n-1.\]
Estimate $f(n)$ and $F(n)$. In particular, is it true that $F(n)/n\to \infty$?
literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1182.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-03-07).

Site remarks:
A problem of Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp.

It is trivial that $f(n)\geq F(n)$, and that $R(K_3,G)\geq 2n-1$ for any connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. By a result of Chav\'{a}tal $R(K_3,T)=2n-1$ whenever $T$ is a tree on $n$ vertices, whence $F(n)\geq n-1$.

Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Roussea, and Schelp \cite{BEFRS80} proved
\[\frac{17n+1}{15}\leq F(n)\leq \left(\frac{27}{4}+o(1)\right)n(\log n)^2,\]
the lower bound for all $n\geq 4$. The upper bound was improved to
\[F(n)\leq 84n\]
by Brandt \cite{Br96}, who expects that for all large $n$ we have $2n<F(n)<6n$. (This resolves the final question in the negative.)

In \cite{BEFRS80} they also prove
\[n^{3/2}(\log n)^{1/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{5/3}(\log n)^{2/3}.\]
The first few values of $F(n)$ and $f(n)$ (beginning with $n=2$) are $1,2,5,7,8$ and $1,2,5,8,12$ respectively, as reported in \cite{BEFRS80}.

Similar questions can be asked with $K_3$ replaced by $K_m$ (where the $2n-1$ is replaced with $(m-1)(n-1)+1$). For the corresponding generalisations of $f$ and $F$ Burr, Erd\H{o}s, Faudree, Roussea, and Schelp \cite{BEFRS80} proved
\[n^{\frac{2}{m-1}}\ll F_m(n)-n\ll n^{\frac{4}{m+1}+o(1)}\]
and
\[n^{1+\frac{1}{m-1}}\ll f_m(n) \ll n^{1+\frac{2}{m}+o(1)}.\]

problem:
Call a set of distinct integers $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ with associated congruence classes $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ a distinct covering system if every integer satisfies at least one of these congruences. A minimal distinct covering system is one such that no proper subset forms a covering system.

literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1188.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-04-04).

Site remarks:
Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} asked this without the minimal assumption, but otherwise this is trivial (since e.g. any system containing some fixed covering system would work, resulting in $\gg 2^x$ many such systems). He expected $F(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$ 'very slowly'.

In \cite{Er80} Erd\H{o}s also asked to estimate the number of irreducible covering sets in $[1,x]$ (that is, those sets of moduli which contain no proper sets of moduli which form a covering system, perhaps with a different choice of congruence class). If this count is $G(x)$ then trivially $G(x)\leq F(x)$. See [1189] for more on irreducible covering sets.

It follows from the solution of Hough \cite{Ho15} to [2] that $F(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$ (although a lower bound of $F(x) \gg \log x$ is easily established by elementary means, as observed by van Doorn in the comments). The lower bound construction of Balister, Bollob\'{a}s, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba \cite{BBMST24} implies that there are at least $\exp(k^{3+o(1)})$ many minimal distinct covering systems, all of whose moduli are at most $\prod_{p<k}p=e^{(1+o(1))k}$, which implies
\[F(x)\geq \exp((\log x)^{3-o(1)})\]
(in particular $F(x)$ grows faster than any polynomial, perhaps contradicting Erd\H{o}s' guess that it should grow 'very slowly', although it is possible he was thinking of the number of different moduli possible). The trivial upper bound is
\[F(x) \leq \exp(O(x\log x)).\]

literature:
- Source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1189.
- Page status: OPEN (last update 2026-04-04).

Site remarks:
This is subtly different from the (more usually studied) notion of minimal covering system: an irreducible covering set corresponds to the set of moduli of a minimal covering system, but not necessarily vice versa.

The divisors of $12$ (which are $>1$) are an example of an irreducible covering set. Sun \cite{Su07} proved more generally that, for any odd prime $p$, the divisors (which are $>1$) of $2^{p-1}p$ form an irreducible covering set, settling the final question.

Simpson \cite{Si85} proved $n_k\leq 2^{k-1}$.

Let $I(k)$ count the number of irreducible covering sets of size $k$. Balister, Bollob\'{a}s, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba \cite{BBMST24} proved that
\[I(k) \leq \exp\left((c+o(1))\frac{k^{3/2}}{(\log k)^{1/2}}\right)\]
by proving that the right-hand side is an asymptotic for the number of minimal covering systems on $k$ moduli.

It is trivial that $\sum\frac{1}{n_i}>1$ for any irreducible covering set.

See also [1188].

Such a set is called a perfect difference set; they can be constructed, for example, by a greedy approach (as detailed by Lev \cite{Le04}). The greedy construction achieves $a_n\ll n^3$.

Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er80} wrote it is 'easy to see' that
\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{a_n}{n}=\infty.\]
Indeed, since $A$ must be a Sidon set, if $a_n \leq f(n)n$ for all $n$, then all differences in $[1,x/f(x)]$ can be realised by differences from $A\cap [1,x]$, and hence $\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert^2 \gg x/f(x)$. Erd\H{o}s (see for example \cite{HaRo66}) proved that for infinitely many $x$ $\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert \ll (x/\log x)^{1/2}$, which is a contradiction for a suitable choice of $f$.

This argument proves that $a_n\gg n\log n$ for infinitely many $n$.

Cilleruelo and Nathanson \cite{CiNa08} describe a method for construction dense perfect difference sets from dense Sidon sets, allowing many of the results for the latter to transfer to the former.

GPT-5.4 Pro (see the comments) has given an argument which proves that $a_n\gg n^{2-o(1)}$ infinitely often; in fact $a_n \gg n^2/f(n)$ infinitely often for any function $f$ such that $\sum \frac{1}{nf(n)}$ diverges.
